clips.text: This is how I sound reading your notes.
Prefix and suffix sums

Answer any range-sum question in O of 1 after one O of n pass, combine best-from-the-left with best-from-the-right around a split, and turn "count the subarrays with property X" into counting equal prefix values.

Many questions ask about blocks of consecutive values: the total from position l to position r, how many marked positions lie between them, or how many blocks add up to exactly k. Adding a block up from scratch costs O of n, so 2 times 10 to the 5 such questions on 2 times 10 to the 5 values take about 4 times 10 to the 10 steps. Testing all n squared over 2 blocks one by one, about 2 times 10 to the 10 of them, is no better. The blocks overlap, so almost all of that adding is repeated work.

Every block is the difference of two prefixes, the blocks that start at the beginning. The values from l to r are the first r plus 1 values with the first l taken away, so once the sum of every prefix is known, the sum of any block is one subtraction.

Call the input A, indexed from 0, and let P of i be the sum of its first i values, A of 0 plus … plus A of i minus 1. One left-to-right pass fills all n plus 1 entries: P of 0 is 0 for the empty prefix, then P of i plus 1 is P of i plus A of i. The block A from l to r, from index l to index r with both ends included, sums to P of r plus 1 minus P of l, so after that O of n pass every question costs O of 1. A grid works the same way with S of i, j, the sum of the top-left block of i rows by j columns. Any rectangle takes four lookups by inclusion–exclusion: the top-left block that ends at the rectangle's bottom-right cell, minus the blocks above it and to its left, plus the block above and to the left that was subtracted twice.
clips.script: Call the input eh, indexed from 0, and let P of i be the sum of its first i values, eh of 0 plus … plus eh of i minus 1. One left-to-right pass fills all n plus 1 entries: P of 0 is 0 for the empty prefix, then P of i plus 1 is P of i plus eh of i. The block eh from l to r, from index l to index r with both ends included, sums to P of r plus 1 minus P of l, so after that O of n pass every question costs O of 1. A grid works the same way with S of i, j, the sum of the top-left block of i rows by j columns. Any rectangle takes four lookups by inclusion–exclusion: the top-left block that ends at the rectangle's bottom-right cell, minus the blocks above it and to its left, plus the block above and to the left that was subtracted twice.

clips.text: Why it is right: P of r plus 1 and P of l both contain A of 0 plus … plus A of l minus 1, and the subtraction cancels exactly those terms, leaving A of l plus … plus A of r. The empty prefix, P of 0 is 0, lets a block that starts at index 0 use the same formula. Since the identity holds for every pair l at most r, any condition on a block can be rewritten as a condition on two prefix values.
clips.script: Why it is right: P of r plus 1 and P of l both contain eh of 0 plus … plus eh of l minus 1, and the subtraction cancels exactly those terms, leaving eh of l plus … plus eh of r. The empty prefix, P of 0 is 0, lets a block that starts at index 0 use the same formula. Since the identity holds for every pair l at most r, any condition on a block can be rewritten as a condition on two prefix values.

clips.text: "The block A from l to r sums to k" becomes P of r plus 1 minus P of l is k, so counting such blocks means counting pairs of prefix positions i less than j with P of i is P of j minus k. Walk j from 1 to n with seen, a map from each prefix value met so far to how often it occurred, seeded with the value 0 once for P of 0: at each j add the count of P of j minus k, then record P of j. That is one O of n log n pass. When k is 0 it is a search for equal prefix values, and sorting them and comparing neighbours works too. Many conditions turn into this one: "the sum is the length" is "the values A i minus 1 sum to 0", and "two kinds of item balance" is "the sum is 0 once one kind is negated".
clips.script: "The block eh from l to r sums to k" becomes P of r plus 1 minus P of l is k, so counting such blocks means counting pairs of prefix positions i less than j with P of i is P of j minus k. Walk j from 1 to n with seen, a map from each prefix value met so far to how often it occurred, seeded with the value 0 once for P of 0: at each j add the count of P of j minus k, then record P of j. That is one O of n log n pass. When k is 0 it is a search for equal prefix values, and sorting them and comparing neighbours works too. Many conditions turn into this one: "the sum is the length" is "the values eh i minus 1 sum to 0", and "two kinds of item balance" is "the sum is 0 once one kind is negated".

clips.text: Prefix values have a mirror image, suffix values computed from the right, and the two together handle splits. Fill L of i, the best answer for a part that ends at index i, from left to right, and R of i, the best for a part that starts at i, from right to left. When the question removes one element, cuts the array once or picks a pivot, each choice combines a left part with a right part, so it costs O of 1 from L and R and trying them all is O of n. The maximum subarray sum fits the same pattern: maximise P of r minus P of l over l less than r, a non-empty block, by keeping the running minimum of P from the left.
Notation
A of i: the input value at index i, counting from 0; A from l to r is the block from index l to index r, both ends included.
clips.script: eh of i: the input value at index i, counting from 0; eh from l to r is the block from index l to index r, both ends included.

clips.text: P of i: the sum of the first i values, A of 0 plus … plus A of i minus 1, with P of 0 is 0; it has n plus 1 entries, and A from l to r sums to P of r plus 1 minus P of l. In countSubarrays, P is a single running total, the prefix sum so far.
clips.script: P of i: the sum of the first i values, eh of 0 plus … plus eh of i minus 1, with P of 0 is 0; it has n plus 1 entries, and eh from l to r sums to P of r plus 1 minus P of l. In countSubarrays, P is a single running total, the prefix sum so far.

clips.text: S of i, j: on a grid g, the sum of the top-left block of i rows by j columns, g from 0 to i minus 1 0 to j minus 1; query(r1, c1, r2, c2) returns the rectangle with those inclusive corners (the TRD version, prefix2D, returns S itself, without query).
seen: in countSubarrays, a map from each prefix value met so far to how many times it occurred, seeded with 0 once for P of 0.
L of i: the best answer for a part of the array that ends at index i, filled left to right; what "best" means depends on the problem, such as the longest increasing run ending at i.
R of i: the mirror image of L of i, the best answer for a part that starts at index i, filled right to left.

n people, up to 10 to the 5, sit around a round table, and each belongs to team A, B or C. Some of them change seats so that every team ends up in one unbroken arc of seats. Find the fewest people who have to move. In the first sample the five seats hold A, B, A, B, C, and the answer is 2.
clips.script: n people, up to 10 to the 5, sit around a round table, and each belongs to team eh, B or C. Some of them change seats so that every team ends up in one unbroken arc of seats. Find the fewest people who have to move. In the first sample the five seats hold eh, B, eh, B, C, and the answer is 2.

clips.text: Fix a final seating. Everyone who already sits in a seat meant for their own team can stay, and the others can swap among the seats they free, since those seats are meant for exactly their teams. So the cost of a final seating is the number of seats that hold the wrong team. Going round the table, the three blocks come in the order A, B, C or A, C, B; any other order is one of these started from another seat. With n start seats that makes 2n final seatings, and comparing each with the table seat by seat costs O of n: 2 times 10 to the 10 steps when n is 10 to the 5.
clips.script: Fix a final seating. Everyone who already sits in a seat meant for their own team can stay, and the others can swap among the seats they free, since those seats are meant for exactly their teams. So the cost of a final seating is the number of seats that hold the wrong team. Going round the table, the three blocks come in the order eh, B, C or eh, C, B; any other order is one of these started from another seat. With n start seats that makes 2n final seatings, and comparing each with the table seat by seat costs O of n: 2 times 10 to the 10 steps when n is 10 to the 5.

clips.text: Team c's block is a run of consecutive seats, and the people who stay in it are the members of team c already sitting there. So each final seating needs three numbers, each the count of one team in a range of seats, and counting in a range is what prefix sums do in O of 1. A block can run past seat n minus 1 and carry on at seat 0. Writing the seating twice, t is s plus s, makes every block an ordinary range of t: a B block on t from 5 to 6 is seats 0 and 1.

Let P of c, i be how many of the first i seats of t hold team c. One left-to-right pass over the 2n seats fills all three rows. Team c's block is as long as the team, P of c, n seats, and if it covers t from l to r minus 1, the members already there number P of c, r minus P of c, l. The three counts add up to the people who stay, and the other n minus that many must move.

Take the order A, B, C with A's block starting at seat 0. A gets seats 0 and 1, B gets seats 2 and 3, and C gets seat 4. The counts are P of A, 2 minus P of A, 0 is 1, P of B, 4 minus P of B, 2 is 1 and P of C, 5 minus P of C, 4 is 1. Three people stay, so two must move, the same count the picture of the table gave.
clips.script: Take the order eh, B, C with eh's block starting at seat 0. A gets seats 0 and 1, B gets seats 2 and 3, and C gets seat 4. The counts are P of eh, 2 minus P of eh, 0 is 1, P of B, 4 minus P of B, 2 is 1 and P of C, 5 minus P of C, 4 is 1. Three people stay, so two must move, the same count the picture of the table gave.

clips.text: Now the order A, C, B starting at seat 2. A takes seats 2 and 3, C takes seat 4, and B takes t from 5 to 6, which are seats 0 and 1 around the table. The same formula works with no special case: P of A, 4 minus P of A, 2 is 1, P of C, 5 minus P of C, 4 is 1 and P of B, 7 minus P of B, 5 is 1. Again three stay and two move.
clips.script: Now the order eh, C, B starting at seat 2. A takes seats 2 and 3, C takes seat 4, and B takes t from 5 to 6, which are seats 0 and 1 around the table. The same formula works with no special case: P of eh, 4 minus P of eh, 2 is 1, P of C, 5 minus P of C, 4 is 1 and P of B, 7 minus P of B, 5 is 1. Again three stay and two move.

clips.text: Of the 10 final seatings, the best moves 2 people, the sample's answer. Each seating costs three subtractions after one O of n pass, so the whole search is O of n, against O of n squared for checking seat by seat. A team with no members has P of c, n is 0 and an empty block, so a table with only one or two teams needs no special case, and the answer is 0 when the teams already sit together, as in sample 3, where the two A's sit in seats 3 and 0, which are neighbours.

clips.text: Reach for it when
Many queries for the sum or count of something over a range l to r, with no updates in between.
Count (or find) subarrays whose sum is k, whose sum is their length, or whose two kinds of items balance out.
Remove one element, cut the array once or choose a pivot: the answer combines something about everything to the left with something about everything to the right.
A small grid (up to about 1000 times 1000) with many rectangle-sum queries.
Common bugs

Off-by-one between inclusive ranges and P: with P of size n plus 1, sum A from l to r is P of r plus 1 minus P of l. Forgetting P of 0 is 0 also forgets every subarray that starts at the first element.
clips.script: Off-by-one between inclusive ranges and P: with P of size n plus 1, sum eh from l to r is P of r plus 1 minus P of l. Forgetting P of 0 is 0 also forgets every subarray that starts at the first element.

clips.text: Overflow: 2 times 10 to the 5 values of 10 to the 9 already pass 2 to the 31, and counts of pairs reach n squared over 2, so keep prefix sums and answers in long long.
unordered map keyed on prefix sums can be broken by anti-hash tests on Codeforces; sort the prefix array, use map, or use a plain array shifted by an offset when the range of values is small.
How it hides in a statement
Count adjacent equal pairs, or positions with some property, inside l to r: that is, prefix count of a zero-one indicator array
Subarray whose sum is its length, or where two kinds of items balance: that is, subtract 1 from every element (or negate one kind), then look for two equal prefix sums
Delete one element / cut the array into parts / choose a pivot: that is, best-from-the-left and best-from-the-right arrays, then try every split in O of n

Best block to reverse, flip or swap: that is, write down the gain of each position, then maximise P of r minus min P of l over l at most r, a maximum subarray sum in which l is r is the empty block (gain 0, for when changing nothing is allowed)
P of i will hold the sum of the first i values of A. Start with P of 0 is 0, the empty prefix.
clips.script: P of i will hold the sum of the first i values of eh. Start with P of 0 is 0, the empty prefix.

clips.text: P of 1 is P of 0 plus A of 0, which is 0 plus 3, so 3.
clips.script: P of 1 is P of 0 plus eh of 0, which is 0 plus 3, so 3.

clips.text: P of 2 is P of 1 plus A of 1, which is 3 plus 1, so 4.
clips.script: P of 2 is P of 1 plus eh of 1, which is 3 plus 1, so 4.

clips.text: P of 3 is P of 2 plus A of 2, which is 4 plus 4, so 8.
clips.script: P of 3 is P of 2 plus eh of 2, which is 4 plus 4, so 8.

clips.text: P of 4 is P of 3 plus A of 3, which is 8 plus 1, so 9.
clips.script: P of 4 is P of 3 plus eh of 3, which is 8 plus 1, so 9.

clips.script: P of 5 is P of 4 plus eh of 4, which is 9 plus 5, so 14.

clips.text: P of 6 is P of 5 plus A of 5, which is 14 plus 9, so 23.
clips.script: P of 6 is P of 5 plus eh of 5, which is 14 plus 9, so 23.

clips.text: P of 7 is P of 6 plus A of 6, which is 23 plus 2, so 25. The last cell is the total of A.
clips.script: P of 7 is P of 6 plus eh of 6, which is 23 plus 2, so 25. The last cell is the total of eh.

clips.text: The sum of A from 2 to 5? Start from P of 6 is 23, the sum of A from 0 to 5: everything up to the right end.
clips.script: The sum of eh from 2 to 5? Start from P of 6 is 23, the sum of eh from 0 to 5: everything up to the right end.

clips.text: P of 2 is 4 is the sum of A from 0 to 1, the part before the range. Subtract it.
clips.script: P of 2 is 4 is the sum of eh from 0 to 1, the part before the range. Subtract it.

clips.text: A of 2 plus … plus A of 5 is P of 6 minus P of 2, which is 23 minus 4, so 19. Any range costs one subtraction: O of 1.
clips.script: eh of 2 plus … plus eh of 5 is P of 6 minus P of 2, which is 23 minus 4, so 19. Any range costs one subtraction: O of 1.

clips.text: A new array A, and the case k is 0: A from l to r sums to 0 exactly when P of l is P of r plus 1. Walk its prefix sums P, counting in seen how often each value has occurred.
clips.script: A new array eh, and the case k is 0: eh from l to r sums to 0 exactly when P of l is P of r plus 1. Walk its prefix sums P, counting in seen how often each value has occurred.

clips.text: P of 1 is P of 0 plus A of 0, so 2, a value not seen before: no zero-sum block ends at 0.
clips.script: P of 1 is P of 0 plus eh of 0, so 2, a value not seen before: no zero-sum block ends at 0.

clips.script: P of 2 is P of 1 plus eh of 1, so 1, a value not seen before: no zero-sum block ends at 1.

clips.text: 3 zero-sum blocks, one per pair of equal prefix values, found in one pass with seen, a map from value to count: O of n log n.
Difference arrays and sweeps

Apply many range updates in O of 1 each and read the result with one prefix pass, stack two levels when the updates come in ranges themselves, and sweep sorted events when coordinates are too large for an array.

The typical question applies many updates of the form "add v to every element from l to r" and reads the array only once they are all done. Applied cell by cell, each update costs up to n steps, so m updates on n elements, both 2 times 10 to the 5, take about 4 times 10 to the 10. Yet inside a range every cell changes in the same way as its neighbour, so most of that work records nothing new.

So look at the differences between neighbours instead of the values. Adding v to the block from l to r makes the step into it, from position l minus 1 to l, larger by v, and the step out of it, from r to r plus 1, smaller by v. Inside the block both neighbours rise together, so their difference does not change. A range update, however long, changes only two differences.

Store those differences in the difference array d: d of i is A of i minus A of i minus 1, with d of 0 is A of 0 as if A of minus 1 were 0. Adding v to A from l to r is then two writes, d of l plus-equals v and d of r plus 1 minus-equals v. The second lands just past the range, possibly one past the end of A, so d needs a spare cell. To read the array, take prefix sums of d: A of i is d of 0 plus d of 1 plus … plus d of i, one left-to-right pass with a running total (build in the template).
clips.script: Store those differences in the difference array d: d of i is eh of i minus eh of i minus 1, with d of 0 is eh of 0 as if eh of minus 1 were 0. Adding v to eh from l to r is then two writes, d of l plus-equals v and d of r plus 1 minus-equals v. The second lands just past the range, possibly one past the end of eh, so d needs a spare cell. To read the array, take prefix sums of d: eh of i is d of 0 plus d of 1 plus … plus d of i, one left-to-right pass with a running total (build in the template).

clips.text: Why it is right: the prefix sums telescope, d of 0 plus … plus d of i is A of 0 plus (A of 1 minus A of 0) plus … plus (A of i minus A of i minus 1), which is A of i. Seen from that pass, d of l plus-equals v adds v to every A of i with i at least l, and d of r plus 1 minus-equals v takes it back from every i at least r plus 1, so exactly A from l to r gains v. Updates only add, so they can arrive in any order and add up in d.
clips.script: Why it is right: the prefix sums telescope, d of 0 plus … plus d of i is eh of 0 plus (eh of 1 minus eh of 0) plus … plus (eh of i minus eh of i minus 1), which is eh of i. Seen from that pass, d of l plus-equals v adds v to every eh of i with i at least l, and d of r plus 1 minus-equals v takes it back from every i at least r plus 1, so exactly eh from l to r gains v. Updates only add, so they can arrive in any order and add up in d.

clips.text: That makes m updates cost O of 1 each plus one O of n pass, O of n plus m instead of O of n times m. When the updates themselves come in ranges, use two levels: if a query runs a whole range of operations, a first difference array over operation numbers counts how often each operation runs, and only after its prefix pass is each operation applied, once, with that weight. Adding the progression 1, 2, …, k to a segment is second order: its differences are constant on the segment, so record them in dd, a difference array of d, and take prefix sums twice (addProgression).

When coordinates reach 10 to the 9 or 10 to the 18 there is no array to index. Keep the same events, +v at l and minus v at r plus 1, sort them by coordinate and sweep. Between two consecutive event coordinates nothing changes, so each gap is a block of identical points: add its length instead of visiting its points. coverage does this for m segments in O of m log m, tracking cover, the number of segments over the current point, and filling len of c, the number of points covered by exactly c segments.
A of i: the array being updated, indexed from 0, and read only after all the updates; A from l to r is the block from index l to index r, both ends included.
clips.script: eh of i: the array being updated, indexed from 0, and read only after all the updates; eh from l to r is the block from index l to index r, both ends included.

clips.text: d of i: the difference array, d of i is A of i minus A of i minus 1 with d of 0, which is A of 0; adding v to A from l to r is d of l plus-equals v and d of r plus 1 minus-equals v (add in the template), and its prefix sums give back a (build). The template sizes it n plus 2; the TRD version, applyRanges, uses n plus 1 and rebuilds a inside d with partial sum.
clips.script: d of i: the difference array, d of i is eh of i minus eh of i minus 1 with d of 0, which is eh of 0; adding v to eh from l to r is d of l plus-equals v and d of r plus 1 minus-equals v (add in the template), and its prefix sums give back a (build). The template sizes it n plus 2; the TRD version, applyRanges, uses n plus 1 and rebuilds a inside d with partial sum.

clips.text: dd of i: a second-order difference array, the differences of d: one prefix pass turns it into d and a second turns it into A. addProgression adds 1, 2, …, r minus l plus 1 on l to r with three writes to it.
clips.script: dd of i: a second-order difference array, the differences of d: one prefix pass turns it into d and a second turns it into eh. addProgression adds 1, 2, …, r minus l plus 1 on l to r with three writes to it.

clips.text: cover: during a sweep, the number of segments that contain the current point.

len of c: in coverage, how many integer points are covered by exactly c of the segments. The TRD version, coveredLength, merges the segments with IntervalContainer.h and returns only the total length covered at least once; it takes half-open int pairs, so an inclusive l to r goes in as l, r plus 1, and coordinates up to 10 to the 18 need coverage's event sweep instead.

The landscape is n points, all at height 0 to begin with, and k edits follow, with n and k up to 2 times 10 to the 5. Raise adds 1 at every point from x1 to x2, and Depress subtracts 1. Hill adds a tent shape: 1 at x1 and x2, 2 one point further in, and so on up to the middle. Valley subtracts the same shape. The output is every final height; the picture shows the first sample's 20 heights after its 13 edits.

An edit can cover all n points, so applying the edits one at a time costs O of n times k: with both at 2 times 10 to the 5, about 4 times 10 to the 10 steps. But the heights are read only once all the edits are in, which is the situation a difference array is for: record each edit in O of 1, then rebuild every height in one pass at the end.

Raise and Depress are the stage's range add: d of x1 plus-equals v and d of x2 plus 1 minus-equals v, with v is 1 for Raise and minus 1 for Depress. A hill is harder: every point changes by a different amount, so recording it in d would take one write per point. Look at its steps instead, the change from one point to the next. On the hill 1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1 they are +1, +1, +1, then 0 between the two middle points, then minus 1 until the height is back to 0. The steps are constant in stretches, so they can go in a difference array of their own: the second-order difference array dd.

So dd records where the step changes. A hill from x1 to x2 starts a step of +1 at x1. With integer division, (x1 plus x2) over 2 and (x1 plus x2 plus 1) over 2 are the middle points, the same point when the hill has an odd number of points, and just after each of them the step drops by 1. The last step down is into x2 plus 1, where the height is back to 0, so at x2 plus 2 the step returns to 0. That makes four writes: dd of x1 plus-equals 1, dd of (x1 plus x2) over 2 plus 1 minus-equals 1, dd of (x1 plus x2 plus 1) over 2 plus 1 minus-equals 1 and dd of x2 plus 2 plus-equals 1. A valley makes the same writes with every sign swapped.

One left-to-right pass rebuilds everything. slope is the running sum of dd, which is the step that the hills and valleys make into point i. Adding d of i for the raises and depressions gives the full step, and h, the running sum of the steps, is the height at point i, printed as soon as it is known. At point 4 of the second sample, dd of 4 is minus 1 takes slope from 1 down to 0, so the height stays at 3.

When the pass ends, the heights are 1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1, 0, exactly the second sample's output. The last write, dd of 8, lies past the last point and is never read. It is still needed: a hill that ends at the last point, x2 is n, puts its fourth write at n plus 2, so d and dd get n plus 3 cells.

Every edit costs two or four writes and the pass costs O of n, so the whole solution is O of n plus k, around 10 to the 6 steps. The heights get large: 2 times 10 to the 5 hills over the whole range each add up to 10 to the 5 in the middle, so a height can reach 2 times 10 to the 10, past the range of int. Keep d, dd, slope and h in long long. A hill on a single point, x1 is x2, writes +1, minus 2 and +1 into three cells in a row and raises only that point, by 1, as the statement says.
Many "add v to every element from l to r" operations, and the values are only read after all of them.
For each point, how many intervals cover it, or how many points are covered by exactly k intervals.
You choose one value x from a large range, and each item contributes a cost that is constant on a few intervals of x.
Operations applied over a range of operation numbers, or operations that add an arithmetic progression to a segment.

The closing update d of r plus 1 lands one past the last index, so d needs n plus 1 cells when A is indexed from 0, and n plus 2 (or the largest coordinate plus 2) when it is indexed from 1. The template allocates n plus 2, which also fits the r plus 2 write of addProgression.
clips.script: The closing update d of r plus 1 lands one past the last index, so d needs n plus 1 cells when eh is indexed from 0, and n plus 2 (or the largest coordinate plus 2) when it is indexed from 1. The template allocates n plus 2, which also fits the r plus 2 write of addProgression.

clips.text: Coordinates up to 10 to the 9 or 10 to the 18 do not fit in an array: switch to sorted (coordinate, ±v) events with r plus 1 as the closing point, and keep r plus 1 and the lengths in long long.
With two levels (how often each operation runs, then what the operations do), finish the prefix pass of the first level before you apply the second.
Reorder the array to maximise the total of fixed range-sum queries: that is, count how many queries cover each index with a difference array, then give the largest values to the most-covered indices

Choose one common target (a pair sum, a temperature, a level) and minimise the changes: that is, each item adds its cost on a few intervals of the target; build a difference array over the target and scan every candidate
Count triples (x, y, z) under an inequality: that is, for each x add +1 over the range of possible sums x plus y, then combine the sum counts with z in one scan

A process where each source is used up by consecutive consumers: that is, prefix sums plus binary search find where each source runs out, and a difference array records the range of consumers it served in full

Range updates without touching every cell. a starts at all 0s, so its difference array d (n plus 1 cells) does too; record where each update starts and stops in d, then rebuild a once. If a starts non-zero, add the rebuilt changes to it.
Add 3 to A from 1 to 4. First d of 1 plus-equals 3: from position 1 on, everything is 3 higher. d of 1 is now 3.

clips.text: DP: states and transitions
Write a DP state as one sentence, add the small extra index the next step needs (last action, run length, time of day), and fill the table with take/skip or count-the-ways transitions.

The questions in this stage make one choice per position, left to right: take or skip an item, pick the day's activity, decide which way a tree falls, and a rule links each choice to the ones just before it. Trying every combination is 2 to the n or 3 to the n, hopeless when n is 10 to the 5. A greedy rule that looks only at the current position fails on tiny cases: with no two neighbours allowed, taking the largest value first in 3, 4, 3 gets 4, while 3 plus 3 is 6.

The rule never needs the whole history. To know what is allowed at the next position, and what it can add, a short summary of the past is enough: what was done last, how long the current run is, what time it is. All histories with the same summary have exactly the same futures, so of those only the best one matters, or, when counting, only how many there are.

So the state is a sentence: dp of i, s is the best answer for the first i positions, given that they end in situation s. The extra index s holds exactly what the next step needs to know about the past and nothing more: the last action, which row the last pick came from, the current run length, or the time of day mod h on an h-hour clock. A transition says how one more position changes s and the answer, for example take (the run grows from s to s plus 1, if that is allowed) or skip (the run resets to 0). Each entry is the max over every way of arriving in it. The empty prefix starts the table: 0 for its one real situation and minus infinity for every other, so that an impossible state never feeds a later one.

Why it is right: if two partial solutions end in the same s, any way of finishing one also finishes the other, with the same gain. So the first i positions of an optimal solution can be swapped for the best ones ending in the same s without losing anything, and that best value is exactly dp of i, s, computed from row i minus 1, which is already final. If a fact the future depends on is left out of s, the swap is no longer safe, and the table mixes histories that should be kept apart.

The cost is (number of states) times (choices per state): n positions with 3 values of s is O of n, and n sleeps on an h-hour clock is O of n times h. Row i plus 1 needs only row i, so the template keeps one row dp of s and builds the next one in nd of s. Counting problems use the same table with plus instead of max: start from one way to build the empty prefix, and reduce modulo 10 to the 9 plus 7 (MOD) after every addition.
dp of i, s: the best answer (or, when counting, the number of ways) for the first i positions, given that they end in situation s.
dp of s: in the template, the current row, dp of i, s for the positions read so far; the i is dropped because only the latest row is kept.
nd of s: the next row, for one more position, built from dp of s and then copied over it.
K: in the template, the most items allowed in a row; s, the current run length, goes from 0 to K.
NEG: the stand-in for minus infinity that marks an unreachable state, LLONG MIN over 4, so that adding a value to it cannot overflow.
MOD: the modulus for counting, 10 to the 9 plus 7 (mod in the TRD version, from ModBinomial.cpp).
ways of i: in a counting DP over lengths, the number of ways to build something of length i; ways of 0 is 1, the empty build.
pre of i: ways of 1 plus … plus ways of i, so pre of b minus pre of A minus 1 counts the ways for every length from A to b.
clips.script: pre of i: ways of 1 plus … plus ways of i, so pre of b minus pre of eh minus 1 counts the ways for every length from eh to b.

clips.text: There are n tasks, up to 3 times 10 to the 5, to be done in a fixed order, and each one is a nail, a screw or a bolt, written 0, 1 and 2. The hammer does nails, the screwdriver does screws and the wrench does bolts. Any task may be skipped, but never revisited, and you may start with any tool. Before a task you may switch to another tool, but the one you drop is lost for good. Find the largest number of tasks you can complete. In the second sample the tasks repeat 0, 1, 2, and the answer is 5.

A dropped tool never comes back, so each tool is held for one unbroken stretch of tasks, and a plan is an order of the tools plus at most two switch points. There are 6 orders and about n squared over 2 pairs of switch points, around 2.7 times 10 to the 11 plans when n is 3 times 10 to the 5. Greedy rules break on small cases. Switching to whatever the next task needs looks sensible, but on the tasks 0, 1, 0, 0 it gives up the hammer for one screw and then misses two nails: it does 2 tasks where keeping the hammer does 3.

The past matters through two facts only: the tool in hand decides whether the next task can be done, and the tools already dropped decide what can be held later. So fix the order in which the tools will be used, one of 6. Then a single number s, how many tools have been dropped so far, gives both facts: the tool in hand is order of s, and the tools before it in the order are gone. dp of s is the most tasks done so far while holding order of s. Before any task all three entries are 0, because tools may be dropped before the first task.

Each task has two transitions. First the drops: holding tool s now means either holding it before, or holding tool s minus 1 and dropping it, so dp of s is max(dp of s, dp of s minus 1), for s is 1 and then s is 2, which also allows two drops at once. Then the task: the state whose tool fits it gains 1, and the other states skip it. For task 4, a nail, the column before is 1, 2, 3. The drops change nothing here, since max(2, 1) is 2 and max(3, 2) is 3. The hammer fits, so dp of 0 becomes 2, and the column is 2, 2, 3.

Filling the rest of the table the same way gives the last column 4, 4, 5, so with the order hammer, screwdriver, wrench at most 5 tasks can be done. Each column depends only on the one before it, so the code keeps one dp of three values and updates it in place, task by task.

To see a plan that reaches 5, walk back from the best cell. If the task fits the tool of the current row, it was done, and the value before it is one less; that value sits in the same row, or in a row above if a tool was dropped just before the task. Here the walk gives the hammer for task 1, the screwdriver for task 2, and then the wrench for the bolts at tasks 3, 6 and 9: five tasks.

Running the same table for each of the 6 orders gives 5, 4, 4, 5, 4 and 4, so the answer is 5, the sample's output. The work is 6 orders times 3 states per task, about 5.4 times 10 to the 6 steps when n is 3 times 10 to the 5, and the counts never pass n, so int is enough. Every state can be reached before the first task by dropping tools, so all of them start at 0 and no minus infinity entry is needed.
Choices are made left to right (days, trees, students in a row) and each choice only restricts the next one or two
The rule mentions the previous step: not the same activity two days running, not the same row twice in a row, at most k in a row
Count the ways, modulo 10 to the 9 plus 7, to build something of length n from blocks or moves
A greedy rule fails on a small hand example, and the number of (position, extra state) pairs is at most about 10 to the 7

Initialising unreachable states to 0 when maximising. A length that cannot be cut exactly, or a day that cannot end in sport, must start at minus infinity (or a sentinel you skip) so it never feeds a later state.
Leaving a fact out of the state. If the transition at i depends on what happened at i minus 1 (which way a tree fell, which row the last student came from), that fact must be an index of dp.

Overflow and negative remainders: sums of 10 to the 5 heights of 10 to the 9 need long long, and (pre of b minus pre of A minus 1) mod MOD can be negative in C plus plus, so add MOD before the final mod.

clips.text: Deleting a value v also deletes every v minus 1 and v plus 1, then group equal values, then run the no-two-adjacent take/skip DP over the value axis (house robber)
Count walks of length n on a small fixed graph: that is, DP over steps whose state is the current vertex, or a class of vertices that symmetry makes interchangeable
Count strings built from blocks of length 1 and k: that is, ways of i is ways of i minus 1 plus ways of i minus k, plus prefix sums when the question asks about a range of lengths
A schedule that keeps drifting around a clock: that is, the state is the time mod h, not the absolute time

Never take two neighbours (the template with K is 1). dp of i, s is the best total from the first i values, with s is 1 if the i-th was taken and s is 0 if not. Row 0 is the empty prefix: 0, and minus infinity for s is 1, which is impossible.
Skip 5: dp of 1, 0 is max(dp of 0, 0, dp of 0, 1), which is max(0, minus infinity), so 0.
Take 5: it may only follow s is 0, so dp of 1, 1 is dp of 0, 0 plus 5, which is 0 plus 5, so 5.
Skip 1: dp of 2, 0 is max(dp of 1, 0, dp of 1, 1), which is max(0, 5), so 5.
Take 1: it may only follow s is 0, so dp of 2, 1 is dp of 1, 0 plus 1, which is 0 plus 1, so 1.
Skip 3: dp of 3, 0 is max(dp of 2, 0, dp of 2, 1), which is max(5, 1), so 5.
Take 3: it may only follow s is 0, so dp of 3, 1 is dp of 2, 0 plus 3, which is 5 plus 3, so 8.
Skip 8: dp of 4, 0 is max(dp of 3, 0, dp of 3, 1), which is max(5, 8), so 8.
Take 8: it may only follow s is 0, so dp of 4, 1 is dp of 3, 0 plus 8, which is 5 plus 8, so 13.
Skip 2: dp of 5, 0 is max(dp of 4, 0, dp of 4, 1), which is max(8, 13), so 13.
Take 2: it may only follow s is 0, so dp of 5, 1 is dp of 4, 0 plus 2, which is 8 plus 2, so 10.
Skip 6: dp of 6, 0 is max(dp of 5, 0, dp of 5, 1), which is max(13, 10), so 13.
Take 6: it may only follow s is 0, so dp of 6, 1 is dp of 5, 0 plus 6, which is 13 plus 6, so 19.
Walk back from the larger entry of the last row, dp of 6, 1 is 19: 6 was taken, so the value before it was skipped. Step to dp of 5, 0.
dp of 5, 0 is 13: 2 was skipped, and 13 is the larger of dp of 4, 0 is 8 and dp of 4, 1 is 13. Step to dp of 4, 1.
dp of 4, 1 is 13: 8 was taken, so the value before it was skipped. Step to dp of 3, 0.
dp of 3, 0 is 5: 3 was skipped, and 5 is the larger of dp of 2, 0 is 5 and dp of 2, 1 is 1. Step to dp of 2, 0.
dp of 2, 0 is 5: 1 was skipped, and 5 is the larger of dp of 1, 0 is 0 and dp of 1, 1 is 5. Step to dp of 1, 1.
dp of 1, 1 is 5: 5 was taken, so the value before it was skipped. Step to dp of 0, 0, the empty prefix: stop.
Best total: 5 plus 8 plus 6 is 19. Each row was built from the row above alone, so two rows of memory and O of n time are enough.
LIS, LDS and their disguises
Compute longest increasing, non-decreasing and decreasing subsequences in O of n log n, rebuild one, and recognise LIS behind problems about removing, nesting, crossing or colouring.

The question: from a sequence A of n numbers, keep as many as possible, in their original order, so that the kept ones strictly increase. They form a longest increasing subsequence (LIS). Trying every subset costs 2 to the n. The DP dp of i is 1 plus max dp of j over j less than i with A of j less than A of i, where dp of i is the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at A of i, costs O of n squared: fine up to n about 5000, but about 2 times 10 to the 10 comparisons when n is 2 times 10 to the 5.
clips.script: The question: from a sequence eh of n numbers, keep as many as possible, in their original order, so that the kept ones strictly increase. They form a longest increasing subsequence (LIS). Trying every subset costs 2 to the n. The DP dp of i is 1 plus max dp of j over j less than i with eh of j less than eh of i, where dp of i is the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at eh of i, costs O of n squared: fine up to n about 5000, but about 2 times 10 to the 10 comparisons when n is 2 times 10 to the 5.

clips.text: That DP remembers more than it needs. Of two increasing subsequences of the same length, the one ending on the smaller value is at least as useful, because any later element that can extend the other can extend it too. So for each length only one number matters: the smallest value an increasing subsequence of that length can end with.

Keep those numbers in an array tails, where tails of k is the smallest end of an increasing subsequence of length k plus 1 among the elements read so far (k counts from 0). The array is strictly increasing, because dropping the last element of a subsequence of length k plus 2 leaves one of length k plus 1 that ends lower. So when A of i arrives, a binary search with lower bound finds the first tail at least A of i, at position k. A of i can follow the length-k subsequence that ends at tails of k minus 1, so it ends one of length k plus 1 and replaces tails of k, or is appended when every tail is smaller.
clips.script: Keep those numbers in an array tails, where tails of k is the smallest end of an increasing subsequence of length k plus 1 among the elements read so far (k counts from 0). The array is strictly increasing, because dropping the last element of a subsequence of length k plus 2 leaves one of length k plus 1 that ends lower. So when eh of i arrives, a binary search with lower bound finds the first tail at least eh of i, at position k. eh of i can follow the length-k subsequence that ends at tails of k minus 1, so it ends one of length k plus 1 and replaces tails of k, or is appended when every tail is smaller.

clips.text: The array tails certifies lengths but is not itself a subsequence, since its entries can come from different subsequences. To rebuild one, keep tailIdx of k, the index of the element now in tails of k, and when A of i lands at position k record par of i is tailIdx of k minus 1, the element it followed ( minus 1 when k is 0). Walking par back from the element in the last tail, then reversing, gives one longest increasing subsequence.

clips.text: Why tails stays exact: the k tails below A of i show that A of i can end an increasing subsequence of every length up to k plus 1, and of none longer, since no subsequence of length k plus 1 ends below A of i. For the shorter lengths the existing tail is already below A of i, and for length k plus 1 the old tail was at least A of i, so tails of k is the only entry that improves. Every entry keeps its meaning after every step, so at the end the size of tails is the LIS length.
clips.script: Why tails stays exact: the k tails below eh of i show that eh of i can end an increasing subsequence of every length up to k plus 1, and of none longer, since no subsequence of length k plus 1 ends below eh of i. For the shorter lengths the existing tail is already below eh of i, and for length k plus 1 the old tail was at least eh of i, so tails of k is the only entry that improves. Every entry keeps its meaning after every step, so at the end the size of tails is the LIS length.

clips.text: Each element costs one binary search, O of n log n in all. The variants are switches on this routine: non-decreasing uses upper bound, which lets A of i follow a tail equal to it; the longest decreasing subsequence (LDS) is the LIS of the negated values; and by Dilworth's theorem the fewest non-decreasing subsequences that cover an array is the length of its longest strictly decreasing subsequence (and the fewest non-increasing ones is the LIS length). When "can follow" compares two coordinates, as in nesting, either keep the O of n squared DP, which accepts any such test, or sort by one coordinate and run LIS on the other.

clips.script: eh of i: the input sequence, indexed from 0, with n elements (S in the TRD version).

clips.text: dp of i: in the O of n squared DP, the length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends at A of i.
clips.script: dp of i: in the O of n squared DP, the length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends at eh of i.

clips.text: tails of k: the smallest value that an increasing subsequence of length k plus 1 can end with, among the elements read so far; it increases strictly with k (in the TRD version, res stores each tail paired with its index).
tailIdx of k: the index in A of the element currently stored in tails of k (the index half of each pair in res in the TRD version).
clips.script: tailIdx of k: the index in eh of the element currently stored in tails of k (the index half of each pair in res in the TRD version).

clips.text: par of i: the index of the element that A of i followed when it was placed, or minus 1 if it started a subsequence (prev in the TRD version, which stores 0 there and stops by counting the length down instead).
clips.script: par of i: the index of the element that eh of i followed when it was placed, or minus 1 if it started a subsequence (prev in the TRD version, which stores 0 there and stops by counting the length down instead).

clips.text: strict: true for strictly increasing (lower bound), false for non-decreasing (upper bound). The TRD version is strict only; its comment says to search for the pair (S of i, i) instead of (S of i, 0) to get non-decreasing.

The problem is Manhattan Mornings. Home, work and n errands, up to 10 to the 5 of them, are points of a street grid, with coordinates up to 10 to the 9. You walk to work along the streets by a shortest route and want to pass as many errands as possible on the way. In the first sample home is at (0, 0), work is at (6, 6), and the errands are at (5, 4), (2, 6) and (3, 1); the best route passes 2 of them.

A shortest route never steps away from work, so in sample 1 it only goes up or right, and x and y never decrease along it. A DP over every street corner between home and work would follow that rule, but with coordinates up to 10 to the 9 there can be 10 to the 18 corners. A DP over the errands, where each errand extends the best route ending at an errand it can follow, is the O of n squared LIS DP: about 5 times 10 to the 9 pairs when n is 10 to the 5.

Errand j can come before errand i on a route exactly when x j at most x i and y j at most y i. Sort the errands by x, and equal x by y, and every route passes its errands in that order. A route is then a subsequence of the sorted errands whose y values never decrease, and any such subsequence is a route. So the answer is the longest non-decreasing subsequence of the y values. In sample 1 the sorted errands are (2, 6), (3, 1) and (5, 4), so the y values are 6, 1, 4, and the longest is 1, 4.

Two steps come before the sort. An errand outside the rectangle between home and work is never on a shortest route, so drop it. And if work is left of home, negate every x, and if work is below home, negate every y; the route then goes up and right as before. Now let A of i be the y value of the i-th remaining errand in sorted order, and run tails on a with upper bound, because two errands with equal y can both be visited.
clips.script: Two steps come before the sort. An errand outside the rectangle between home and work is never on a shortest route, so drop it. And if work is left of home, negate every x, and if work is below home, negate every y; the route then goes up and right as before. Now let eh of i be the y value of the i-th remaining errand in sorted order, and run tails on a with upper bound, because two errands with equal y can both be visited.

clips.text: In sample 1, A is 6, 1, 4. 6 starts tails. 1 is below 6, so upper bound finds tails of 0, and 1 replaces 6: a route through one errand can now end as low as y is 1, which leaves more room above it. 4 is above every tail, so it is appended, and tails ends as 1, 4. Its size, 2, is the answer: the route through (3, 1) and then (5, 4).
clips.script: In sample 1, eh is 6, 1, 4. 6 starts tails. 1 is below 6, so upper bound finds tails of 0, and 1 replaces 6: a route through one errand can now end as low as y is 1, which leaves more room above it. 4 is above every tail, so it is appended, and tails ends as 1, 4. Its size, 2, is the answer: the route through (3, 1) and then (5, 4).

clips.text: In sample 2, after flipping both axes and dropping (3, 1), the errands sorted by x and then y are ( minus 2, minus 1), ( minus 2, 0), (0, minus 1) and (0, 0), so A is minus 1, 0, minus 1, 0. When the second minus 1 arrives, upper bound passes over the tail equal to it and lands at tails of 1: an errand can follow another on the same street. tails ends as minus 1, minus 1, 0, so the answer is 3. With lower bound the second minus 1 would replace the first and the answer would be 2, and sorting equal x by y descending would also give 2, because errands on the same avenue could then not chain.
clips.script: In sample 2, after flipping both axes and dropping (3, 1), the errands sorted by x and then y are ( minus 2, minus 1), ( minus 2, 0), (0, minus 1) and (0, 0), so eh is minus 1, 0, minus 1, 0. When the second minus 1 arrives, upper bound passes over the tail equal to it and lands at tails of 1: an errand can follow another on the same street. tails ends as minus 1, minus 1, 0, so the answer is 3. With lower bound the second minus 1 would replace the first and the answer would be 2, and sorting equal x by y descending would also give 2, because errands on the same avenue could then not chain.

clips.text: Errands at home or at work lie in the rectangle and count, as in sample 2, where the best route passes the errand at home, the one at (0, 1) and the one at work. Errands at the same point give equal pairs, which upper bound lets chain, so in sample 3 both errands at (100, 100) count. Sorting and one binary search per errand take O of n log n, fast for 10 to the 5 errands, and the coordinates and their negatives fit in int.
Keep, or remove, as many items as possible so that what is left is in order
Items are pairs such as (width, height) or (entry hole, exit hole), and one item fits inside, follows or crosses another
A graph whose edges join inverted pairs (a bigger value before a smaller one): its independent sets are increasing subsequences and its cliques are decreasing ones
The fewest groups, colours or passes such that each group on its own is sorted

Mixing up strict and non-strict: lower bound builds a strictly increasing subsequence, upper bound a non-decreasing one. "Remove the fewest so the rest is sorted" usually allows equal values, so it needs upper bound.
Treating tails as an actual subsequence. It only certifies the length; to rebuild one, store for each i the index that ended the previous length (par of i) and walk back from the end of the longest.

Sorting pairs by the first coordinate and running LIS on the second when equal first coordinates may not chain. Sort ties by the second coordinate descending, or compare both coordinates in an O of n squared DP.
Fewest items to remove or move so the rest is sorted: that is, n minus the longest non-decreasing subsequence
Nest envelopes, boxes or dolls: that is, sort by one dimension, then LIS on the other (equal first coordinates must not chain)
Largest group of pairwise crossing segments between two parallel lines: that is, longest decreasing subsequence of exit positions listed in entry order (pairwise non-crossing: that is, LIS)
Fewest colours so that each colour class is sorted: that is, length of the longest strictly decreasing subsequence (Dilworth)
tails of k holds the smallest value an increasing subsequence of length k plus 1 can end with. Each new value binary-searches tails.
tails is empty: 4 becomes tails of 0, the end of a length-1 subsequence.
2: is tails of 0 is 4, the length-1 tail, less than 2? No: search this length and shorter.
The first tail at least 2 is tails of 0 is 4, the length-1 tail. Replace it: length 1 can now end lower, at 2.
9: is tails of 0 is 2, the length-1 tail, less than 9? Yes, so 9 can go after it: search longer lengths.
9 is bigger than every tail, so it follows tails of 0 is 2 and becomes tails of 1, the end of a length-2 subsequence.
3: is tails of 1 is 9, the length-2 tail, less than 3? No: search this length and shorter.
3: is tails of 0 is 2, the length-1 tail, less than 3? Yes, so 3 can go after it: search longer lengths.
The first tail at least 3 is tails of 1 is 9, the length-2 tail. Replace it: length 2 can now end lower, at 3.
6: is tails of 1 is 3, the length-2 tail, less than 6? Yes, so 6 can go after it: search longer lengths.
6 is bigger than every tail, so it follows tails of 1 is 3 and becomes tails of 2, the end of a length-3 subsequence.
10: is tails of 1 is 3, the length-2 tail, less than 10? Yes, so 10 can go after it: search longer lengths.
10: is tails of 2 is 6, the length-3 tail, less than 10? Yes, so 10 can go after it: search longer lengths.

LCS, edit distance and two-sequence DP
Set up dp of i, j over prefixes of two sequences to align, count, score or edit them, and spot the hidden second sequence when it is a reverse, a permutation order or a pattern automaton.

This stage compares two sequences, a with n items and b with m. The model question is the longest common subsequence (LCS): the longest sequence that both contain, its items in order but not necessarily adjacent. Testing every subsequence of a against b costs 2 to the n, about 10 to the 9 already when n is 30. Matching greedily goes wrong: for A is XAB and b is ABX, matching X first leaves nothing after it for A and B, so it finds 1 instead of 2.
clips.script: This stage compares two sequences, a with n items and b with m. The model question is the longest common subsequence (LCS): the longest sequence that both contain, its items in order but not necessarily adjacent. Testing every subsequence of a against b costs 2 to the n, about 10 to the 9 already when n is 30. Matching greedily goes wrong: for eh is XAB and b is ABX, matching X first leaves nothing after it for eh and B, so it finds 1 instead of 2.

clips.text: Look only at the last items. If A and b end with the same item, some LCS pairs those two, so the answer is 1 plus the LCS of what is left of both. If they differ, at least one of the two is not used, so the answer is the better of dropping the last item of A or the last item of b. Either way what remains is again a prefix of a against a prefix of b, and there are only (n plus 1)(m plus 1) such pairs.

clips.text: So let dp of i, j be the answer for the prefixes A from 0 up to i and b from 0 up to j, the first i items of A and the first j of b; row 0 and column 0 are the empty prefixes, worth 0. Cell (i, j) compares the last items A of i minus 1 and b of j minus 1: if they are equal, dp of i, j is dp of i minus 1, j minus 1 plus 1, otherwise dp of i, j is max(dp of i minus 1, j, dp of i, j minus 1). Filling the rows top to bottom, each left to right, has those neighbours ready in time, and dp of n, m is the LCS length. To print an LCS, walk back from (n, m): when the two last items match, take the item and move diagonally, otherwise move to the neighbour holding the larger value.

clips.text: Why the rule is right: when A of i minus 1 is b of j minus 1, any common subsequence of the two prefixes can have its last matched pair moved onto these two items, or gain them as a new last pair, so pairing them never loses. When they differ they cannot be paired with each other, and pairing each with something earlier would make the two pairs cross, so at least one of them is unused and dropping it loses nothing.

clips.text: Edit distance, the fewest single-item inserts, deletes and replacements that turn a into b, uses the same table. dp of i, j is now the fewest operations turning A from 0 up to i into b from 0 up to j. The three neighbours become: delete A of i minus 1 (from (i minus 1, j), plus 1), insert b of j minus 1 (from (i, j minus 1), plus 1), or turn A of i minus 1 into b of j minus 1 (from (i minus 1, j minus 1), plus 1 only if they differ). Row 0 costs j insertions and column 0 costs i deletions.

clips.text: Both tables take O of nm time: 2.5 times 10 to the 7 cells when both lengths are 5000, which is quick, but a full table of int is then 100 MB. When only the value is needed, keep two rows, prv and cur, for O of m memory, and keep the full table only to walk back. Twists change what a cell stores (a count, a score, a piece counter, an automaton state), not the shape of the table, and the second sequence may be hidden: the reverse of the first, the order of another permutation, or a pattern automaton.

The problem is Prince and Princess. The squares of an n times n board are numbered 1 to n squared, with n up to 250. The Prince visits the squares A, p plus 1 of them, and the Princess visits the squares b, q plus 1 of them; neither visits a square twice, and both start at square 1 and end at square n squared. Each may skip squares, and we want the longest route that both can follow. In the sample A is 1, 7, 5, 4, 8, 3, 9 and b is 1, 4, 3, 5, 6, 2, 8, 9, and the longest common route has 4 squares, for example 1, 4, 8, 9.

clips.text: A route both can follow is a common subsequence of A and b, so the answer is their longest common subsequence, and the table dp of i, j computes it. But each route can visit up to n squared is 62 500 squares, so the table has about 62 500 times 62 500 about 3.9 times 10 to the 9 cells: seconds of work for one test case, against a time limit of 1 second.

clips.text: No route visits a square twice, so each square of A is at most one square of b, and each row of the table has at most one match. A common route is a set of matched pairs, and its pairs never cross, because both routes visit them in order. So of the 3.9 times 10 to the 9 cells at most 62 500 are matches, the only places where the value grows, and the answer depends only on them.

clips.text: Let pos of v be the index of square v in A, or minus 1 if the Prince never visits it. Walk along b and replace each square by its pos, dropping the squares that are not on A. Two pairs do not cross exactly when their positions in a increase along b, so a common route is an increasing subsequence of this list, and the answer is its longest increasing subsequence. The positions are all different, so lower bound and upper bound agree, and tails finds the length in O of q log q.

Then 2 replaces 3: a common route of two squares, 1 then 5, can end at A of 2, earlier on the Prince's route than A of 3. 4 replaces 5 in the same way, and 6 is appended, so tails ends as 0, 2, 4, 6. Its size, 4, is the answer.

clips.text: Two strings or arrays of length up to about 5000, and the statement talks about subsequences, matching, aligning, merging or interleaving them.
Operations insert, delete and replace, or "fewest characters to change or remove so that A becomes B".
A score that rewards matched characters and penalises unmatched ones, often over substrings rather than whole strings.
Palindromes, or a process that grows outwards from a point: compare the sequence with its own reverse.

Off-by-one between table and string indices: with an (n plus 1) times (m plus 1) table, cell (i, j) compares A of i minus 1 with b of j minus 1, and row 0 and column 0 are the empty-prefix base cases (0 for LCS, i or j for edit distance).

Memory: a 5000 times 5000 int table is 100 MB. Keep two rows when you only need the value, and the full table only when you must walk back to reconstruct the answer.
Fewest deletions from both strings to make them equal: that is, the size of A plus the size of b minus 2 times LCS(A, b).

Longest common subsequence of several permutations: that is, a common subsequence is a chain in the order "x before y in every permutation", so it is a longest path in a DAG; with two permutations, relabel by positions and it becomes LIS.
Longest common subsequence that must avoid (or contain) a pattern P: that is, add a third index, the KMP automaton state: how much of P the chosen characters currently end with.

Knapsack and subset sums
Recognise a knapsack under any wording, decide what the capacity dimension measures, and use the right loop direction for zero-one, unbounded and bounded items.

The model question: n items, item i with weight w of i and value v of i, and a capacity W. Choose a set of total weight at most W with the largest total value, each item used at most once (the zero-one knapsack). Trying every subset costs 2 to the n, about 10 to the 30 when n is 100. Greedy by value per unit of weight fails: with a capacity of 4 and items of (weight, value) (3, 5), (2, 3) and (2, 3), it takes the first, has no room left and scores 5, while the two small items score 6.

What a partial choice leaves for the remaining items depends only on how much weight it has used. Two choices that used the same weight face exactly the same future, so only the one with more value is worth keeping. With integer weights there are only W plus 1 possible amounts, so the work grows with W, not with 2 to the n.

Let dp of c be the best value of a set of the items considered so far with total weight at most c; before any item, every dp of c is 0. Item i is added in one pass over c: dp of c is max(dp of c, dp of c minus w i plus v of i) for every c at least w of i, which either skips the item or puts it on top of the best set that leaves w of i free. After the last item, dp of W is the answer.

The update is right only if dp of c minus w i still means "without item i". Sweeping c downwards guarantees that, because the smaller index has not been touched yet in this pass. So after item i, each dp of c is the best over subsets of the first i items, and that is the whole proof. Sweeping upwards, dp of c minus w i may already include item i, so the item can be taken again and again: wrong for zero-one, and exactly right when every item has unlimited copies (the unbounded knapsack).

Each item costs O of W, so the DP is O of n times W time and O of W memory. Starting from 0 everywhere means "weight at most c"; starting from dp of 0 is 0 and minus infinity everywhere else means "weight exactly c". An item with cnt of i copies is split into packs of 1, 2, 4 and so on copies plus a remainder, each run as a zero-one item. When only feasibility matters, a bitset can, whose bit s says some subset sums to s, takes each item with can or-equals can shifted left by w of i in O of MAXS over 64.

The real work is choosing what the index measures. It must be additive over the chosen items and small enough to loop over: weight, elapsed time, the number of items covered, the peak storage in use during a step, a small total value when the weights are huge (then store the least weight for each value), or a sum shifted by an offset when per-item amounts can be negative.
w of i: the weight of item i (in the TRD version each item is a pair, and its weight is wt).
v of i: the value of item i (val in the TRD version).
W: the capacity, the largest total weight allowed (C in the TRD version).

dp of c: the best total value of a set of the items processed so far with total weight at most c, or exactly c with the minus infinity start. The diagram keeps one row per item, dp of i, c for the first i items; the code keeps only the latest row.
cnt of i: how many copies of item i exist, in the bounded version.
can: the subset-sum bitset; bit s is set when some subset sums to exactly s (built by reachable in the TRD version).
MAXS: the largest sum the bitset tracks (S in the TRD version).

The problem is A Musical Question. Bob has two CDs that each hold W minutes (c in the statement), with W up to 1000, and n songs, up to 1000 of them, each at most 1000 minutes long. Each song goes whole onto one CD or is left out, and he wants as many minutes as possible on the two CDs together. Among the best totals, the two CDs should differ as little as possible, and the output gives the fuller CD first. In the second sample W is 100 and the songs last 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 minutes: all 150 minutes fit, split 80 and 70.

Each song goes on the first CD, on the second or nowhere, so there are 3 to the n choices, about 10 to the 477 when n is 1000. Filling one CD as full as possible and then the other is not safe either. With W is 8 and songs of 2, 2, 4, 5 and 5 minutes, the only way to fill the first CD to 8 is 2 plus 2 plus 4, and then the second CD takes one 5: 13 minutes. Putting 5 plus 2 on each CD makes 14. Even when the total comes out right, the split can be wrong: on sample 2 this gives 100 and 50 instead of 80 and 70.

This is a zero-one knapsack whose weight is a pair. What the remaining songs can still achieve depends only on the minutes already on each CD, c1 on the first and c2 on the second, so that pair is the state. Only reachability matters, so keep it in bitsets: bit c2 of can of c1 is set when some songs fill the CDs with exactly c1 and c2 minutes. That is (W plus 1) squared states, about 10 to the 6, and before any song only can of 0, 0 is set.

Song i, of length w of i, is added in one pass over the rows. Putting it on the second CD shifts a row by w of i: can of c1 shifted left by w of i. Putting it on the first CD takes the row w of i lower: can of c1 minus w i. So can of c1 or-equals (can of c1 shifted left by w of i) or can of c1 minus w i. Sweeping c1 from W downwards means the lower row has not been touched in this pass yet, and the shift is taken from the row's old value, so each song is used at most once. With 64 bits to a word, this is O of n times W squared over 64, about 1.6 times 10 to the 7 operations, where a plain bool table would take 10 to the 9.

Each song only adds pairs. After song 30, for example, (30, 30) is reachable, with 10 plus 20 on one CD and 30 on the other. Song 50 adds pairs such as (100, 50): 10 plus 40 plus 50 on the first CD and 20 plus 30 on the second. The shifts also set bits above W, such as bit 110 of can of 0, from 10 plus 20 plus 30 plus 50 on the second CD. Those bits are never read, so they need no clearing.

After the last song, read the answer off the table. The largest total c1 plus c2 is 150, on the diagonal from (100, 50) to (50, 100). Of those pairs, (80, 70) and (70, 80) differ least, so the output is 80 70. The table is symmetric, because the two CDs can swap, so it is enough to scan c2 at most c1, which also puts the fuller CD first. A song longer than W fits on neither CD: its shift only sets bits above W, and c1 at least w of i never holds.
You pick a subset of items, each with a cost and a gain, under a total budget that is at most about 10⁵ or can be capped there.
"Can we make exactly S" or "which totals are reachable": subset-sum feasibility, often as a bitset.
One quantity is huge (up to 10⁹) and another is small (total at most 10⁵): index by the small one and store the best of the huge one.
A condition such as "ratio is k" or "the two sums are equal": rewrite it as a sum of per-item differences that must equal 0.
Wrong loop direction: sweeping capacity upwards in a zero-one knapsack lets one item be taken many times. With a negative weight the safe direction flips; when unsure, copy the row.

"At most c" versus "exactly c": all zeros means at most, minus infinity except dp of 0 is 0 means exactly. If you computed exactly, take the maximum over all c at most W (or make the table monotone) before reading the answer, otherwise a capacity that cannot be filled exactly looks impossible.

A capacity W far larger than the total weight sum of w of i of all the items: cap W at sum of w of i before allocating the table. In 1633D the capacity reaches 10⁶, but the weights add up to at most 12n.
Each paid item gives time to take t other items for free, pay as little as possible: that is, each paid item covers t plus 1 items; a min-cost knapsack whose capacity is "items covered", capped at n.

Items with a duration and a deadline, maximise the value finished in time: that is, sort by deadline (exchange argument), then a zero-one knapsack over elapsed time where an item fits only if its finish time is before its deadline.
Total taste divided by total calories must equal k: that is, weight A minus k times b per item, possibly negative; a knapsack over that sum with an offset, target exactly 0.
clips.script: Total taste divided by total calories must equal k: that is, weight eh minus k times b per item, possibly negative; a knapsack over that sum with an offset, target exactly 0.

clips.text: Grid DP, interval DP and choosing the state

Design DP states over grid cells, over segments dp of l, r filled by length, and over small tuples such as the last item on each line, and spot the reorder or delete problems that collapse into one of them.

The questions here come in two shapes. One is a walk across a grid that moves only right or down and is scored by the cells it visits; the other is a row of items that is merged, deleted or folded in place, where the neighbours close up after every step. Listing the possibilities is hopeless: a 20 times 20 grid has about 3.5 times 10 to the 10 right/down paths from corner to corner, and a row of 20 piles can be merged into one by about 1.2 times 10 to the 17 different sequences of merges.

Most of those possibilities share their future. A walk that has reached a cell can go on in exactly the same ways however it got there, and it can only have arrived from the cell above or the cell to the left. In a row whose neighbours close up, every item on the table is built from a contiguous segment of the original row, so what happens to the segment l to r depends only on the items inside it. The last step on it splits it into shorter segments that never interact again.

For a grid, let best of i, j be the best value of a path from the top-left cell (0, 0) to the cell (i, j), and g of i, j the value written in that cell. Then best of i, j is g of i, j plus max(best of i minus 1, j, best of i, j minus 1), and filling the table row by row has both neighbours ready in time, O of nm for n rows and m columns. Running the same pass from the other corners gives the best piece from each corner to every cell, so two paths that meet can be glued together at the meeting cell.

For a row, let dp of l, r be the best answer for the items l to r on their own. In the template, piles A from 0 to n minus 1 are merged until one is left, and each merge costs the size of the new pile. The last merge of l to r joins l to k and k plus 1 to r for some split point k and costs the whole segment's total, pre of r plus 1 minus pre of l from prefix sums, so dp of l, r is the minimum over k of dp of l, k plus dp of k plus 1, r, plus that total. The template fills every segment of one length len before any longer one, so the shorter segments it reads are already final.
clips.script: For a row, let dp of l, r be the best answer for the items l to r on their own. In the template, piles eh from 0 to n minus 1 are merged until one is left, and each merge costs the size of the new pile. The last merge of l to r joins l to k and k plus 1 to r for some split point k and costs the whole segment's total, pre of r plus 1 minus pre of l from prefix sums, so dp of l, r is the minimum over k of dp of l, k plus dp of k plus 1, r, plus that total. The template fills every segment of one length len before any longer one, so the shorter segments it reads are already final.

clips.text: Every way of merging l to r has a last merge at some k, and the two halves before it were merged independently. So the cheapest way with that k uses the cheapest way for each half, and trying every k covers every way. In general, a state must be the smallest description of a partial solution that still decides every future move: two partial solutions with equal states can be finished in exactly the same ways, so only the better needs keeping. Examples are the cell a walk has reached, the segment still on the table, or the last item placed on each of three lines (UKIEPC 2025 Klaus).

There are O of n squared segments and trying every split costs O of n each, so interval DP is usually O of n cubed, which is why these problems have n at most 500. When a segment only looks at its two ends, as for palindromes or a block that grows at one end, it is O of n squared and n can reach 5000. Points on a circle become a row once the circle is cut at one point, and each choice then splits an arc into independent smaller arcs. UKIEPC 2023 Clearing Space also cuts its circle, at the first chosen post, but then runs a chain DP over (last post, posts used) instead of splitting arcs.
best of i, j: in a grid DP, the best value of a path from the top-left cell (0, 0) to the cell (i, j) that moves only right or down.
g of i, j: the value in the grid cell in row i and column j, both counted from 0.
dp of l, r: in an interval DP, the best answer for the items l to r on their own, as if nothing outside them existed; l and r are the first and last index, both included.
A of i: item i of the row, counted from 0; in the template, the size of pile i. A from l to r is the part from index l to index r, both included.
clips.script: eh of i: item i of the row, counted from 0; in the template, the size of pile i. eh from l to r is the part from index l to index r, both included.

clips.text: s from l to r: the substring of a string s from index l to index r, both included.
k: the split point, so that the last step joins l to k and k plus 1 to r. In a deletion problem k is instead the later element that is removed together with element l.
len: the length r minus l plus 1 of a segment; every segment of one length is filled before any longer one.
pre of i: the prefix sum A of 0 plus … plus A of i minus 1, so the items l to r total pre of r plus 1 minus pre of l (P in the TRD version).
clips.script: pre of i: the prefix sum eh of 0 plus … plus eh of i minus 1, so the items l to r total pre of r plus 1 minus pre of l (P in the TRD version).

clips.text: The input is one string of at most 200 capital letters. A block A that appears m times in a row, for m at least 2, can be written once, in brackets, to the power m, and the block inside can be factored again. The weight of a factoring is the number of letters still written, not counting brackets and exponents, and the task is the least weight. In the first sample, PRATTATTATTIC, writing ATT once, cubed, leaves seven letters: P, R, A, T, T, I and C.
clips.script: The input is one string of at most 200 capital letters. A block A that appears m times in a row, for m at least 2, can be written once, in brackets, to the power m, and the block inside can be factored again. The weight of a factoring is the number of letters still written, not counting brackets and exponents, and the task is the least weight. In the first sample, PRATTATTATTIC, writing ATT once, cubed, leaves seven letters: P, R, eh, T, T, I and C.

clips.text: Shortening the first repeat you see goes wrong. Writing each TT as T squared leaves P, R, A, T squared, A, T squared, A, T squared, I, C: ten letters, and the three copies of ATT can no longer be joined into one. Trying every factoring is hopeless too: a run of 40 G's alone has about 2.4 times 10 to the 13 different factorings, and the input can have 200 letters.
clips.script: Shortening the first repeat you see goes wrong. Writing each TT as T squared leaves P, R, eh, T squared, eh, T squared, eh, T squared, I, C: ten letters, and the three copies of ATT can no longer be joined into one. Trying every factoring is hopeless too: a run of 40 G's alone has about 2.4 times 10 to the 13 different factorings, and the input can have 200 letters.

clips.text: Look at the outermost step of a factoring of the substring s from l to r. Either it is two factorings side by side, split after some position k, or it is one block written to a power. In both cases the pieces are shorter substrings, and how one piece is factored does not affect the other. That is an interval DP: solve every substring, shortest first. A string of 200 letters has about 2 times 10 to the 4 substrings, each with fewer than 200 split points, so O of n cubed is fast.

Let dp of l, r be the least weight of s from l to r. It starts at the length, r minus l plus 1, the weight of writing every letter. A split after position k offers dp of l, k plus dp of k plus 1, r. For a repeat, let d be the length of the block: if d divides the length and s from l to r minus d is s from l plus d to r, the substring is its first d letters repeated, and writing that block once costs dp of l, l plus d minus 1. Filling the table by length makes every entry it reads final, and the answer is dp of 0, n minus 1.

Back to PRATTATTATTIC, with positions counted from 0. At length 2, the TT at positions 3 and 4 is T repeated, so dp of 3, 4 is dp of 3, 3, so 1. At length 3, ATT is not a repeat, but splitting it after the A costs dp of 2, 2 plus dp of 3, 4 is 1 plus 1, so 2. So dp of 2, 4 is 2, for A followed by T squared.

At length 9, positions 2 to 10 hold ATTATTATT. The block length d is 3 divides 9, and s from 2 to 7 is s from 5 to 10, so it is ATT three times. Writing the block once costs what ATT costs, so dp of 2, 10 is dp of 2, 4, so 2, and the block keeps its own factoring, A followed by T squared. The best split of the same substring costs 4.

The whole string is the last entry. Its first split, after the P, gives dp of 0, 0 plus dp of 1, 12 is 1 plus 5, so 6, and nothing does better, so the answer is 6: P, R, then A with T squared, all cubed, then I, C. A single letter weighs 1, and a run of nine G's is G to the power 9, weight 1, with no special cases. At n is 200 the splits take about 1.3 times 10 to the 6 steps and the repeat checks at most 5.4 times 10 to the 6 letter comparisons, well within the time limit.
n at most 500 (or n at most 5000 with an O of n to the 2 DP) and an operation that removes or merges a contiguous block, after which the neighbours close up.
A grid walk with right/down moves where you optimise or test something about the path, or two walkers whose paths interact.
Questions about every substring or subarray: how many palindromes inside s from l to r, can A from l to r collapse into one element.
clips.script: Questions about every substring or subarray: how many palindromes inside s from l to r, can eh from l to r collapse into one element.

clips.text: Points on a circle or a polygon where choices must not cross: cut the circle once, and each choice splits an arc into independent smaller arcs.
Filling dp of l, r with l and r both increasing reads dp of l plus 1, r before it exists. Loop over the length, or run l downward and r upward.

Transitions such as dp of l plus 1, k-1 reach empty segments (l greater than r). Size the table n plus 2 and leave those entries at 0 (or whatever an empty segment costs) instead of special-casing every branch.
A 5000 times 5000 table of int is 100 MB and of long long is 200 MB. Store flags as bool or char and check the memory limit before choosing the type.

Delete palindromes or blocks of equal letters until nothing is left: that is, dp of l, r where the first element, l, either goes alone or goes with a later equal element k once l plus 1 to k-1 is cleared. What is left is k plus 1 to r when the pair closes a palindrome (607B, where an adjacent pair still costs 1), or k to r when element l rides along with element k's later deletion (1132F)

Choose an order that minimises a sum of (max - min) over prefixes: that is, sort first; the items placed so far are always a contiguous block of the sorted array, so dp of l, r grows the block at one end
Fewest trailing zeros of a product along a grid path: that is, two independent min-sum grid DPs, one counting factors of 2 and one counting factors of 5

Assign items in input order to one of several lines, where the cost depends on the previous item on the same line: that is, dp over the index of the last item on each line; one of them is always the current index - 1, which removes a dimension
dp of l, r is the longest palindromic subsequence of s from l to r: row l, column r. Fill by length, so every shorter interval inside is ready.
Length 1: every single letter is a palindrome, so dp of i, i is 1 down the diagonal.
