clips.text: 5 edges is n minus 1, so stop: B to C (7) and B to D (10) are never examined. MST weight 1 plus 2 plus 3 plus 4 plus 6 is 16.
Topological sort and DAG DP
Turn "x before y" constraints into a directed graph, find an order or prove none exists, and run DP along that order for longest paths, path counts and minimal layer numbers.

Some statements hand you rules of the form "x must come before y": prerequisites, dependencies, a list sorted under an unknown alphabet. They ask for an order that obeys every rule, or a proof that none exists, or something computed along the rules, such as the longest chain or the number of routes from a start. Trying orders one by one is hopeless: 26 letters can be ordered in about 4 times 10 to the 26 ways. A computation along the rules must handle each item after everything that has to precede it, and input order or label order does not promise that. Sweeping over all the rules until nothing changes can take n sweeps, about 10 to the 10 steps for n is 10 to the 5 items and m is 10 to the 5 rules.

Make each item a vertex and each rule "x before y" a directed edge x to y. An order of the vertices in which every edge points forward is a topological order, and one exists exactly when the graph has no cycle: on a cycle, each vertex would have to come before itself. A graph without a cycle always has a vertex with no incoming edges, because walking backwards along incoming edges would otherwise repeat a vertex within n steps and close a cycle. Such a vertex can safely go first.

Kahn's algorithm applies that observation over and over. Keep adj of v, the vertices that v has an edge to; indeg of v, the number of edges into v from vertices not yet placed; and a queue q of the vertices whose indeg has reached 0. Pop a vertex v, append it to order, and delete its outgoing edges: for each u in adj of v, decrease indeg of u and push u when it reaches 0. Each vertex and each edge is handled once, so this is O of n plus m. Listing the vertices in reverse order of when a DFS finishes them also gives a topological order.

Why it works: a vertex enters order only once all its incoming edges are deleted, that is, after every vertex that points into it, so every edge points forward. Removing a vertex from a graph with no cycle leaves a graph that still has no cycle, so by the observation another vertex is always ready, the queue never runs dry early, and all n vertices are placed. With a cycle, no vertex on it ever reaches indeg 0, and neither does anything reachable from it, so order ends with fewer than n vertices: that is the "impossible", minus 1 or "infinite" case.

Once you have order, any DP whose transitions follow edges takes one pass over it. Visit each v in order and push its value along each edge v to u: len of u is max(len of u, len of v plus 1) gives the longest path, counted in edges, ending at u, and ways of u plus-equals ways of v (mod 10 to the 9 plus 7) counts the paths from a start vertex src. Every vertex that points into u comes earlier in order, so u's value is final before u passes it on, the same argument as the children-first pass on a rooted tree.

Each pass is O of n plus m. The variations change what is pushed along an edge, and sometimes where the values start. A cost of 0 or 1 per edge counts passes or rounds. Once the items that must be equal are merged with DSU, the smallest values that satisfy every rule A less than b are longest-path layers. For shortest paths from src in a DAG, start with 0 at src and infinity everywhere else, skip any vertex still at infinity when its turn comes, and push min instead of max; negative weights are fine, because a vertex is only used once everything before it is final. A min-heap in place of the queue gives the lexicographically smallest order, in O of (n plus m) log n.
clips.script: Each pass is O of n plus m. The variations change what is pushed along an edge, and sometimes where the values start. A cost of 0 or 1 per edge counts passes or rounds. Once the items that must be equal are merged with DSU, the smallest values that satisfy every rule eh less than b are longest-path layers. For shortest paths from src in a DAG, start with 0 at src and infinity everywhere else, skip any vertex still at infinity when its turn comes, and push min instead of max; negative weights are fine, because a vertex is only used once everything before it is final. A min-heap in place of the queue gives the lexicographically smallest order, in O of (n plus m) log n.

clips.text: adj of v: the vertices u with an edge v to u, that is, the items that v must come before (gr in the TRD version).
indeg of v: how many edges into v come from vertices not yet placed; v can be placed once it is 0 (in of v in the diagram).
q: the queue of vertices whose indeg has reached 0 and that wait to be placed (in the TRD version's topoSort, one list q is both the queue and the returned order).
order: the topological order, the vertices in the order Kahn's algorithm removes them; it has fewer than n entries exactly when the graph has a cycle (returned by topoSort in the TRD version).
len of v: the most edges on any path that ends at v (dp in the TRD version's longestPath).
ways of v: the number of paths from src to v, mod 10 to the 9 plus 7.
src: the start vertex; ways of v counts the paths that begin there.

There are n topics, up to 4 times 10 to the 5, each settled in its own meeting, one meeting at a time. Topic i needs e i minutes, up to 10 to the 6, and lists the topics that must be discussed before it. There are at most 4 times 10 to the 5 such rules, and they have no cycle. Each meeting starts with a recap of one minute per meeting already held, so the meeting at position pos, counting from 0, lasts e i plus pos. Print the shortest possible length of the longest meeting, over all orders that obey the rules.

Trying every order is hopeless: 10 topics with no rules can already be ordered in 10!, about 3.6 times 10 to the 6, ways. A natural greedy goes from the front and always holds the longest ready topic next, since later meetings carry more recap. It fails. Say topic A takes 1 minute and must come before B, which takes 100, and C takes 50. The ready topics are A and C, so the greedy holds C first, then A, then B, which lasts 100 plus 2 is 102. The order A, B, C does better: B lasts 101 and C lasts 52. From the front, the greedy cannot see the long topic waiting behind a short one.
clips.script: Trying every order is hopeless: 10 topics with no rules can already be ordered in 10!, about 3.6 times 10 to the 6, ways. A natural greedy goes from the front and always holds the longest ready topic next, since later meetings carry more recap. It fails. Say topic A takes 1 minute and must come before B, which takes 100, and C takes 50. The ready topics are eh and C, so the greedy holds C first, then eh, then B, which lasts 100 plus 2 is 102. The order eh, B, C does better: B lasts 101 and C lasts 52. From the front, the greedy cannot see the long topic waiting behind a short one.

clips.text: An order that obeys "this before that" rules is a topological order, so the question is which ready topic goes where. The recap grows with position, and the last meeting has the largest, n minus 1 minutes, so decide it first. The last topic must be one that no other topic needs, and among those, put the shortest last. Suppose an optimal order ends with such a topic s, while a shorter one, t, comes earlier. Move t to the end. Nothing needs t, so the order still obeys the rules. Every meeting after t's old place moves one slot earlier and gets a minute shorter, and t now lasts e t plus n minus 1, less than s did. So the longest meeting does not grow, and the same choice repeats for the n minus 1 topics left.

This is Kahn's algorithm run backwards. Reverse every rule: adj of v lists the topics that v needs first, and indeg of b counts the unplaced topics that need b. A topic with indeg 0 can take the latest free position, so it waits in q, a min-heap ordered by e. Fill the positions from n minus 1 down to 0, each time with the topic popped from q, and record e v plus pos. Placing v deletes its arrows: each b in adj of v loses 1 from indeg of b, and joins q when it reaches 0. The answer is the largest e v plus pos.

In sample 2, no topic needs topic 1 or topic 6, so q starts with both. Topic 1 is shorter, so it takes pos 5 and lasts 2 plus 5 is 7; putting 6 there instead would cost 4 plus 5 is 9. Deleting 1's arrows lowers indeg of 4 and indeg of 3 to 1, so only 6 is ready. It takes pos 4 and lasts 4 plus 4 is 8. Deleting its arrow to 3 brings indeg of 3 to 0, and 3 joins q.

Topic 3 takes pos 3 and lasts 1 plus 3 is 4. Deleting its arrows frees both 2 and 4, so q holds 4, with e is 3, and 2, with e is 4. The shorter, 4, takes pos 2 and lasts 3 plus 2 is 5. Then 2 takes pos 1 and lasts 4 plus 1 is 5, which frees topic 5, and 5 takes pos 0 and lasts 2 plus 0 is 2.

The order is 5, 2, 4, 3, 6, 1, and the meetings last 2, 5, 5, 4, 8 and 7 minutes, so the answer is 8, as in the sample. With m rules, every topic enters and leaves the heap once and every rule is handled once, so the run is O of (n plus m) log n. When two ready topics have the same e, either can go later. Lengths stay below 1.4 times 10 to the 6, so int is enough.
The statement gives pairwise constraints: "a must come before b", "x is smaller than y", prerequisites, dependencies, or a list that is sorted under some unknown order.
You must answer "impossible", -1 or "infinite" when the requirements contradict each other or a walk could repeat forever: that is cycle detection.
The graph is promised to be acyclic ("no cyclic routes", "a task never depends on itself") and you want the best or the number of paths.
You must give items the smallest ranks, levels or values that respect a set of less than and is relations.

Not checking for a cycle: after Kahn's algorithm, compare the number of removed vertices with n. With DFS you need three colours (unvisited, on the stack, finished); a plain visited flag cannot tell a back edge from a harmless cross edge.

Running the DP in input order or vertex-number order, or starting Kahn's algorithm only from the source: start from every vertex with in-degree 0, or vertices fed by unreachable ones are never processed.
In "sorted under some order" problems, a word followed by its own proper prefix ("care" before "car") can never be sorted, and it produces no letter edge, so it must be checked separately.

Find an alphabet or ranking under which a given list is sorted: that is, compare neighbouring items; each first difference gives one edge "x before y", and any topological order of the letters is an answer.
How many passes, rounds or semesters until everything is done: that is, longest path in the dependency DAG, where an edge costs 1 when it forces a new pass and 0 otherwise.

Assign the smallest positive values satisfying A less than b and A is b: that is, merge the is groups with DSU, then a group's value is 1 plus the longest chain of less than edges ending at it; a cycle, or A less than inside one group, means no assignment.
clips.script: Assign the smallest positive values satisfying eh less than b and eh is b: that is, merge the is groups with DSU, then a group's value is 1 plus the longest chain of less than edges ending at it; a cycle, or eh less than inside one group, means no assignment.

clips.text: Orient undirected edges, or choose which edges to keep, so that no cycle appears: that is, fix one vertex order (a topological order of the forced edges) and point everything forward in it; edges that all go forward in one order can never form a cycle.
Kahn's algorithm. in of v counts the edges into v. b and e have none, so they start in the queue.
Dequeue b and append it to the order. Now delete its outgoing edge.
Delete b to A: in of a drops from 2 to 1. One more edge still points into A.
clips.script: Delete b to eh: in of a drops from 2 to 1. One more edge still points into eh.

clips.text: Dequeue e and append it to the order. Now delete its 2 outgoing edges, one at a time.
Delete e to A: in of a drops from 1 to 0. Nothing else has to come before A, so enqueue it.
clips.script: Delete e to eh: in of a drops from 1 to 0. Nothing else has to come before eh, so enqueue it.

clips.text: Delete e to c: in of c drops from 1 to 0. Nothing else has to come before c, so enqueue it.
Dequeue A and append it to the order. Now delete its outgoing edge.
clips.script: Dequeue eh and append it to the order. Now delete its outgoing edge.

clips.text: Delete A to g: in of g drops from 2 to 1. One more edge still points into g.
clips.script: Delete eh to g: in of g drops from 2 to 1. One more edge still points into g.

clips.text: Dequeue c and append it to the order. Now delete its 2 outgoing edges, one at a time.
Delete c to g: in of g drops from 1 to 0. Nothing else has to come before g, so enqueue it.
Delete c to d: in of d drops from 1 to 0. Nothing else has to come before d, so enqueue it.
Dequeue g and append it to the order. Now delete its outgoing edge.
Delete g to f: in of f drops from 2 to 1. One more edge still points into f.

Delete d to f: in of f drops from 1 to 0. Nothing else has to come before f, so enqueue it.

Order: b, e, A, c, g, d, f. Every edge points forward in it. If the queue empties before all 7 are output, the graph has a cycle.

clips.text: Dijkstra, Floyd–Warshall and state graphs
Compute single-source and all-pairs shortest paths, run Dijkstra over expanded states, and reuse a distance table to answer "what if this road changes" questions.

The question: the least total cost from a start to every vertex, or to one target, when each edge has a weight. BFS answers it only when every edge costs the same: from S, the edge S to A of weight 4 is a single edge, but S to B to A with weights 1 and 2 costs 3. Listing every path is exponential, and improving distances edge by edge until nothing changes can take n minus 1 passes over all m edges, about 10 to the 10 steps for n is 10 to the 5 vertices and m is 10 to the 5 edges.
clips.script: The question: the least total cost from a start to every vertex, or to one target, when each edge has a weight. BFS answers it only when every edge costs the same: from S, the edge S to eh of weight 4 is a single edge, but S to B to A with weights 1 and 2 costs 3. Listing every path is exponential, and improving distances edge by edge until nothing changes can take n minus 1 passes over all m edges, about 10 to the 10 steps for n is 10 to the 5 vertices and m is 10 to the 5 edges.

clips.text: Suppose no weight is negative. Among the vertices whose distance is not yet known, take the one with the smallest tentative distance, the best found so far through vertices already known: no other route can beat it, because such a route has to leave the known vertices somewhere, already costs at least as much at that point, and can only add more. So distances can be fixed one vertex at a time in increasing order, much as BFS fixes them layer by layer.

Dijkstra's algorithm does this with a priority queue. dist of v holds the best distance found so far from the start src (INF until v is reached, 0 for src), and the min-heap pq holds pairs (d, v), each meaning "v can be reached at cost d". Pop the smallest pair. If d differs from dist of v, the pair is stale, left over from before an improvement, so skip it. Otherwise v is settled, meaning dist of v is final. Relax each edge in adj of v from v to u with weight w: if d plus w less than dist of u, set dist of u is d plus w, record par of u is v and push (dist of u, u). Pushing a new pair instead of updating the old one keeps the code short. Following par of u back from any vertex u gives a shortest path to it.

Why it is right: suppose some path to v were shorter than the popped d, and let u be its first vertex that is not yet settled. The vertex before u on that path is settled, so its edge into u was relaxed and dist of u is at most the path's length up to u, which is below d because the rest of the path costs at least 0. Then (dist of u, u) would have come out of pq before (d, v). Each vertex is settled once and each edge relaxed once, so at most m plus 1 pairs are pushed and the total is O of (n plus m) log m. A negative weight breaks the argument, which is why Dijkstra needs every weight at least 0.

Dijkstra never looks at what a vertex means, only at its edges, so a vertex can be a state: (city, best bike owned), (vertex, riding or not), (city, coupons used). When the cost of an edge depends on something you carry or have done, put that thing in the vertex. If it takes K values c from 0 to K minus 1, number the state (v, c) as v times K plus c: the graph has n times K vertices, and the same dijkstra runs on it unchanged.

For all pairs at once, Floyd–Warshall keeps a table d of i, j that starts as the edge weights (INF where there is no edge, 0 on the diagonal) and, for k is 0 to n minus 1 in the outer loop, sets d of i, j is min(d of i, j, d of i, k plus d of k, j) for every i and j. After the pass for k, d of i, j is the shortest path from i to j whose stopovers all lie among vertices 0 to k, so the outer loop can add vertices one at a time, in any order you choose. It costs O of n cubed, about 1.25 times 10 to the 8 for n is 500. With the finished table, "change one road", "add a road" or "visit these places in some order" become arithmetic or a small DP over table entries.

adj of v: the edges out of v, as pairs (u, w): an edge from v to u with weight w (the TRD version stores the same pairs but names the popped vertex u and its neighbour v: adj of u holds v, w, and it sets par of v is u).
src: the start vertex (s in the TRD version).

dist of v: the best distance from src to v found so far, final once v is settled, and INF if v is unreachable (LLONG MAX in the TRD version). In the worked problem, dist of v, f is the cheapest way to reach city v with f units of fuel.
pq: a min-heap of pairs (d, v), each saying v can be reached at cost d; a popped pair whose d differs from dist of v is stale and skipped.
par of u: the vertex before u on a shortest path from src; the edges from par of u to u form the shortest-path tree (in the TRD version, path(t) follows them back).
INF: the stand-in for "unreachable", LLONG MAX over 4, so that adding to it cannot overflow (inf, which is 2 to the 62, in KACTL's FloydWarshall.h).
d of i, j: the Floyd–Warshall table: edge weights at first, the shortest distance from i to j at the end (m of i, j in the TRD version).
k: the Floyd–Warshall outer loop; after its pass for k, d of i, j uses only vertices 0 to k as stopovers.
K: in a state graph, how many values c is 0 to K minus 1 the thing you carry can take; state (v, c) is vertex v times K plus c (stateId(city, c, K) in the TRD version).
d1 of v: in a two-person problem, the distance to v from the first person's start, from one Dijkstra run.
d2 of v: the distance to v from the second person's start, from a second run.

There are n cities, up to 1000, joined by m two-way roads, up to 10 to the 4, each at most 100 long. Fuel costs p v a unit in city v, at most 100, and the car burns one unit per unit of distance. Each of up to 100 queries gives a tank capacity c, at most 100, a start city src and a goal city t. The car starts with an empty tank and may buy fuel in any city it is in, as long as the tank never holds more than c. For each query, print the cheapest cost of reaching t, or "impossible".

In the sample, with c is 10, the trip from city 0 to city 3 shows the difficulty. The shortest route, 0, then 2, then 3, needs 15 units of fuel. The tank holds 10, so at least 5 units must be bought in city 2, where fuel costs 20, and the trip costs at least 10 times 10 plus 5 times 20 is 200. The longer route 0, then 1, then 2, then 3 needs 17 units, but buys 9 in city 0 and 8 in city 1, all at 10, for 170. Dijkstra over cities alone cannot see this: what a road costs depends on where its fuel was bought, and on how much is still in the tank.

What decides the cost of the next move is the city you are in and the fuel in the tank, so make that pair the vertex: state (v, f) means being in city v with f units of fuel, where f runs from 0 to c. With K is c plus 1 fuel levels, number state (v, f) as v times K plus f, as in the template, and keep dist of v, f at that index; that is at most 1000 times 101, about 10 to the 5 states. Every move costs a price or nothing, never a negative amount, so Dijkstra runs on these states unchanged.

Two kinds of move leave state (v, f). Buying one unit goes to (v, f plus 1) and costs p v, if f less than c. Driving a road of length d to city u goes to (u, f minus d) and costs nothing, if f at least d. Buying several units is the same as buying them one at a time, so single units are enough, and they keep the graph small: an edge for every amount would give up to c edges per state, about 10 to the 7 per query, while single units leave 1 plus deg(v), where deg(v) counts the roads at v. Start at (src, 0) with cost 0. The first state of city t to leave pq has the lowest cost of any state in city t, so it is the answer; if pq empties first, print impossible.

Dijkstra first pops the states of city 0 in order of cost, each buying a unit at 10, so row 0 fills with 0, 10, 20 and so on. From (0, 8), at 80, the road of length 8 reaches (2, 0) at 80, and from there a unit bought in city 2 costs 20, so dist of 2, 1 becomes 100. Popping (0, 9) at 90 drives the road of length 9 to (1, 0) at 90, and the road of length 8 to (2, 1), also at 90, which lowers dist of 2, 1 from 100: fuel carried from city 0 beats fuel bought in city 2.

From (1, 0), at 90, row 1 fills at 10 a unit, while buying in city 2 costs 20 a unit. When (1, 8) is popped at 170, the road of length 1 reaches (2, 7) at 170, below the 180 it cost to buy those units in city 2. Then (2, 7) is popped, and the road of length 7 reaches (3, 0), also at 170.

The first state of city 3 to leave pq is (3, 0) at 170, so the answer is 170: buy 9 units in city 0, drive to city 1, buy 8 more, and drive through city 2 to city 3. The second query, from city 1 to city 4, prints impossible: city 4 has no roads, so pq empties without reaching it. Each query handles at most n times K states, about 10 to the 5, and about 2 times 10 to the 6 edges, so it costs O of (n plus m) times K log(n times K), and stopping at the first state of t often ends it sooner. A trip never needs to cost more than 100 times 100 times 999, below 10 to the 7, so int is enough.
Weighted edges with non-negative weights, and the question asks for the least total time, cost or distance from a start.
The cost of an edge depends on something you carry or have done (a bike, a horse, a ticket, fuel, discounts used): make that part of the vertex.

n is at most a few hundred and the question involves many pairs, or vertices and roads are added over time (or removed, if you can read the removals in reverse as additions): Floyd–Warshall, then an O of n squared relaxation per addition.
You may change one road, or must visit a few special places: precompute distances from the relevant sources once, then combine table entries.

Missing the stale-entry check: without "if (d is not dist of v) continue" a vertex popped many times rescans its edges, which can blow up to O of n times m. Also use a min-heap (greater), not the default max-heap.
Overflow: 10 to the 5 edges of weight 10 to the 6 or more need long long, and an INF of LLONG MAX overflows as soon as you add to it; use LLONG MAX over 4 or skip INF entries.
Floyd–Warshall with k not as the outermost loop: the result is wrong but often still passes small tests.
Delete vertices one by one and report a sum over all pairs before each deletion: that is, reverse the order and add the vertices as the k of Floyd–Warshall.
Costs depend on an item picked up earlier (a bike, a horse, a coupon): that is, Dijkstra over states (vertex, item), n states per item value.
Two people travel and meet at a vertex as early as possible: that is, one Dijkstra from each start; meeting at v takes max(d1 of v, d2 of v), so minimise that over v.

Make one road free, or add one road, and minimise a sum of route lengths: that is, with all-pairs distances, route A to b becomes min(d of A, b, d of A, x plus w plus d of y, b, d of A, y plus w plus d of x, b) for road x to y of new length w.
clips.script: Make one road free, or add one road, and minimise a sum of route lengths: that is, with all-pairs distances, route eh to b becomes min(d of eh, b, d of eh, x plus w plus d of y, b, d of eh, y plus w plus d of x, b) for road x to y of new length w.

clips.text: Dijkstra from S. Every distance starts at infinity except dist of S is 0, and the priority queue holds (0, S). Entries are (distance, vertex).
Pop (0, S), the smallest entry, and settle S at 0: with no negative edges, no later path can be shorter.
Edge S to A (4): 0 plus 4 is 4 less than infinity, so dist of A is 4. Push (4, A).
clips.script: Edge S to A (4): 0 plus 4 is 4 less than infinity, so dist of eh is 4. Push (4, eh).

clips.text: Edge S to B (1): 0 plus 1 is 1 less than infinity, so dist of B is 1. Push (1, B).
Pop (1, B), the smallest entry, and settle B at 1: with no negative edges, no later path can be shorter.
Edge B to A (2): 1 plus 2 is 3 less than 4, so dist of A is 3. Push (3, A); the old (4, A) stays in the queue, now out of date.
clips.script: Edge B to A (2): 1 plus 2 is 3 less than 4, so dist of eh is 3. Push (3, eh); the old (4, eh) stays in the queue, now out of date.

clips.text: Edge B to C (5): 1 plus 5 is 6 less than infinity, so dist of C is 6. Push (6, C).
Edge B to D (4): 1 plus 4 is 5 less than infinity, so dist of D is 5. Push (5, D).
Pop (3, A), the smallest entry, and settle A at 3: with no negative edges, no later path can be shorter.
clips.script: Pop (3, eh), the smallest entry, and settle eh at 3: with no negative edges, no later path can be shorter.

clips.text: Edge A to C (1): 3 plus 1 is 4 less than 6, so dist of C is 4. Push (4, C); the old (6, C) stays in the queue, now out of date.
clips.script: Edge eh to C (1): 3 plus 1 is 4 less than 6, so dist of C is 4. Push (4, C); the old (6, C) stays in the queue, now out of date.

clips.text: Pop (4, A). A is already settled at 3, so this entry is out of date: skip it.
clips.script: Pop (4, eh). eh is already settled at 3, so this entry is out of date: skip it.

clips.text: Pop (4, C), the smallest entry, and settle C at 4: with no negative edges, no later path can be shorter.
Edge C to T (3): 4 plus 3 is 7 less than infinity, so dist of T is 7. Push (7, T).
Pop (5, D), the smallest entry, and settle D at 5: with no negative edges, no later path can be shorter.
Edge D to T (3): 5 plus 3 is 8 is not less than 7, so nothing changes.
Pop (6, C). C is already settled at 4, so this entry is out of date: skip it.
Pop (7, T), the smallest entry, and settle T at 7: with no negative edges, no later path can be shorter. T has no outgoing edges.
Shortest-path tree in green. S to T costs 7: S to B to A to C to T. The direct edge S to A (4) lost to S to B to A (3).
clips.script: Shortest-path tree in green. S to T costs 7: S to B to eh to C to T. The direct edge S to A (4) lost to S to B to A (3).

clips.text: Binary lifting and LCA
Build jump tables up of j, v on trees and on "next" pointers to answer k-th ancestor, LCA, distance and path-maximum queries in O of log n, and count how many greedy steps lead from l to r.

The questions come on a fixed rooted tree, many at a time: the k-th ancestor of v, the lowest common ancestor (LCA) of A and b, the distance between them, the heaviest edge on their path. Walking up one parent at a time answers each in O of depth, and on a path-shaped tree with n is 2 times 10 to the 5 vertices and 2 times 10 to the 5 queries that is about 4 times 10 to the 10 steps. Storing every ancestor of every vertex would make each jump O of 1, but needs O of n squared memory.
clips.script: The questions come on a fixed rooted tree, many at a time: the k-th ancestor of v, the lowest common ancestor (LCA) of eh and b, the distance between them, the heaviest edge on their path. Walking up one parent at a time answers each in O of depth, and on a path-shaped tree with n is 2 times 10 to the 5 vertices and 2 times 10 to the 5 queries that is about 4 times 10 to the 10 steps. Storing every ancestor of every vertex would make each jump O of 1, but needs O of n squared memory.

clips.text: Every jump length is a sum of distinct powers of two, its binary digits: a jump of 13 is a jump of 8, then 4, then 1. So it is enough to know, for each vertex, where jumps of 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on land, and each of those is built from the one before, because a jump of 2 to the j is two jumps of 2 to the j minus 1.

Binary lifting stores up of j, v, the vertex 2 to the j steps above v, for every level j from 0 to LOG minus 1, where 2 to the LOG is larger than any jump (LOG is 18 when n is up to 2 times 10 to the 5). Row 0 holds the parents, found by a BFS from the root, with the root pointing to itself so that a jump past the top stops at the root. Every later row follows from the one below it: up of j, v is up of j minus 1, up j minus 1, v. Filling the table one row at a time, for every vertex, costs O of n log n. Then kth(v, k), the k-th ancestor of v, makes one jump v is up of j, v for each power 2 to the j in the binary form of k, at most LOG jumps.

For lca(A, b), the deepest vertex that is an ancestor of both, first lift the deeper vertex by the difference in depth, where dep of v counts the edges from the root to v; if the two now coincide, that vertex is the answer. Otherwise the LCA is some s at least 1 steps above both, and their 2 to the j-th ancestors are equal exactly when 2 to the j at least s. Trying j from LOG minus 1 down to 0 and jumping both only when up of j, A is not up of j, b climbs s minus 1 steps, one binary digit at a time, and leaves A and b as two different children of the LCA, which is up of 0, A. Distances follow: dist(A, b) is dep of A plus dep of b minus 2 times dep of lca(A, b).
clips.script: For lca(eh, b), the deepest vertex that is an ancestor of both, first lift the deeper vertex by the difference in depth, where dep of v counts the edges from the root to v; if the two now coincide, that vertex is the answer. Otherwise the LCA is some s at least 1 steps above both, and their 2 to the j-th ancestors are equal exactly when 2 to the j at least s. Trying j from LOG minus 1 down to 0 and jumping both only when up of j, eh is not up of j, b climbs s minus 1 steps, one binary digit at a time, and leaves eh and b as two different children of the LCA, which is up of 0, eh. Distances follow: dist(eh, b) is dep of eh plus dep of b minus 2 times dep of lca(eh, b).

clips.text: Whenever a condition holds on a bottom part of the path from v towards the root and fails above it, such as "the sum of positive weights climbed is at most x", try the jumps from the largest down and take each one that still lands on a vertex satisfying it: the jumps taken spell out, in binary, how far the condition reaches. An aggregate stored next to each jump, such as the heaviest edge among those 2 to the j edges, combines the same way as the jumps and answers path-maximum or path-sum queries during the climb.

Nothing in the table needs a tree. For any function next(x) that gives each position one successor, setting up of 0, x is next(x) and doubling as before answers "where am I after k steps", as long as there is a level for every bit of k: LOG is 60 for k up to 10 to the 18, while the template's LOG is 18 only covers k below 2 to the 18. The same descent answers "how many greedy steps lead from l past r", which never takes more than n steps. UKIEPC 2023 Fast Forward jumped through "next ad break" pointers this way. Building costs O of n times LOG time and memory, 1.2 times 10 to the 7 entries for n is 2 times 10 to the 5 and LOG is 60, and every query O of LOG.

up of j, v: the vertex 2 to the j steps above v, or the root if v is less than 2 to the j deep; j is the level, never a step count. Over a function next, it is next applied 2 to the j times (tbl of j, v in the TRD version, built by treeJump).

LOG: the number of levels, j is 0 to LOG minus 1; 2 to the LOG must exceed the longest jump, so 18 for depths below 2 to the 18 and 60 for k up to 10 to the 18 (in the TRD version treeJump picks it as the number of rows of tbl, which only covers jumps shorter than about 2n, so stepTable builds its own 60).
dep of v: the number of edges from the root down to v (depth in the TRD version).
kth(v, k): the k-th ancestor of v, one jump for each bit set in k (jmp(tbl, v, k) in the TRD version).
lca(A, b): the lowest common ancestor of A and b, the deepest vertex that has both in its subtree; a vertex counts as its own ancestor (lca(tbl, depth, A, b) in the TRD version).
clips.script: lca(eh, b): the lowest common ancestor of eh and b, the deepest vertex that has both in its subtree; a vertex counts as its own ancestor (lca(tbl, depth, eh, b) in the TRD version).

clips.text: dist(A, b): the number of edges on the path between A and b (treeDist in the TRD version).
clips.script: dist(eh, b): the number of edges on the path between eh and b (treeDist in the TRD version).

clips.text: next(x): the successor of position x under any function that gives each position one successor, such as "the furthest point one greedy step reaches"; jumping along it needs no tree (in the TRD version, stepTable(next) builds the 60 levels once and afterSteps(up, x, k) answers each query).

Tree City has n attractions, up to 2 times 10 to the 5, labelled 1 to n and joined by n minus 1 roads into a tree. A tourist at x goes on to every y greater than x that is a multiple of x, along the path between them. The length of that trip is the number of attractions on the path, counting x and y. Print the sum of the lengths over all such pairs. In the sample, the trip from 2 to 6 passes 2, 8, 10, 1, 4 and 6, so its length is 6, and the 17 trips add up to 55.

Count the pairs first. x has floor of n over x minus 1 multiples above it, and adding these up over all x gives about 2.3 times 10 to the 6 pairs when n is 2 times 10 to the 5. That many pairs is fine, but their paths are not. Walking from x to y one edge at a time costs O of depth, and on a path of 2 times 10 to the 5 vertices labelled in order the walks add up to about 2.2 times 10 to the 11 steps. A BFS from every x is no better: n searches of n steps each, 4 times 10 to the 10.

The tree is fixed and only the pairs change, so this is millions of distance queries on one tree, which is what binary lifting is for. Root the tree at 1. The path from x to y climbs from x to their lowest common ancestor, lca(x, y), and comes down to y, so it has dist(x, y) is dep of x plus dep of y minus 2 times dep of lca(x, y) edges, and one more vertex than edges. Building up of j, v costs O of n log n once, and after that every lca(x, y) costs O of log n.

A BFS from vertex 1, without recursion, gives every depth dep of v and every parent up of 0, v, with vertex 1 pointing to itself so that a jump past the top stops there. Each level doubles the one below it: up of j, v is up of j minus 1, up j minus 1, v. No vertex is 2 to the 18 deep when n is at most 2 times 10 to the 5, so 18 levels are enough: LOG is 18. The sample tree is only 3 deep, so levels 0 and 1 already cover it, and every higher level holds 1. For example, up of 1, 2 is up of 0, up 0, 2, which is up of 0, 8, so 10.

Take the pair 2 and 6. Vertex 2 is at depth 3 and 6 is at depth 2, so first lift 2 by the difference, one step: kth(2, 1) is up of 0, 2, so 8. Now 8 and 6 are level but different, so the LCA is higher up. Try the levels from the top. At j is 1, up of 1, 8 and up of 1, 6 are both 1. That is a common ancestor, but it may be above the lowest one, so neither vertex jumps.

At j is 0, up of 0, 8 is 10 and up of 0, 6 is 4 are different, so both jump, to 10 and 4. The levels have run out, and 10 and 4 are two children of the lowest common ancestor, so it is their parent: lca(2, 6) is up of 0, 10, so 1. Then dist(2, 6) is dep of 2 plus dep of 6 minus 2 times dep of 1, which is 3 plus 2 minus 0, so 5 edges, and the path has 6 vertices, as in the statement.

Doing the same for all 17 pairs of the sample gives the lengths in the table, which add up to 55. There are O of n log n pairs and each lca costs O of log n, so the whole solution is O of n log squared n, plus O of n log n to build the table. On a path of 2 times 10 to the 5 vertices the sum is about 2.2 times 10 to the 11, so it needs long long. With 2.3 times 10 to the 6 pairs, reading the table takes most of the time, so lca(A, b) skips every level whose jump is longer than dep of A: such a jump would land both vertices on the root, so it can never be taken.
clips.script: Doing the same for all 17 pairs of the sample gives the lengths in the table, which add up to 55. There are O of n log n pairs and each lca costs O of log n, so the whole solution is O of n log squared n, plus O of n log n to build the table. On a path of 2 times 10 to the 5 vertices the sum is about 2.2 times 10 to the 11, so it needs long long. With 2.3 times 10 to the 6 pairs, reading the table takes most of the time, so lca(eh, b) skips every level whose jump is longer than dep of eh: such a jump would land both vertices on the root, so it can never be taken.

clips.text: Many queries about paths between two vertices of a fixed tree: distances, whether a vertex lies on a path, the heaviest edge on a path.
For each vertex, "the highest ancestor that still satisfies X", where X is monotone along the root path (sums of positive weights, depths).
A greedy step "from position x go as far as possible" repeated many times, with many queries asking how many steps get from l to r.
Applying the same function k times with k up to 10 to the 9 or 10 to the 18: teleporters, permutations, successor graphs.

LOG must satisfy 2 to the LOG greater than the longest jump: depths up to 2 times 10 to the 5 minus 1 need LOG is 18, because 2 to the 17 is 131072 is too small, and k up to 10 to the 18 steps needs 60.
Give the root (or a sentinel such as position n plus 1) a jump to itself. Otherwise up of j of the root reads garbage or index 0, and a "jump while the condition holds" loop walks off the tree.

Fill row j only after row j minus 1 is complete for every vertex (j as the outer loop), or fill all levels of a vertex once its ancestors are done, in BFS order. A recursive DFS on a path of 2 times 10 to the 5 vertices can overflow the stack.

Minimum spanning tree that must contain a given edge: that is, MST weight minus the heaviest MST edge on the path between its endpoints plus its own weight; the path maximum comes from binary lifting (609E)
Fewest pieces or intervals covering l to r, over many queries: that is, a greedy "furthest reach" pointer next(x), and the answer is how often you apply it: jump tables over next (1516D, 1175E)

Is there one simple path through all these vertices?: that is, the deepest vertex and the deepest vertex off its root path are the ends; check dist(A, x) plus dist(x, b) is dist(A, b) with LCA (1702G2)
clips.script: Is there one simple path through all these vertices?: that is, the deepest vertex and the deepest vertex off its root path are the ends; check dist(eh, x) plus dist(x, b) is dist(eh, b) with LCA (1702G2)

clips.text: For each vertex count the descendants that "reach" it within a budget: that is, each descendant is counted by a contiguous run of ancestors; find the top of the run by lifting and add 1 along it with a tree difference array (739B)
Many paths in a tree, and for each edge count the paths that use it: that is, +1 at A and at b, minus 2 at lca(A, b), then subtree sums (191C)
clips.script: Many paths in a tree, and for each edge count the paths that use it: that is, +1 at eh and at b, minus 2 at lca(eh, b), then subtree sums (191C)

clips.text: up of j, v is v's 2 to the j-th ancestor. Depth runs left to right, and the root, 0, points to itself so a jump can't fall off the top.
Row 0 is the parent: up of 0, v is parent of v, with up of 0, 0 is 0. Each later row doubles the jump.
up of 1, 7 is up of 0, up 0, 7, which is up of 0, 6, so 5: two jumps of 1 make one of 2.
up of 1, 10 is up of 0, up 0, 10, which is up of 0, 9, so 8: two jumps of 1 make one of 2.
Row 1 is filled the same way for every vertex. A jump past the root stops there: 1 is only 1 deep, so up of 1, 1 is 0.
up of 2, 7 is up of 1, up 1, 7, which is up of 1, 5, so 3: two jumps of 2 make one of 4.
up of 2, 10 is up of 1, up 1, 10, which is up of 1, 8, so 1: two jumps of 2 make one of 4.
Row 2 is filled the same way for every vertex. A jump past the root stops there: 3 is only 3 deep, so up of 2, 3 is 0.
Query: the 5th ancestor of 7. 5 is 101 in binary, so jump 4, then 1.
Bit 2 of 5 is 1: jump 4 with up of 2, 7 is 3.
Bit 1 of 5 is 0: no jump of 2. Stay at 3.
Bit 0 of 5 is 1: jump 1 with up of 0, 3 is 2.
The 5th ancestor of 7 is 2, at depth 7 minus 5 is 2: 2 jumps instead of 5. Any k takes at most log base 2 of n.
LCA(7, 10). 7 is at depth 7 and 10 at depth 5: first lift 7 by the difference, 2, so both are level.
Bit 1 of 2 is set: 7 jumps to up of 1, 7 is 5. Both are at depth 5 now, and 5 is not 10.
up of 2, 5 is up of 2, 10, so 1: a common ancestor, but maybe above the lowest one. Don't jump.
up of 1, 5 is 3 and up of 1, 10 is 8 differ, so the LCA is higher still: both jump 2.
up of 0, 3 is up of 0, 8, so 2: a common ancestor, but maybe above the lowest one. Don't jump.
3 and 8 are now children of the meeting point, so LCA is up of 0, 3, so 2.
LCA(7, 10) is 2. The path between them has dep of 7 plus dep of 10 minus 2 times dep of 2 is 8 edges.
Binary and ternary search on the answer
Turn "find the best value" into "is this value achievable?" and binary search the boundary, or ternary search a convex cost over one free parameter.

Some questions ask for the best value outright: the most cookies you can bake, the least time in which everyone can meet, the largest gap you can keep between chosen points. There is often no formula, and trying candidates one by one is too slow: the answer can be anywhere up to 2 times 10 to the 9, and if checking one candidate is an O of n pass over n is 2 times 10 to the 5 items, a scan costs about 4 times 10 to the 14 steps.

Ask an easier question instead: is x achievable? Write ok(x) for that check. It is usually a short greedy pass, and it is monotone: if the answer can be at least x, it can be at least every smaller x, so as x grows ok(x) reads true … true, false … false and the answer is the last true. For a minimum, such as the least time, it reads false … false, true … true and the answer is the first true.

Finding where a monotone sequence switches is binary search. Keep two numbers lo and hi with the answer between them, and test the middle value mid. If ok(mid) is true the answer is at least mid, so set lo is mid; if it is false, everything from mid up fails, so set hi is mid minus 1. Each check halves the range, so 2 times 10 to the 9 candidates need about 31 checks; lastTrue in the template is this loop.

It is correct because of an invariant: ok(lo) is true and everything above hi is false. Start lo where ok is known to hold (or check it first), and each step keeps the invariant while shrinking the range, so the loop ends with lo is hi on the boundary. The true branch sets lo is mid, so mid must round up, mid is lo plus (hi minus lo plus 1) over 2, because rounding down gives mid is lo once hi, which is lo plus 1 and the loop never ends.

In total that is O of log range checks of O of n each, so O of n log range. When the answer is a real number, such as a time printed to 10 to the -6, run a fixed 60 to 100 halvings, as firstTrueReal does, instead of looping until hi minus lo less than eps. Near 10 to the 9 neighbouring doubles are about 10 to the -7 apart, so with eps is 10 to the -9 the gap never gets that small and the loop never ends.

Ternary search handles a different shape: you choose one parameter x, such as a meeting point or a shift, to minimise a cost f(x) that falls and then rises, often a max or sum of convex (V- or U-shaped) pieces like the size of A i minus x. There is no yes/no check, but comparing f at two probe points m1 less than m2, a third and two thirds of the way from lo to hi, shows which part to drop: if f(m1) less than f(m2) the minimum is not right of m2, otherwise it is not left of m1. Each round keeps 2 over 3 of the range, so argminReal runs 100 rounds. On integers, argminInt binary searches for the first x with f(x) at most f(x plus 1), the sign of f(x plus 1) minus f(x). Either way f must have no flat stretch away from the minimum.
clips.script: Ternary search handles a different shape: you choose one parameter x, such as a meeting point or a shift, to minimise a cost f(x) that falls and then rises, often a max or sum of convex (V- or U-shaped) pieces like the size of eh i minus x. There is no yes/no check, but comparing f at two probe points m1 less than m2, a third and two thirds of the way from lo to hi, shows which part to drop: if f(m1) less than f(m2) the minimum is not right of m2, otherwise it is not left of m1. Each round keeps 2 over 3 of the range, so argminReal runs 100 rounds. On integers, argminInt binary searches for the first x with f(x) at most f(x plus 1), the sign of f(x plus 1) minus f(x). Either way f must have no flat stretch away from the minimum.

clips.text: ok(x): the check "is x achievable?"; it must be monotone, true up to some point and false after it (or the reverse when minimising).

lo, hi: the ends of the range that still holds the answer. In lastTrue ok(lo) is true and everything above hi is false; in firstTrueReal (and the TRD's firstTrue) ok(hi) is true and everything below lo is false.
mid: the candidate tested in one round, halfway between lo and hi (rounded up in lastTrue).
lastTrue: the largest x in lo to hi with ok(x) true (the TRD version has firstTrue instead: the smallest x with ok(x) true, for a check that goes false … false, true … true).
firstTrueReal: the smallest real x with ok(x) true, found with 100 halvings.
f(x): in ternary search, the cost being minimised, which falls and then rises.
A i: the i-th number in the input, such as a person's position or how much of an ingredient one cookie needs.
clips.script: eh i: the i-th number in the input, such as a person's position or how much of an ingredient one cookie needs.

clips.text: m1, m2: the two probe points, a third and two thirds of the way from lo to hi.
argminReal: ternary search for the real x that minimises f.
argminInt: the integer version, the first x with f(x) at most f(x plus 1) (the TRD version's peak uses KACTL's ternSearch instead, written for a maximum).

A freight train of N wagons, up to 10 to the 9, stands in Belgium. W of the wagons, at most 10 to the 4 and given in increasing order, hold freight that must go to Luxembourg, and the rest are empty. Each of the L locomotives, at most 10 to the 4, takes a run of consecutive wagons, so the train is cut into at most L trains. A train with any freight in it goes to Luxembourg, where shorter is faster, and a train of only empty wagons can go back to the Netherlands at any length. Print the smallest possible length of the longest train to Luxembourg. In the first sample case there are 6 wagons, freight in wagons 1 and 2, and two locomotives: wagons 1 and 2 go to Luxembourg and wagons 3 to 6 go back, so the answer is 2.

N reaches 10 to the 9, so a solution can't even look at every wagon, let alone try every way to place the cuts. Asking, for D is 1, 2, 3 and so on, whether some cut keeps every train to Luxembourg within D wagons, and stopping at the first D that works, can take 10 to the 9 checks, and there are up to 100 test cases.

The statement asks for the smallest possible longest train, and a fixed limit is much easier to test. Let ok(D) say whether at most L trains can carry everything with every train to Luxembourg at most D wagons long. A cut that works for D also works for D plus 1, so ok reads false … false, true … true, and the answer is the first true. That mirrors lastTrue: keep ok(hi) true and everything below lo false, starting from lo is 1 and hi is N, because one train of all N wagons always works. A true check moves hi down to mid and a false one moves lo up to mid plus 1, so mid rounds down: rounded up, mid would equal hi once hi is lo plus 1, and a true check would leave hi where it was.

ok(D) builds the trains from the front. Let p be the first wagon not yet in a train. The next train can take D wagons, which is always allowed, or every empty wagon before next, the next freight wagon, which is allowed at any length because it goes back. Take whichever reaches further: p becomes the larger of p plus D and next. Ending a train later never hurts, because any cut of the wagons after an earlier end, with its first train trimmed, also cuts the wagons after a later end. Count the trains until p passes N; ok(D) is true if there are at most L. On the first sample case the search starts with lo is 1 and hi is 6 and checks mid is 3: one train takes wagons 1 to 3, the next takes 4 to 6, two trains in all, so ok(3) is true and hi is 3.

Next, mid is 1 plus (3 minus 1) over 2, so 2. The first train takes wagons 1 and 2. From wagon 3 there is no freight left, so the next train takes all four remaining wagons back to the Netherlands. That is longer than D, which is fine, since only trains to Luxembourg are limited. Two trains, so ok(2) is true and hi is 2.

Then mid is 1 plus (2 minus 1) over 2, so 1. With trains of one wagon, wagons 1 and 2 need a train each, and wagons 3 to 6 make a third, one more than the two locomotives. So ok(1) is false and lo is 2. Now lo and hi are both 2, and the answer is 2 after three checks. The other two sample cases give 3 and 2 the same way.

About 30 checks cover every D from 1 to 10 to the 9. Each check stops after L plus 1 trains and moves past each freight wagon once, so it costs O of W plus L, and a test case costs O of (W plus L) log N: about 6 times 10 to the 5 steps, and 6 times 10 to the 7 for 100 cases. After the last freight wagon there is nothing left to carry, so next is N plus 1 and one train takes all the remaining wagons back, as wagons 3 to 6 did in the sample. p plus D can reach 2 times 10 to the 9, just under the int limit of about 2.1 times 10 to the 9, so the solution keeps positions in long long to be safe.
The statement asks for the largest or smallest value of something (cookies, time, radius, median) and a fixed candidate is easy to test, often greedily
Feasibility is monotone in the answer: more time, a larger radius or a lower target can only make the check easier
A real-valued output with tolerance 10 to the -6 together with a question of the form "can everything fit, or everyone meet, within T"
You pick one free parameter, such as a meeting point, a shift x or a final height, and the cost is a max or sum of the size of something minus parameter terms, which is convex in it

Mid rounding: with lo is mid you must take mid, which is lo plus (hi minus lo plus 1) over 2, or the loop never ends when hi is lo plus 1. Write the invariant (ok(lo) true, everything above hi false) before coding.
Overflow inside the check: A i times guess can pass 10 to the 18. Pick hi so the products fit in long long, and stop summing once the running total exceeds the budget.
clips.script: Overflow inside the check: eh i times guess can pass 10 to the 18. Pick hi so the products fit in long long, and stop summing once the running total exceeds the budget.

clips.text: while (hi minus lo greater than 1e-9) can loop forever once doubles stop changing; use a fixed iteration count. Ternary search also needs a function with no flat stretch away from the optimum: on a plateau f(m1) is f(m2) and it can discard the side holding the minimum.
The k-th smallest value of a huge implicit set (a multiplication table, all pairwise sums): that is, binary search on the value v and count the entries at most v
Maximise the minimum, minimise the maximum, or the largest radius that still fits: that is, binary search on the threshold and check greedily whether every part can meet it
Minimum time for everyone to gather: that is, binary search on T; each person can reach an interval of positions and the check is whether all intervals intersect
Choose a point or shift that minimises a worst-case or total distance: that is, the cost is convex in that parameter, so ternary search it, even when each evaluation is itself an O of n scan

Find the largest x in 0 to 15 with ok(x): x squared at most 120, which reads true … true, then false … false. ok(0) is true, so start at lo is 0, hi is 15, and keep ok(lo) true and everything above hi false.
lo is 0, hi is 15, so mid is lo plus (hi minus lo plus 1) over 2, so 8: the middle, 7.5, rounded up.
ok(8): 8 squared is 64 at most 120, so it's true.
True, so everything up to 8 is true too: the answer is at least 8. lo is mid, so 8.
lo is 8, hi is 15, so mid is lo plus (hi minus lo plus 1) over 2, so 12: the middle, 11.5, rounded up.
ok(12): 12 squared is 144 greater than 120, so it's false.
False, so everything from 12 up is false too: the answer is below 12. hi is mid minus 1, so 11.
lo is 8, hi is 11, so mid is lo plus (hi minus lo plus 1) over 2, so 10: the middle, 9.5, rounded up.
ok(10): 10 squared is 100 at most 120, so it's true.
True, so everything up to 10 is true too: the answer is at least 10. lo is mid, so 10.
lo is 10, hi is 11, so mid is lo plus (hi minus lo plus 1) over 2, so 11: the middle, 10.5, rounded up. Rounded down it would be 10 is lo, already known true, so lo is mid would never move.
ok(11): 11 squared is 121 greater than 120, so it's false.
False, so everything from 11 up is false too: the answer is below 11. hi is mid minus 1, so 10.
lo is hi, so 10: the loop stops and 10 is the answer, after 4 checks.
Scanning 0, 1, 2, … up to the first false would take 12 checks; binary search takes about log base 2 of 16 is 4. Over 0 to 10 to the 18 that's about 60.
Ternary search for the minimum of a function that falls, then rises. Start with lo to hi is 0 to 10 and shrink it by a third each round.
Round 1: lo to hi is 0.00 to 10.00. m1 is lo plus (hi minus lo) over 3, so 3.33, m2 is hi minus (hi minus lo) over 3, so 6.67.
f(m1) is 3.464 greater than f(m2), so 1.038: the minimum can't be left of m1, where f only falls.
Drop the left third: lo is m1, so 3.33. lo to hi is now 3.33 to 10.00, 2 over 3 as wide.
Round 2: lo to hi is 3.33 to 10.00. m1 is lo plus (hi minus lo) over 3, so 5.56, m2 is hi minus (hi minus lo) over 3, so 7.78.
f(m1) is 1.155 less than f(m2), so 1.611: the minimum can't be right of m2, where f only rises.
Drop the right third: hi is m2, so 7.78. lo to hi is now 3.33 to 7.78, 2 over 3 as wide.
Round 3: lo to hi is 3.33 to 7.78. m1 is lo plus (hi minus lo) over 3, so 4.81, m2 is hi minus (hi minus lo) over 3, so 6.30.
f(m1) is 1.618 greater than f(m2), so 1.000: the minimum can't be left of m1, where f only falls.
Drop the left third: lo is m1, so 4.81. lo to hi is now 4.81 to 7.78, 2 over 3 as wide.
Round 4: lo to hi is 4.81 to 7.78. m1 is lo plus (hi minus lo) over 3, so 5.80, m2 is hi minus (hi minus lo) over 3, so 6.79.
f(m1) is 1.069 greater than f(m2), so 1.067: the minimum can't be left of m1, where f only falls.
Drop the left third: lo is m1, so 5.80. lo to hi is now 5.80 to 7.78, 2 over 3 as wide.
Round 5: lo to hi is 5.80 to 7.78. m1 is lo plus (hi minus lo) over 3, so 6.46, m2 is hi minus (hi minus lo) over 3, so 7.12.
f(m1) is 1.007 less than f(m2), so 1.188: the minimum can't be right of m2, where f only rises.
Drop the right third: hi is m2, so 7.12. lo to hi is now 5.80 to 7.12, 2 over 3 as wide.
After 5 rounds lo to hi is 5.80 to 7.12, around the true minimum at 6.30. Each round keeps 2 over 3, so 100 rounds is plenty for doubles.
Geometry: cross products, polygons and sweeps
Answer turn, side, intersection, area and inside/outside questions exactly with integer cross products, and process geometric events in sorted order with a sweep line.

Geometry questions here come with integer coordinates up to 10 to the 9 and ask something discrete: does the path turn left at this corner, do two segments touch, is a point inside a polygon, outside it or on its edge. The obvious tools, angles from atan2, slopes y over x and intersection points in doubles, are not exact. The directions (10 to the 9, 10 to the 9 minus 1) and (10 to the 9 minus 1, 10 to the 9 minus 2) differ by about 5 times 10 to the -19 radians, far below the spacing of doubles near π/4 (about 10 to the -16), so atan2 returns the same angle for both and their slopes come out equal too. Slopes also fail on vertical lines.

One exact number decides almost all of these: the cross product of two vectors, cross(A, b) is A x times b y minus A y times b x. It is twice the signed area of the triangle with corners at the origin, A and b: positive when b is counter-clockwise from A, negative when clockwise, zero when they are collinear. It needs only multiplication and subtraction, so with integer input it is exact; for the two directions that atan2 could not tell apart, it is exactly minus 1, a definite clockwise turn.
clips.script: One exact number decides almost all of these: the cross product of two vectors, cross(eh, b) is eh x times b y minus eh y times b x. It is twice the signed area of the triangle with corners at the origin, eh and b: positive when b is counter-clockwise from eh, negative when clockwise, zero when they are collinear. It needs only multiplication and subtraction, so with integer input it is exact; for the two directions that atan2 could not tell apart, it is exactly minus 1, a definite clockwise turn.

clips.text: The other tests are built from it, with each point stored as an integer vector P. orient(A, b, c) is the sign of cross(b minus A, c minus A): +1 if the walk A to b to c turns left at b, minus 1 if it turns right, 0 if the three points are collinear. Segments ab and cd cross properly when c and d lie strictly on opposite sides of ab and A and b strictly on opposite sides of cd. Otherwise they can only meet where an endpoint of one lies on the other, which onSeg(A, b, p) checks: p is collinear with A and b, and dot(A minus p, b minus p) at most 0, so p lies between them, ends included. segInter(A, b, c, d) combines the two cases.
clips.script: The other tests are built from it, with each point stored as an integer vector P. orient(eh, b, c) is the sign of cross(b minus eh, c minus eh): +1 if the walk eh to b to c turns left at b, minus 1 if it turns right, 0 if the three points are collinear. Segments ab and cd cross properly when c and d lie strictly on opposite sides of ab and eh and b strictly on opposite sides of cd. Otherwise they can only meet where an endpoint of one lies on the other, which onSeg(eh, b, p) checks: p is collinear with eh and b, and dot(eh minus p, b minus p) at most 0, so p lies between them, ends included. segInter(eh, b, c, d) combines the two cases.

clips.text: A polygon is its vertices p 0, …, p n minus 1 in order, with the last edge wrapping from p n minus 1 back to p 0. The shoelace formula area2 adds cross(p i, p i plus 1) over the edges. Each term is twice the signed area of the triangle from the origin to that edge, and the total is twice the polygon's area, positive when the vertices run counter-clockwise. inPoly tests a point by casting a ray from it to the right and counting the edges the ray crosses, an odd count meaning inside. An edge counts when exactly one of its ends is strictly above the point. So a vertex level with the point counts as below it: a ray through a vertex is counted once where the boundary crosses the line and 0 or 2 times where it only touches, and a horizontal edge never counts. The edge must also pass to the point's right, which one orient call settles: the point must be left of an upward edge or right of a downward one.

The origin triangles in the shoelace sum also cover ground outside the polygon, but each such patch is counted as often with A plus sign as with A minus sign, so it cancels. Each crossing moves the ray between inside and outside, and its far end is outside, so the parity of the count gives the answer. And every decision is an exact integer sign: with the size of coordinates at most 10 to the 9, differences reach 2 times 10 to the 9 and a cross product of differences at most 8 times 10 to the 18, inside long long (about 9.2 times 10 to the 18); anything larger, such as a product of two cross products, needs _ int128.
clips.script: The origin triangles in the shoelace sum also cover ground outside the polygon, but each such patch is counted as often with eh plus sign as with eh minus sign, so it cancels. Each crossing moves the ray between inside and outside, and its far end is outside, so the parity of the count gives the answer. And every decision is an exact integer sign: with the size of coordinates at most 10 to the 9, differences reach 2 times 10 to the 9 and a cross product of differences at most 8 times 10 to the 18, inside long long (about 9.2 times 10 to the 18); anything larger, such as a product of two cross products, needs _ int128.

clips.text: Each test is O of 1, and area and point in polygon are O of n. Print an area exactly from area2, as a whole number or a whole number and a half: twice the area can reach 8 times 10 to the 18, and a double holds integers exactly only up to 2 to the 53, about 9 times 10 to the 15. Keep floating point for a printed length only. Even angles are compared exactly: first by half-plane, upper or lower, then by the sign of their cross product. When many objects interact along one axis, such as 10 to the 5 segments where checking every pair is 5 times 10 to the 9 tests, a sweep line sorts their start and end events by coordinate and walks through them, keeping the active objects in a set or Fenwick tree. That brings the work down to about O of n log n.
P: a point with long long coordinates x and y, also used as the vector from the origin to it (the TRD version uses Point of ll, where cross and dot are member functions, as in A.cross(b)).
clips.script: P: a point with long long coordinates x and y, also used as the vector from the origin to it (the TRD version uses Point of ll, where cross and dot are member functions, as in eh.cross(b)).

clips.text: cross(A, b): A x times b y minus A y times b x, also written A times b; twice the signed area of the triangle 0, A, b, positive when b is counter-clockwise from A.
clips.script: cross(eh, b): eh x times b y minus eh y times b x, also written eh times b; twice the signed area of the triangle 0, eh, b, positive when b is counter-clockwise from eh.

clips.text: dot(A, b): A x times b x plus A y times b y, the dot product; it is at most 0 exactly when the angle between A and b is at least 90°.
clips.script: dot(eh, b): eh x times b x plus eh y times b y, the dot product; it is at most 0 exactly when the angle between eh and b is at least 90°.

clips.text: orient(A, b, c): the sign of cross(b minus A, c minus A): +1 for a left turn at b, 0 for collinear points, minus 1 for a right turn (turn in the TRD version, which calls sideOf).
clips.script: orient(eh, b, c): the sign of cross(b minus eh, c minus eh): +1 for a left turn at b, 0 for collinear points, minus 1 for a right turn (turn in the TRD version, which calls sideOf).

clips.text: onSeg(A, b, p): whether p lies on the segment from A to b, ends included (onEdge in the TRD version, which calls onSegment).
clips.script: onSeg(eh, b, p): whether p lies on the segment from eh to b, ends included (onEdge in the TRD version, which calls onSegment).

clips.text: segInter(A, b, c, d): whether the closed segments ab and cd share at least one point.
clips.script: segInter(eh, b, c, d): whether the closed segments ab and cd share at least one point.

clips.text: p i: the i-th vertex of a polygon, p 0 to p n minus 1 in order round it; p n means p 0 again.
area2(g): twice the signed area of the polygon g by the shoelace formula (polygonArea2 in the TRD version; the TRD's area2 returns its absolute value).
inPoly(g, p): 1 if p is inside the polygon g, 0 if it is on the boundary, minus 1 if outside (the TRD version's inside calls inPolygon and returns true or false, counting the boundary as inside).

A times x plus b times y plus c: for a line given as A times x plus b times y plus c is 0, with integer coefficients A, b and c (numbers here, not points), its sign at a point (x, y) says which side of the line the point is on.
clips.script: eh times x plus b times y plus c: for a line given as eh times x plus b times y plus c is 0, with integer coefficients eh, b and c (numbers here, not points), its sign at a point (x, y) says which side of the line the point is on.

clips.text: There are up to 10 to the 5 rectangles with sides parallel to the axes and integer coordinates up to 10 to the 9 in absolute value. Print 1 if the outlines of some two of them share a point, and 0 otherwise. Only the outlines count: a rectangle lying wholly inside another does not touch it. The statement also promises that no two x coordinates are equal, and no two y coordinates. In the first sample A and B overlap, so their outlines meet, and the answer is 1.
clips.script: There are up to 10 to the 5 rectangles with sides parallel to the axes and integer coordinates up to 10 to the 9 in absolute value. Print 1 if the outlines of some two of them share a point, and 0 otherwise. Only the outlines count: a rectangle lying wholly inside another does not touch it. The statement also promises that no two x coordinates are equal, and no two y coordinates. In the first sample eh and B overlap, so their outlines meet, and the answer is 1.

clips.text: The direct approach tests every pair of rectangles. With 10 to the 5 rectangles that is about 5 times 10 to the 9 pairs, each needing up to 16 tests of one edge against another, and when the answer is 0 none of them can be skipped. Testing whether two rectangles overlap is the wrong question too. In the second sample B, C and D overlap A, because they lie inside it, but no two outlines meet, so the answer is 0.
clips.script: The direct approach tests every pair of rectangles. With 10 to the 5 rectangles that is about 5 times 10 to the 9 pairs, each needing up to 16 tests of one edge against another, and when the answer is 0 none of them can be skipped. Testing whether two rectangles overlap is the wrong question too. In the second sample B, C and D overlap eh, because they lie inside it, but no two outlines meet, so the answer is 0.

clips.text: The distinct coordinates narrow down how two outlines can meet. Two vertical edges of different rectangles have different x values, so they never meet, and two horizontal edges never meet either. A corner of one rectangle cannot lie on the other's outline, since that would need an equal x or an equal y. So two outlines meet exactly where a horizontal edge of one crosses a vertical edge of the other, strictly inside both edges. To find such crossings among many axis-parallel edges, sort the vertical edges by x and process them from left to right with a sweep line.

A vertical line sweeps from left to right and stops at each of the 2n vertical edges in order of x. The set active holds the heights of the horizontal edges that the line crosses: a rectangle's bottom and top go in at its left edge and come out at its right edge. A vertical edge from y1 to y2 crosses another rectangle's horizontal edge exactly when that edge is active and its height lies strictly between y1 and y2. One lookup checks this: active.upper bound(y1) is the lowest active height above y1, and there is a crossing if it is below y2. If there is none, a left edge inserts its rectangle's two heights and a right edge erases them. In the second sample at x is 2, C's left edge runs from 10 to 12, and the lowest active height above 10 is 20, so nothing crosses it.

In the first sample the vertical edges, in order of x, are at 0, 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6. At x is 0, A's left edge finds the set empty, so nothing crosses it, and A's heights 0 and 2 go in. At x is 1, B's left edge runs from 1 to 4. The lowest active height above 1 is 2, which is below 4, so A's top edge crosses B's left edge at the point (1, 2). The sweep prints 1 after looking at two of the six edges.
clips.script: In the first sample the vertical edges, in order of x, are at 0, 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6. At x is 0, eh's left edge finds the set empty, so nothing crosses it, and eh's heights 0 and 2 go in. At x is 1, B's left edge runs from 1 to 4. The lowest active height above 1 is 2, which is below 4, so eh's top edge crosses B's left edge at the point (1, 2). The sweep prints 1 after looking at two of the six edges.

clips.text: A right edge is checked before its rectangle's heights are erased. In the second sample at x is 3, B's right edge runs from 1 to 4, and B's own heights 1 and 4 are still in the set. The lowest height above 1 is 4, B's own top edge, and 4 is not strictly below 4, so it does not count. A rectangle's own heights are always exactly y1 and y2, so the strict test never mistakes them for a crossing. C's heights, 10 and 12, are active too, but they lie above 4. After the check, 1 and 4 are erased.

A's heights, 0 and 20, go in at x is 0 and stay until x is 20. Every other rectangle lies inside A, so each of their vertical edges runs strictly between 0 and 20, and neither of A's heights is ever strictly inside one of them. At x is 11, for example, D's left edge runs from 3 to 18, the set holds only 0 and 20, and the lowest height above 3 is 20, which is not below 18. All eight vertical edges pass the check, so the sweep prints 0, as the statement requires for nested rectangles.
clips.script: eh's heights, 0 and 20, go in at x is 0 and stay until x is 20. Every other rectangle lies inside eh, so each of their vertical edges runs strictly between 0 and 20, and neither of eh's heights is ever strictly inside one of them. At x is 11, for example, D's left edge runs from 3 to 18, the set holds only 0 and 20, and the lowest height above 3 is 20, which is not below 18. All eight vertical edges pass the check, so the sweep prints 0, as the statement requires for nested rectangles.

clips.text: Sorting the 2n vertical edges takes O of n log n. Each edge then makes one lookup and two insertions or two erasures in the set, each O of log n, so the whole sweep is O of n log n, a few million steps for 10 to the 5 rectangles. The coordinates are only compared, never multiplied or added, so int is enough and nothing is ever rounded. A single rectangle has nothing to meet, so it prints 0, and the sweep stops at the first crossing it finds.
Integer coordinates up to 10 to the 9 and a yes/no or counting question about turns, sides of lines, intersections or containment
A polygon given as a vertex list, with questions about its area, convexity, orientation or which points lie inside it
Lines or segments where only the order of the objects at certain x positions, or the order of their endpoints, matters
Many axis-parallel segments or rectangles whose interactions must be counted: sort by one coordinate and sweep

Overflow: with coordinates up to 10 to the 9 a cross product of differences can reach 8 times 10 to the 18, at the edge of long long; anything larger, such as a product of two cross products, needs _ int128. Never multiply two signed values just to compare their signs.

Floating-point decisions: testing collinearity, "strictly inside" or ties with doubles and an epsilon gives wrong answers on boundary tests. Keep every predicate in integers and convert only a final length; print an area from area2 exactly, since doubles hold integers exactly only up to 2 to the 53 about 9 times 10 to the 15.

Boundary cases: points on an edge, collinear consecutive vertices, segments that touch without crossing, a ray through a vertex (use the half-open test), and the wrap-around from the last vertex back to the first.
Is a turn dangerous, or which side of a road is a point on: that is, the sign of one cross product (or of A times x plus b times y plus c), computed exactly in integers
clips.script: Is a turn dangerous, or which side of a road is a point on: that is, the sign of one cross product (or of eh times x plus b times y plus c), computed exactly in integers

clips.text: How many lines separate two points: that is, count the lines for which the two points give A times x plus b times y plus c of different signs
clips.script: How many lines separate two points: that is, count the lines for which the two points give eh times x plus b times y plus c of different signs

clips.text: Do two lines cross inside a vertical strip: that is, sort the lines by height at the left edge and look for an inversion at the right edge
Compare angles between vectors: that is, compare the (dot, the size of cross) pairs with another cross product instead of calling atan2
cross(A, b) is A x times b y minus A y times b x is one number that says which way b turns from A. Build it term by term.
clips.script: cross(eh, b) is eh x times b y minus eh y times b x is one number that says which way b turns from eh. Build it term by term.

clips.text: A x times b y is 4 times 3, so 12: the 4 times 3 rectangle.
clips.script: eh x times b y is 4 times 3, so 12: the 4 times 3 rectangle.

clips.text: Subtract A y times b x is 1 times 2, so 2, the 2 times 1 rectangle: cross(A, b) is 12 minus 2, so 10.
clips.script: Subtract eh y times b x is 1 times 2, so 2, the 2 times 1 rectangle: cross(eh, b) is 12 minus 2, so 10.

clips.text: cross(A, b) is 10 greater than 0: b is counter-clockwise from A, a left turn. 10 is also the parallelogram's area.
clips.script: cross(eh, b) is 10 greater than 0: b is counter-clockwise from eh, a left turn. 10 is also the parallelogram's area.

clips.text: Now b is (3, minus 1). A x times b y is 4 times ( minus 1), so minus 4: the 4 times 1 rectangle, negative because b points below the x-axis.
clips.script: Now b is (3, minus 1). eh x times b y is 4 times ( minus 1), so minus 4: the 4 times 1 rectangle, negative because b points below the x-axis.

clips.text: Subtract A y times b x is 1 times 3, so 3, the 3 times 1 rectangle: cross(A, b) is minus 4 minus 3, so minus 7.
clips.script: Subtract eh y times b x is 1 times 3, so 3, the 3 times 1 rectangle: cross(eh, b) is minus 4 minus 3, so minus 7.

clips.text: cross(A, b) is minus 7 less than 0: b is clockwise from A, a right turn. The parallelogram's area is still 7.
clips.script: cross(eh, b) is minus 7 less than 0: b is clockwise from eh, a right turn. The parallelogram's area is still 7.

clips.text: b is (8, 2), so 2a: cross is 4 times 2 minus 1 times 8, so 0. Zero means collinear: no turn at all.
Which way does A to b to c turn? Measure both from A: b minus A is (4, 1) and c minus A is (5, 3), then take their cross product.
clips.script: Which way does eh to b to c turn? Measure both from eh: b minus eh is (4, 1) and c minus eh is (5, 3), then take their cross product.

clips.text: orient(A, b, c): cross(b minus A, c minus A) is 4 times 3 minus 1 times 5, so 7 greater than 0, a left turn at b.
clips.script: orient(eh, b, c): cross(b minus eh, c minus eh) is 4 times 3 minus 1 times 5, so 7 greater than 0, a left turn at b.

clips.text: With c is (8, 1): c minus A is (7, 0), and cross is 4 times 0 minus 1 times 7, so minus 7 less than 0, a right turn at b.
clips.script: With c is (8, 1): c minus eh is (7, 0), and cross is 4 times 0 minus 1 times 7, so minus 7 less than 0, a right turn at b.

clips.text: Shoelace: area is the size of sum of cross(p i, p i plus 1) over 2. Each term is twice the signed area of the triangle from the origin (0, 0) to one edge.
cross(p0, p1) is 1 times 1 minus 1 times 6, so minus 5: clockwise around the origin, so it subtracts.
cross(p1, p2) is 6 times 3 minus 1 times 7, so 11: counter-clockwise around the origin, so it adds.
cross(p2, p3) is 7 times 4 minus 3 times 4, so 16: counter-clockwise around the origin, so it adds.
cross(p3, p4) is 4 times 3 minus 4 times 1, so 8: counter-clockwise around the origin, so it adds.
cross(p4, p0) is 1 times 1 minus 3 times 1, so minus 2: clockwise around the origin, so it subtracts.
Sum is 28, so the area is 28 over 2 is 14. The three added triangles cover the polygon and the two red ones outside it; the red terms, minus 5 and minus 2, cancel those. Integer input keeps it exact.
Convex hulls and the convex hull trick
Build a convex hull with the monotone chain, use it for containment and extreme-point questions, recognise hulls hiding in prefix sums and parabolas, and speed up DP with the convex hull trick.

Hull questions are about the outermost points of a set: the shortest fence around n trees, which points can be extreme in some direction, whether one shape fits inside another. A hull edge joins two points with every other point on one side of the line through them, but testing all n squared pairs against all n points is O of n cubed, about 10 to the 15 steps for n is 10 to the 5. The convex hull, the smallest convex polygon containing every point, can be built in O of n log n instead.

Walking counter-clockwise round a convex polygon, every corner is a left turn. So sort the points by x, breaking ties by y, and walk along the bottom from the leftmost point to the rightmost; that walk is the lower hull, the part of the hull seen from below. A point where the walk would turn right or go straight on lies on or above the line joining its neighbours, so it is not a corner.

Andrew's monotone chain, convexHull in the template, does this with a stack h. Scan the sorted points. Before pushing each point q, measure the turn from o, the second-to-top point of h, through A, the top one, to q: cross(o, A, q), the cross product of A minus o and q minus o, is positive for a left turn. While that turn is not a left turn, pop the top: it is not on the lower hull. A second scan from right to left builds the upper hull the same way, and joining the two chains gives the hull counter-clockwise.
clips.script: Andrew's monotone chain, convexHull in the template, does this with a stack h. Scan the sorted points. Before pushing each point q, measure the turn from o, the second-to-top point of h, through eh, the top one, to q: cross(o, eh, q), the cross product of eh minus o and q minus o, is positive for a left turn. While that turn is not a left turn, pop the top: it is not on the lower hull. A second scan from right to left builds the upper hull the same way, and joining the two chains gives the hull counter-clockwise.

clips.text: A popped point lies on or above the segment from the point below it to q, both of which are in the set, so it can never be a lower-hull corner, however many points come later. So h always holds the lower hull of the points scanned so far. Each point is pushed once and popped at most once, so each scan is O of n and the sort dominates: O of n log n in all.

The convex hull trick is the same idea for lines. In a DP like dp of i is min over j less than i of (dp of j plus m j times x i), each earlier j is a line with slope m j and intercept dp of j, and dp of i is the lowest of those lines at x is x i, a point on their lower envelope, which is a convex chain. Trying every j is O of n squared, 5 times 10 to the 11 steps for n is 10 to the 6.
