When slopes arrive in decreasing order and queries in increasing order, MonoCHT keeps the envelope in a deque L of lines (m, c), each meaning y is m times x plus c. Adding a line with add(m, c) first pops the last line l2 while useless(l1, l2, l3) says it can never again be strictly lowest, where l1 is the line before it and l3 the new one. query(x) pops from the front any line already beaten at x, since it stays beaten for every larger x.

Each line enters the deque once and leaves it at most once, so the whole DP is O of n. With unsorted queries, binary search the envelope instead of popping from the front; with unsorted slopes too, use a Li Chao tree or KACTL's LineContainer, at O of log n per operation. Many hull problems need only one chain: the lines through two points with no point strictly above them are the upper-hull edges, prefix sums drawn as points (i, S i) turn block averages into slopes so the lower hull gives the smallest averages, and parabolas y is x squared plus bx plus c become lines once you subtract x squared from y.
cross(o, A, b): the cross product of A minus o and b minus o, positive when o to A to b turns left (in the TRD version it is the member function o.cross(A, b) of Point of ll).
clips.script: cross(o, eh, b): the cross product of eh minus o and b minus o, positive when o to eh to b turns left (in the TRD version it is the member function o.cross(eh, b) of Point of ll).

clips.text: convexHull: Andrew's monotone chain, returning the hull counter-clockwise without duplicates or points in the middle of an edge (ConvexHull.h in the TRD has the same name and output).
h: the stack holding the chain built so far; its top two points and the next point form the turn being tested.
dp of i: the DP value at i, a minimum over earlier j.
m j, x i: in dp of i is min over j of (dp of j plus m j times x i), the slope that j contributes and the point at which i queries.

MonoCHT: the monotone convex hull trick, keeping the lower envelope of lines (the TRD version uses KACTL's LineContainer instead, which keeps the maximum, writes lines as k times x plus m with slope k, and takes lines and queries in any order at O of log n each; for a minimum, add( minus k, minus m) and negate query(x)).
L: the deque of lines (m, c), each meaning y is m times x plus c, in decreasing order of slope.
add(m, c): adds the line y is m times x plus c at the back, first popping the lines it makes useless.
query(x): the lowest value of the lines at x, after popping lines from the front that can no longer be lowest.
useless(l1, l2, l3): for the last two lines l1, l2 of L and a new line l3, true when l2 is never strictly below both l1 and l3, so l2 can go.
A i, b j: input numbers, as in the disguise dp of i is min j dp of j plus b j times A i, where b j becomes line j's slope and A i the query point.
clips.script: eh i, b j: input numbers, as in the disguise dp of i is min j dp of j plus b j times eh i, where b j becomes line j's slope and eh i the query point.

clips.text: S i: the prefix sum A 1 plus … plus A i, with S 0 is 0.
clips.script: S i: the prefix sum eh 1 plus … plus eh i, with S 0 is 0.

clips.text: Up to 10 to the 6 points along a walkway, given in increasing order at positions up to 10 to the 9, must all be covered. A roof from position A to position b costs c plus (b minus A) squared, where c is a fixed charge of up to 10 to the 9, and a roof over a single point costs c. Find the cheapest set of roofs. A long roof pays the square of its length, and many short roofs pay c each time. In the sample, with c is 5000, one roof over everything costs 1041324, and a separate roof for each of the 10 points costs 50000.
clips.script: Up to 10 to the 6 points along a walkway, given in increasing order at positions up to 10 to the 9, must all be covered. A roof from position eh to position b costs c plus (b minus eh) squared, where c is a fixed charge of up to 10 to the 9, and a roof over a single point costs c. Find the cheapest set of roofs. A long roof pays the square of its length, and many short roofs pay c each time. In the sample, with c is 5000, one roof over everything costs 1041324, and a separate roof for each of the 10 points costs 50000.

clips.text: A roof only needs to start and end at points, and two roofs never need to overlap, so each roof covers a run of consecutive points. Let dp of i be the cheapest cover of the first i points, with dp of 0 is 0. If the last roof runs from point j to point i, the rest is the cheapest cover of the first j minus 1 points, so dp of i is the minimum over j at most i of dp of j minus 1 plus c plus (x i minus x j) squared. For dp of 5 in the sample the best last roof covers points 4 and 5: dp of 3 is 6936, plus 5000, plus 34 squared, gives 13092. Trying every j for every i is about n squared over 2 steps, 5 times 10 to the 11 for 10 to the 6 points.

Expand the square: (x i minus x j) squared is x i squared minus 2 times x j times x i plus x j squared. The terms x i squared and c do not depend on j, and the only term that mixes i and j is minus 2 times x j times x i. So each j is a line with slope minus 2 times x j and intercept dp of j minus 1 plus x j squared, and dp of i is x i squared plus c plus the lowest of those lines at x i. The positions increase, so the slopes arrive in decreasing order and the query points in increasing order, which is what MonoCHT from the template needs. At i is 2 the lines are those of points 1 and 2. At x is 23 line 1 is lower, at minus 45, so dp of 2 is 23 squared plus 5000 minus 45, so 5484.

For each i from 1 to n, first add the line of the roof that starts at point i, with add( minus 2 times x i, dp of i minus 1 plus x i squared), then set dp of i is x i squared plus c plus query(x i). Adding first lets a roof cover point i alone. add pops lines from the back of the deque L while useless says they can never again be strictly lowest. At i is 3 the new line has slope minus 90 and intercept 7509. It meets line 1 at x about 85.3, where line 2 is about 1604, far above both, and on either side line 1 or line 3 is lower still. So line 2 is popped: for every later point, a roof starting at point 1 or 3 is at least as cheap as one starting at point 2. query(45) still finds line 1 lowest, at minus 89, so dp of 3 is 6936.

At i is 5 the deque holds lines 1, 3 and 4 and the new line 5. At x is 101 they give minus 201, minus 1581, minus 2109 and minus 845. query compares the first two lines and pops the front one while the second is at least as low: line 3 beats line 1, then line 4 beats line 3, and line 5 does not beat line 4. Each popped line has a gentler slope than the line that beat it, so it stays higher for every larger x, and the queries only move right. Line 4 is now in front, so the last roof starts at point 4, and dp of 5 is 101 squared plus 5000 minus 2109, so 13092, the split shown earlier.

The run ends with dp of 10 is 30726. Following each dp of i back to the point where its last roof starts gives five roofs: points 1 to 4, 5 and 6, 7 alone, 8 alone, and 9 and 10, costing 9356, 5529, 5000, 5000 and 5841. Each line is added once and popped at most once, so the DP is O of n. x i squared reaches 10 to the 18, still inside long long, and the statement promises that the answer fits. The useless test multiplies an intercept difference of up to about 10 to the 18 by a slope difference of up to 2 times 10 to the 9, so it needs _ int128, as in the template. Two points at the same position give two lines with the same slope, and the template's tests still give the right answer.
Questions about the outermost points of a set: the length of a fence around everything, which points can be extreme, whether one shape fits inside another
A DP transition dp of i is min or max over j of (dp of j plus f(j) times g(i)), a product of something about j and something about i, with n up to 10 to the 5 or 10 to the 6
Averages, slopes or rates built from prefix sums, such as choosing blocks with the smallest average
Curves like y is x squared plus bx plus c through pairs of points, which become straight lines after a change of variables

Collinear and duplicate points: decide whether points on hull edges belong to the hull (popping on at most 0, as in the template, drops them) and remove duplicates first; a hull of one or two points must still work.

Overflow in the convex hull trick: the test for a useless line multiplies an intercept difference (up to about 10 to the 18) by a slope difference, so use _ int128 or long double. Lines with equal slopes need explicit handling (keep the better intercept).

The monotone trick assumes sorted slopes and sorted queries. If queries are unsorted, binary search over the envelope instead of popping from the front; if slopes are unsorted too, use a Li Chao tree.

Repeatedly averaging segments to get the lexicographically smallest sequence: that is, the lower convex hull of the prefix-sum points (i, S i); each hull edge is a block whose value is the edge's slope
Parabolas y is x squared plus bx plus c with no point strictly above: that is, set Y is y minus x squared, which turns them into lines, and count upper-hull edges

Splitting time between activities with different rates to reach several targets: that is, the achievable rates form the convex hull of the activity vectors; find where the ray towards the target leaves it
dp of i is min j dp of j plus b j times A i with sorted A and b: that is, each j is a line with slope b j, and each step is a query on the lower envelope
clips.script: dp of i is min j dp of j plus b j times eh i with sorted eh and b: that is, each j is a line with slope b j, and each step is a query on the lower envelope

clips.text: Andrew's monotone chain. The labels number the points sorted by x, then y: 1 (1, 2), 2 (2, 4), 3 (3, 1), 4 (4, 3), 5 (5, 0), 6 (6, 4), 7 (7, 2), 8 (9, 3). Scan left to right for the lower hull, keeping only left turns.
Lower hull: push 1 and 2. A stack of fewer than two points has no turn to check.
Turn 1, then 2, then 3: cross is minus 5 at most 0, a right turn, so 2 isn't on the lower hull. Pop 2.
Only 1 is left, so there's no turn to check. Push 3.
Turn 1, then 3, then 4: cross is 5 greater than 0, a left turn. Push 4.
Turn 3, then 4, then 5: cross is minus 5 at most 0, a right turn, so 4 isn't on the lower hull. Pop 4.
Turn 1, then 3, then 5: cross is 0, a straight line, so 3 adds nothing. Pop 3.
Only 1 is left, so there's no turn to check. Push 5.
Turn 1, then 5, then 6: cross is 18 greater than 0, a left turn. Push 6.
Turn 5, then 6, then 7: cross is minus 6 at most 0, a right turn, so 6 isn't on the lower hull. Pop 6.
Turn 1, then 5, then 7: cross is 12 greater than 0, a left turn. Push 7.
Turn 5, then 7, then 8: cross is minus 2 at most 0, a right turn, so 7 isn't on the lower hull. Pop 7.
Turn 1, then 5, then 8: cross is 20 greater than 0, a left turn. Push 8.
Lower hull: 1, then 5, then 8. Every point was pushed once and popped at most once.
Upper hull, right to left: push 8 and 7. A stack of fewer than two points has no turn to check.
Turn 8, then 7, then 6: cross is minus 5 at most 0, a right turn, so 7 isn't on the upper hull. Pop 7.
Only 8 is left, so there's no turn to check. Push 6.
Turn 8, then 6, then 5: cross is 13 greater than 0, a left turn. Push 5.
Turn 6, then 5, then 4: cross is minus 7 at most 0, a right turn, so 5 isn't on the upper hull. Pop 5.
Turn 8, then 6, then 4: cross is 5 greater than 0, a left turn. Push 4.
Turn 6, then 4, then 3: cross is 3 greater than 0, a left turn. Push 3.
Turn 4, then 3, then 2: cross is minus 5 at most 0, a right turn, so 3 isn't on the upper hull. Pop 3.
Turn 6, then 4, then 2: cross is minus 4 at most 0, a right turn, so 4 isn't on the upper hull. Pop 4.
Turn 8, then 6, then 2: cross is 4 greater than 0, a left turn. Push 2.
Turn 6, then 2, then 1: cross is 8 greater than 0, a left turn. Push 1.
Upper hull: 8, then 6, then 2, then 1. Together with the lower hull it goes all the way round.

Hull: 1, 5, 8, 6, 2. Points 3, 4, 7 are inside or on an edge. O of n log n to sort, O of n per scan. Popping only on cross less than 0 keeps collinear points, but then input that is all on one line comes back with its middle points twice.
Each query counts positions i in l up to r with s i is s i plus 1. Whether a single position i counts does not depend on the query at all.
Mark c i is 1 when s i is s i plus 1. Every query is then a sum of c over a range, a prefix-sum query; with 10 to the 5 queries you cannot rescan the string each time.
Build P of k is c 1 plus … plus c k with P of 0, so 0 and answer each query with P of r minus 1 minus P of l minus 1. O of n plus m overall.

Let c i is 1 if s i is s i plus 1 (1 at most i less than n) and P of k is c 1 plus … plus c k. A query counts i from l to r minus 1, which is P of r minus 1 minus P of l minus 1. Using P of r instead of P of r minus 1 is the usual wrong answer: it also counts the pair (r, r plus 1), which lies outside the query. O of n plus m.
Both question types ask for the total cost of stones l to r, once in the original order and once in sorted order. The stones never change between questions.
Two fixed orders means two prefix-sum arrays: one over the costs as given, one over the costs sorted. Each question is then a single subtraction.

Copy v, sort the copy, build P over v and Q over the sorted copy, and print P of r minus P of l minus 1 or Q of r minus Q of l minus 1. Keep the sums in 64 bits: 10 to the 5 stones of cost 10 to the 9 overflow int.

Build prefix sums P over the original costs and Q over the sorted costs. Type 1 prints P of r minus P of l minus 1 and type 2 prints Q of r minus Q of l minus 1. O of n log n plus m. The totals reach 10 to the 14, so both arrays and the output must be long long; that is the only common wrong answer.
Iulia’s juice is her date’s juice exactly when (odd-glass juice) minus (even-glass juice) is zero over the chosen range. What if every even-numbered glass counted with A minus sign?
clips.script: Iulia’s juice is her date’s juice exactly when (odd-glass juice) minus (even-glass juice) is zero over the chosen range. What if every even-numbered glass counted with eh minus sign?

clips.text: With b i is A i for odd i and b i is minus A i for even i, you need a non-empty block of b with sum 0. A block sum P of r minus P of l minus 1 is zero exactly when two prefix sums are equal, so the question becomes "does the prefix array contain a repeated value?".
clips.script: With b i is eh i for odd i and b i is minus eh i for even i, you need a non-empty block of b with sum 0. A block sum P of r minus P of l minus 1 is zero exactly when two prefix sums are equal, so the question becomes "does the prefix array contain a repeated value?".

clips.text: Compute P of 0 is 0 and P from 1 to n with the signed amounts, sort the n plus 1 values (or insert them into a set) and check for a duplicate. O of n log n per test; avoid unordered map here, it is a known anti-hash target.

Negate the even-numbered glasses: b i is A i for odd i, minus A i for even i. A range l to r is balanced exactly when b l plus … plus b r is 0 exactly when P of r is P of l minus 1. So the answer is YES exactly when the values P from 0 to n contain a duplicate; sort them and compare neighbours. The sums reach 2 times 10 to the 14, so use long long, and leaving out P of 0 misses ranges that start at the first glass.
clips.script: Negate the even-numbered glasses: b i is eh i for odd i, minus eh i for even i. A range l to r is balanced exactly when b l plus … plus b r is 0 exactly when P of r is P of l minus 1. So the answer is YES exactly when the values P from 0 to n contain a duplicate; sort them and compare neighbours. The sums reach 2 times 10 to the 14, so use long long, and leaving out P of 0 misses ranges that start at the first glass.

clips.text: If you remove A i, the new increasing run through the gap is a run ending at A i minus 1 glued to a run starting at A i plus 1, provided A i minus 1 less than A i plus 1. How could you know those two run lengths in O of 1 for every i?
clips.script: If you remove eh i, the new increasing run through the gap is a run ending at eh i minus 1 glued to a run starting at eh i plus 1, provided eh i minus 1 less than eh i plus 1. How could you know those two run lengths in O of 1 for every i?

clips.text: This is the left/right precomputation pattern: L of i is the length of the strictly increasing run ending at i (filled left to right) and R of i the length of the run starting at i (filled right to left). With both arrays, each possible removal is evaluated in O of 1.
Answer is max(max over i of L of i, max over interior i with A i minus 1 less than A i plus 1 of L of i minus 1 plus R of i plus 1). Two passes to build L and R and one scan to combine them: O of n.
clips.script: Answer is max(max over i of L of i, max over interior i with eh i minus 1 less than eh i plus 1 of L of i minus 1 plus R of i plus 1). Two passes to build L and R and one scan to combine them: O of n.

clips.text: Compute L of i is L of i minus 1 plus 1 if A i minus 1 less than A i else 1, and R of i symmetrically from the right. With no removal the answer is max L of i. Removing an interior A i joins the two runs when A i minus 1 less than A i plus 1, giving L of i minus 1 plus R of i plus 1. Take the maximum of all candidates in O of n. The common miss is forgetting the no-removal case, which is the answer for an already increasing array such as the second sample.
clips.script: Compute L of i is L of i minus 1 plus 1 if eh i minus 1 less than eh i else 1, and R of i symmetrically from the right. With no removal the answer is max L of i. Removing an interior eh i joins the two runs when eh i minus 1 less than eh i plus 1, giving L of i minus 1 plus R of i plus 1. Take the maximum of all candidates in O of n. The common miss is forgetting the no-removal case, which is the answer for an already increasing array such as the second sample.

clips.text: Brightness changes with time, so one 2D prefix sum of brightness cannot serve every view. But c at most 10, and each star’s brightness cycles with period c plus 1. What do all stars that start with the same brightness have in common at time t?

Group the stars by initial brightness s (at most 11 groups). Every star in group s has brightness (s plus t) mod (c plus 1) at time t, so for each group you only need how many of its stars lie in the rectangle: one 2D prefix count per group on the 100 times 100 sky.

Build cnt of s, x, y and turn each layer into a 2D prefix sum. For a view, for every s get the rectangle count k s by inclusion–exclusion and add k s times ((s plus t) mod (c plus 1)). O of c times 100 squared plus q times c.

Let cnt of s, x, y count the stars at (x, y) with initial brightness s, and make each of the c plus 1 layers a 2D prefix sum. A view (t, x1, y1, x2, y2) adds, for each s from 0 to c, k is S of x2, y2 minus S of x1 minus 1, y2 minus S of x2, y1 minus 1 plus S of x1 minus 1, y1 minus 1 times (s plus t) mod (c plus 1). Several stars can share a point, so count rather than mark, and the rectangle includes its border. O of c times 100 squared plus q times c.
The condition "sum is length" compares two quantities that both grow with the subarray. Can you charge the length to the elements one at a time?

The sum of A l to A r is r minus l plus 1 exactly when the sum of (A i minus 1) over l to r is 0. With prefix sums P of A i minus 1 that means P of r is P of l minus 1, so you are counting pairs of equal prefix values.
clips.script: The sum of eh l to eh r is r minus l plus 1 exactly when the sum of (eh i minus 1) over l to r is 0. With prefix sums P of eh i minus 1 that means P of r is P of l minus 1, so you are counting pairs of equal prefix values.

clips.text: Walk left to right with a count of every prefix value seen so far, starting with P of 0 is 0 seen once; at each r add the count of P of r, then record P of r. P stays within minus n to 8n, so an array shifted by n works. O of n per test, answer in long long.

Replace each digit A i with A i minus 1; a good subarray is then a block with sum 0, i.e. a pair l minus 1 less than r with P of l minus 1 is P of r. Count equal pairs in one pass with a frequency table seeded with P of 0 is 0. The answer can reach about n squared over 2 is 5 times 10 to the 9, so use long long. Forgetting the initial P of 0 drops every good prefix: the second sample then gives 4 instead of 6.
clips.script: Replace each digit eh i with eh i minus 1; a good subarray is then a block with sum 0, i.e. a pair l minus 1 less than r with P of l minus 1 is P of r. Count equal pairs in one pass with a frequency table seeded with P of 0 is 0. The answer can reach about n squared over 2 is 5 times 10 to the 9, so use long long. Forgetting the initial P of 0 drops every good prefix: the second sample then gives 4 instead of 6.

clips.text: Reverse a block of odd length: does any element change the parity of its position? Then reverse a block of even length and watch what happens to neighbouring pairs.

An odd-length reversal keeps every element on its parity, so it never helps. An even-length reversal starting at l has the same effect on the even-position sum as swapping each pair (l, l plus 1), (l plus 2, l plus 3), …, so each pair has a fixed gain and you want the contiguous run of pairs with the largest total gain: a maximum subarray sum.

Build two gain arrays: pairs (0,1), (2,3), … with gain A of 2i plus 1 minus A of 2i, and pairs (1,2), (3,4), … with gain A of 2i minus 1 minus A of 2i. For each, the best block is max over r of P of r minus min over l at most r of P of l (at least 0, the empty block). Add the larger one to the initial even sum. O of n.
clips.script: Build two gain arrays: pairs (0,1), (2,3), … with gain eh of 2i plus 1 minus eh of 2i, and pairs (1,2), (3,4), … with gain eh of 2i minus 1 minus eh of 2i. For each, the best block is max over r of P of r minus min over l at most r of P of l (at least 0, the empty block). Add the larger one to the initial even sum. O of n.

clips.text: Start from base is A 0 plus A 2 plus …. Only even-length reversals matter, and they act as swaps of aligned pairs. Blocks starting at an even index give gains A 2i plus 1 minus A 2i; blocks starting at an odd index give gains A 2i minus 1 minus A 2i. The answer is base plus the larger maximum subarray sum (empty allowed, so never negative) of the two gain arrays, each computed with a running prefix minimum in O of n. Sums reach 2 times 10 to the 14, so use long long.
clips.script: Start from base is eh 0 plus eh 2 plus …. Only even-length reversals matter, and they act as swaps of aligned pairs. Blocks starting at an even index give gains eh 2i plus 1 minus eh 2i; blocks starting at an odd index give gains eh 2i minus 1 minus eh 2i. The answer is base plus the larger maximum subarray sum (empty allowed, so never negative) of the two gain arrays, each computed with a running prefix minimum in O of n. Sums reach 2 times 10 to the 14, so use long long.

clips.text: If the whole array sums to S, what must each of the three parts sum to? What does that force the prefix sum to be at each of the two cut points?

The parts are equal exactly when S is divisible by 3, the first part ends at some p with P of p is S over 3, and the second ends at some q greater than p with P of q is 2S over 3 (the third part then sums to S over 3 automatically). So you are counting pairs p less than q, which one left-to-right pass with a running count handles.

If S mod 3 is not 0, print 0. Otherwise scan q from 2 to n minus 1: first add 1 to cnt if P of q minus 1 is S over 3 (p is q minus 1 becomes available), then if P of q is 2S over 3 add cnt to the answer. O of n, answer in long long.

Let P be the prefix sums and S is P of n. If S is not divisible by 3 the answer is 0. Otherwise count pairs 1 at most p less than q at most n minus 1 with P of p is S over 3 and P of q is 2S over 3 by sweeping q and keeping how many valid p lie strictly before it. The strict p less than q matters when S is 0 (then S over 3 is 2S over 3, as in an all-zero array), q must stop at n minus 1 so the third part is non-empty, and the count reaches about n squared over 2, so use long long. O of n.
There are up to 2 times 10 to the 5 recipes, each covering a range of temperatures. Adding 1 to every temperature of every recipe is too slow; what is the cheapest way to record "+1 on l to r"?

Record each recipe as d of l plus-equals 1, d of r plus 1 minus-equals 1; one prefix pass over d gives how many recipes recommend each temperature. A question then asks how many temperatures in A to b are admissible, which is an ordinary prefix sum over zero-one admissible flags.
clips.script: Record each recipe as d of l plus-equals 1, d of r plus 1 minus-equals 1; one prefix pass over d gives how many recipes recommend each temperature. A question then asks how many temperatures in eh to b are admissible, which is an ordinary prefix sum over zero-one admissible flags.

clips.text: Temperatures are at most 200000, so plain arrays work. In one pass: cover of t is cover of t minus 1 plus d of t and good of t is good of t minus 1 plus (cover of t at least k). Answer good of b minus good of A minus 1. O of n plus q plus 200000.
clips.script: Temperatures are at most 200000, so plain arrays work. In one pass: cover of t is cover of t minus 1 plus d of t and good of t is good of t minus 1 plus (cover of t at least k). Answer good of b minus good of eh minus 1. O of n plus q plus 200000.

clips.text: Mark every recipe in a difference array (d of l plus plus, d of r plus 1 minus minus), prefix it to get the number of recipes per temperature, turn that into a zero-one admissible flag, and prefix the flags. Each question is good of b minus good of A minus 1. Allocate room for index 200001, where the closing update of a recipe ending at 200000 lands. O of n plus q plus T with T is 200000.
clips.script: Mark every recipe in a difference array (d of l plus plus, d of r plus 1 minus minus), prefix it to get the number of recipes per temperature, turn that into a zero-one admissible flag, and prefix the flags. Each question is good of b minus good of eh minus 1. Allocate room for index 200001, where the closing update of a recipe ending at 200000 lands. O of n plus q plus T with T is 200000.

clips.text: Each query applies a whole range of operations, and each operation adds to a whole range of the array. What single number do you need to know about each operation before touching the array?

Two levels of range updates: a difference array over operation numbers counts how many times each operation i runs (times of i); then operation i is one range update of times of i times d i on the array, recorded in a second difference array.

For each query do times of x plus plus, times of y plus 1 minus minus, and prefix it. Then for each operation add times of i times d i at l i and subtract it at r i plus 1 in the array’s difference array, prefix that and add it to A. O of n plus m plus k, all in long long.
clips.script: For each query do times of x plus plus, times of y plus 1 minus minus, and prefix it. Then for each operation add times of i times d i at l i and subtract it at r i plus 1 in the array’s difference array, prefix that and add it to eh. O of n plus m plus k, all in long long.

clips.text: First difference array over operations: each query (x, y) does times of x plus plus, times of y plus 1 minus minus; after a prefix pass times of i is how often operation i runs. Second difference array over the array: operation i adds times of i times d i on l i to r i. Prefix it and add the initial A. Values reach 10 to the 5 times 10 to the 5 times 10 to the 5 is 10 to the 15, so 32-bit ints overflow; that is the common wrong answer. O of n plus m plus k.
clips.script: First difference array over operations: each query (x, y) does times of x plus plus, times of y plus 1 minus minus; after a prefix pass times of i is how often operation i runs. Second difference array over the array: operation i adds times of i times d i on l i to r i. Prefix it and add the initial eh. Values reach 10 to the 5 times 10 to the 5 times 10 to the 5 is 10 to the 15, so 32-bit ints overflow; that is the common wrong answer. O of n plus m plus k.

clips.text: Write the total of all query answers as a sum over positions: each position contributes its value times the number of queries that cover it. Which positions deserve the biggest values?

How often each position is covered depends only on the queries, and one difference array (+1 at l, minus 1 at r plus 1, then prefix) gives all those counts. What is left is a rearrangement problem: put the largest value on the most-covered position.
Compute freq of i with the difference array, sort freq and sort A, and add A of i times freq of i at matching ranks. O of n log n plus q, answer in long long.
clips.script: Compute freq of i with the difference array, sort freq and sort eh, and add eh of i times freq of i at matching ranks. O of n log n plus q, answer in long long.

clips.text: The total is sum of A i times freq i, where freq i is the number of queries covering position i. Compute freq with a difference array, then sort both freq and the values and multiply them rank by rank (largest with largest). Filling freq by looping over every query range is O of n times q and times out, and the answer reaches about 8 times 10 to the 15, so use long long.
clips.script: The total is sum of eh i times freq i, where freq i is the number of queries covering position i. Compute freq with a difference array, then sort both freq and the values and multiply them rank by rank (largest with largest). Filling freq by looping over every query range is O of n times q and times out, and the answer reaches about 8 times 10 to the 15, so use long long.

clips.text: Follow one sort of tea instead of one taster: tea i is offered to tasters i, i plus 1, i plus 2, … in that order, each taking up to b j. When does it run out?

With prefix sums B of b, tasters i to j all drink their full b j from tea i as long as B of j minus B of i minus 1 at most A i; binary search finds the last such j, and taster j plus 1 gets whatever is left. "Tasters i to j each drink their full amount once more" is a range update, so record it in a difference array of counts.
clips.script: With prefix sums B of b, tasters i to j all drink their full b j from tea i as long as B of j minus B of i minus 1 at most eh i; binary search finds the last such j, and taster j plus 1 gets whatever is left. "Tasters i to j each drink their full amount once more" is a range update, so record it in a difference array of counts.

clips.text: For each tea i: find the largest j with B of j at most B of i minus 1 plus A i, do cnt of i plus plus, cnt of j plus 1 minus minus, and if j less than n add A i minus (B of j minus B of i minus 1) to extra of j plus 1. After prefixing cnt, taster k drinks cnt k times b k plus extra k. O of n log n.
clips.script: For each tea i: find the largest j with B of j at most B of i minus 1 plus eh i, do cnt of i plus plus, cnt of j plus 1 minus minus, and if j less than n add eh i minus (B of j minus B of i minus 1) to extra of j plus 1. After prefixing cnt, taster k drinks cnt k times b k plus extra k. O of n log n.

clips.text: Each tea i is drunk by tasters i, i plus 1, … in order. Using prefix sums B of b, binary search the largest j at least i minus 1 with B of j minus B of i minus 1 at most A i: tasters i to j drink in full (range +1 on a count difference array) and, if j less than n, taster j plus 1 drinks the remainder A i minus (B of j minus B of i minus 1). Taster k’s total is (prefix of counts at k) times b k plus remainder k. Totals reach about 2 times 10 to the 14, so use long long; simulating the steps directly is O of n squared.
clips.script: Each tea i is drunk by tasters i, i plus 1, … in order. Using prefix sums B of b, binary search the largest j at least i minus 1 with B of j minus B of i minus 1 at most eh i: tasters i to j drink in full (range +1 on a count difference array) and, if j less than n, taster j plus 1 drinks the remainder eh i minus (B of j minus B of i minus 1). Taster k’s total is (prefix of counts at k) times b k plus remainder k. Totals reach about 2 times 10 to the 14, so use long long; simulating the steps directly is O of n squared.

clips.text: Coordinates go up to 10 to the 18, so you cannot keep a counter for every point. Between two consecutive segment endpoints, can the number of covering segments change?

This is a difference array without the array: each segment contributes +1 at l and minus 1 at r plus 1, and coverage only changes at those 2n event coordinates. Sort the events and sweep; each gap between consecutive event coordinates is a block of points with the same coverage.
Sort pairs (coordinate, ±1) with the closing event at r plus 1. Walk them while tracking cover; before applying event i, add x i minus x i minus 1 to cnt of cover. O of n log n, lengths in long long.

Create events (l, +1) and (r plus 1, minus 1), sort by coordinate and sweep. Between consecutive events x i minus 1 and x i the coverage is constant, so do cnt of cover plus-equals x i minus x i minus 1 before applying event i, then print cnt from 1 to n. Closing at r instead of r plus 1 drops every right endpoint, and r plus 1 can be 10 to the 18 plus 1, so use long long. O of n log n.
Fix the target sum x. For one pair (A i, A n minus i plus 1), how many of its two numbers must be replaced: 0, 1 or 2? How does that depend on x?
clips.script: Fix the target sum x. For one pair (eh i, eh n minus i plus 1), how many of its two numbers must be replaced: 0, 1 or 2? How does that depend on x?

clips.text: For a pair with lo is min and hi is max: cost 0 when x is lo plus hi, cost 1 when x is in lo plus 1 to hi plus k (keep one number, set the other to x minus it), otherwise 2. That is a constant cost plus a range update and a point update over x, so a difference array over x in 2 to 2k gives the total cost for every x at once.
Start every x at n (2 per pair). For each pair add minus 1 on lo plus 1 to hi plus k and another minus 1 at x is lo plus hi. Prefix over x from 2 to 2k and take the minimum. O of n plus k per test.

Each x in 2 to 2k costs 2 per pair by default. A pair (u, v) with lo at most hi needs one replacement when lo plus 1 at most x at most hi plus k (the kept number plus a new value in 1 to k reaches x) and none when x is u plus v. Encode the minus 1 range and the minus 1 point in a difference array over x, prefix it, and take the minimum of n plus diff over all x. Size the array 2k plus 2 so the closing index hi plus k plus 1 fits. O of n plus k per test, which is fine because sum of k at most 2 times 10 to the 5.
Because x at most y at most z, the only triangle inequality that can fail is x plus y greater than z. So a choice of (x, y) matters only through s is x plus y. How many pairs (x, y) give each sum s?

For a fixed x, y ranges over B to C, so x adds +1 to every s in x plus B to x plus C: a range update. A difference array over s (at most B plus C at most 10 to the 6) gives ways of s for every s after one prefix pass.
For each s the valid z are C at most z at most min(D, s minus 1), so add ways of s times max(0, min(D, s minus 1) minus C plus 1). O of B plus C, answer in long long.

With x at most y at most z the triangle condition reduces to x plus y greater than z. For each x in A to B add +1 on the sums x plus B to x plus C in a difference array; prefixing gives ways of s, the number of (x, y) pairs with sum s. The answer is sum of over s of ways of s times max(0, min(D, s minus 1) minus C plus 1). The count can be around 10 to the 15, so use long long. O of B plus C.
clips.script: With x at most y at most z the triangle condition reduces to x plus y greater than z. For each x in eh to B add +1 on the sums x plus B to x plus C in a difference array; prefixing gives ways of s, the number of (x, y) pairs with sum s. The answer is sum of over s of ways of s times max(0, min(D, s minus 1) minus C plus 1). The count can be around 10 to the 15, so use long long. O of B plus C.

clips.text: Look at the last element b n. Which progressions reach it, and which of them adds the most to it? Once b n is satisfied, does the same argument work for b n minus 1?

Greedy from the right: the rightmost unsatisfied position i should get progressions that end exactly at i (or at k when i less than k), because they add the maximum possible amount to i and as much as possible to the positions on its left. Applying "k, k minus 1, …, 1" fast is a range update of a range update: track how many progressions are active and their total at the current position.

Sweep i from n down to 1 keeping sum (amount added at i) and cnt (active progressions). Moving left, sum minus-equals cnt, then cnt drops by the progressions whose left end was i plus 1 (kept in a close array). If b i greater than sum, place x is ceiling of (b i minus sum) over g progressions with g, which is min(i, k), and update the answer, sum, cnt and the close array. O of n.

Process positions from right to left. At position i every active progression adds one less than at i plus 1, so sum minus-equals cnt, then remove the progressions whose left end was i plus 1. If b i minus sum greater than 0, place x is ceiling of (b i minus sum) over g progressions with right end max(i, k) (1-indexed), where g is min(i, k) is what each adds at i; add x to the answer, x times g to sum and x to cnt, and schedule their removal at their left end. A progression ending further left gives i less and does nothing for positions to the right, so the greedy is optimal. O of n, with b up to 10 to the 12 so use long long throughout.
Suppose you already knew the best answer for every length shorter than n. What does the last piece you cut leave behind?

Let dp of len is the most pieces whose lengths add up to exactly len. The last piece is A, b or c, so dp of len is one more than the best of dp of len minus A, dp of len minus b, dp of len minus c. Greedy (cut as many of the shortest piece as possible) fails because the leftover may not be cuttable: n is 7 with pieces 5, 5, 2 leaves 1 after three 2s.
clips.script: Let dp of len is the most pieces whose lengths add up to exactly len. The last piece is eh, b or c, so dp of len is one more than the best of dp of len minus eh, dp of len minus b, dp of len minus c. Greedy (cut as many of the shortest piece as possible) fails because the leftover may not be cuttable: n is 7 with pieces 5, 5, 2 leaves 1 after three 2s.

clips.text: Set dp of 0 is 0 and every other entry to minus infinity, then for len is 1 to n take the max of dp of len minus p plus 1 over p in A, b, c with p at most len and dp of len minus p reachable. Print dp of n; O of n.
clips.script: Set dp of 0 is 0 and every other entry to minus infinity, then for len is 1 to n take the max of dp of len minus p plus 1 over p in eh, b, c with p at most len and dp of len minus p reachable. Print dp of n; O of n.

clips.text: dp of len is the maximum number of pieces whose lengths sum to exactly len, with dp of 0 is 0 and all other entries minus infinity (unreachable). For len from 1 to n, dp of len is max(dp of len minus A, dp of len minus b, dp of len minus c) plus 1, skipping a piece that is longer than len or whose source is unreachable. The statement guarantees dp of n is reachable, so print it; O of n. Initialising with 0 instead of minus infinity is the usual wrong answer: it lets an uncuttable leftover count as zero pieces.
clips.script: dp of len is the maximum number of pieces whose lengths sum to exactly len, with dp of 0 is 0 and all other entries minus infinity (unreachable). For len from 1 to n, dp of len is max(dp of len minus eh, dp of len minus b, dp of len minus c) plus 1, skipping a piece that is longer than len or whose source is unreachable. The statement guarantees dp of n is reachable, so print it; O of n. Initialising with 0 instead of minus infinity is the usual wrong answer: it lets an uncuttable leftover count as zero pieces.

clips.text: Walk the columns from left to right. To know whether you may take the top or the bottom student of column i, what is the only fact you need about the team chosen so far?

Only the row of the last chosen student matters, so put it in the state: a take/skip DP over columns with the row of the last pick as the extra index. Taking the taller student greedily fails: with columns (5 over 4) and (10 over 1), taking 5 first forces you to 1, while 4 then 10 gives 14.

Let r1 of i / r2 of i is the largest total from columns 1 to i whose last chosen student is in row 1 / row 2 (the empty team counts as 0 for both). Then r1 of i is max(r1 of i minus 1, r2 of i minus 1 plus h1 of i) and r2 of i is max(r2 of i minus 1, r1 of i minus 1 plus h2 of i); print max(r1 of n, r2 of n). O of n.

Define r1 of i and r2 of i as the maximum total height of a valid team drawn from columns 1 to i whose last chosen student is in row 1 or row 2, with r1 of 0 is r2 of 0, so 0. Either the team does not use column i, or its last pick is in column i and the pick before it is in the other row, which gives r1 of i is max(r1 of i minus 1, r2 of i minus 1 plus h1 of i) and symmetrically r2 of i is max(r2 of i minus 1, r1 of i minus 1 plus h2 of i). Print max(r1 of n, r2 of n). Heights reach 10 to the 9 and n reaches 10 to the 5, so use long long; two rolling variables give O of n time and O of 1 memory.
The only rule links today to yesterday. If you knew what Vasya did yesterday, which of today's options would be open?

Make the last day's activity part of the state: dp of i, s with s in rest, contest, sport. Greedily doing any available activity fails: on input 3 2, doing sport on day 1 forces a rest on day 2, while a contest on day 1 avoids it.

dp of i, rest is min over all s of dp of i minus 1, s plus 1; dp of i, contest is min(dp of i minus 1, rest, dp of i minus 1, sport) if A i is 1 or 3; dp of i, sport is min(dp of i minus 1, rest, dp of i minus 1, contest) if A i is 2 or 3; every other state is +infinity. Start from dp of 0, rest is 0 and print the minimum at day n; O of n.
clips.script: dp of i, rest is min over all s of dp of i minus 1, s plus 1; dp of i, contest is min(dp of i minus 1, rest, dp of i minus 1, sport) if eh i is 1 or 3; dp of i, sport is min(dp of i minus 1, rest, dp of i minus 1, contest) if eh i is 2 or 3; every other state is +infinity. Start from dp of 0, rest is 0 and print the minimum at day n; O of n.

clips.text: Let dp of i, s be the fewest rest days among the first i days when day i ends in state s (rest, contest, sport), with dp of 0, rest is 0 and unavailable states +infinity. Resting costs one and may follow anything; a contest may follow rest or sport when A i has bit 0 set (A i is 1 or 3); sport may follow rest or contest when A i has bit 1 set (A i is 2 or 3). Print the minimum of the three states after day n; O of n. Reading A i as two bits avoids case-by-case mistakes for A i is 3.
clips.script: Let dp of i, s be the fewest rest days among the first i days when day i ends in state s (rest, contest, sport), with dp of 0, rest is 0 and unavailable states +infinity. Resting costs one and may follow anything; a contest may follow rest or sport when eh i has bit 0 set (eh i is 1 or 3); sport may follow rest or contest when eh i has bit 1 set (eh i is 2 or 3). Print the minimum of the three states after day n; O of n. Reading eh i as two bits avoids case-by-case mistakes for eh i is 3.

clips.text: The positions in the sequence do not matter at all. If you take one copy of the value v, is there any reason not to take every copy of v?

Taking v deletes all copies of v minus 1 and v plus 1 but no other copy of v, so the game is: choose a set of values, no two consecutive, each worth v times cnt of v. That is the no-two-adjacent take/skip DP (house robber), run over the values 1 to 10 to the 5 instead of over the array.

Count cnt of v, then dp of v is max(dp of v minus 1, dp of v minus 2 plus v times cnt of v) for v up to the largest value, and print the last entry. Use long long: the score can reach 10 to the 5 times 10 to the 5 is 10 to the 10.

Taking one copy of v removes every v minus 1 and v plus 1 but leaves the other copies of v, which you then take as well, so the answer is the best set of values with no two consecutive, where value v is worth v times cnt of v. Let dp of v be the best score using only values 1 to v: dp of v is max(dp of v minus 1, dp of v minus 2 plus v times cnt of v). Iterate over every v up to 10 to the 5, including values with count 0, for O of n plus max a total. The answer reaches 10 to the 10, so an int accumulator overflows.
Process the trees from left to right. When you decide what tree i does, which earlier tree can get in its way, and what do you need to know about it?

Tree i can only collide with tree i minus 1 (on its left) and with the point of tree i plus 1 (on its right). The one fact about the past that matters is where tree i minus 1's occupied stretch ends, which depends only on whether it fell right. So use a DP with state "did tree i fall right".

Keep stay of i (tree i stands or fell left, so it occupies up to x i) and right of i (fell right, occupying up to x i plus h i; allowed only if x i plus h i less than x i plus 1 or i is the last tree). Tree i may fall left only if x i minus h i is strictly greater than the end of the stretch in the state you come from. O of n.

Let stay of i be the most trees felled among the first i when tree i ends at x i (standing or fallen left), and right of i the same when tree i fell right. stay of i is max(stay of i minus 1, right of i minus 1) for standing, improved to stay of i minus 1 plus 1 if x i minus h i greater than x i minus 1 and to right of i minus 1 plus 1 if x i minus h i greater than x i minus 1 plus h i minus 1; right of i is max(stay of i minus 1, right of i minus 1) plus 1 when i is n or x i plus h i less than x i plus 1, and minus infinity otherwise. The first tree can always fall left, and all comparisons are strict because a fallen tree may not touch an occupied point. Print max(stay of n, right of n); x i plus h i reaches 2 times 10 to the 9, so use long long.
To count walks that end at D you do not need to know which of A, B, C the ant is on, only whether it is on D. Why are A, B and C interchangeable?
clips.script: To count walks that end at D you do not need to know which of eh, B, C the ant is on, only whether it is on D. Why are eh, B and C interchangeable?

clips.text: This is counting DP over steps with a two-value state: d of k is walks of length k that end at D, o of k is walks of length k that end at any of A, B, C. Symmetry collapses four vertices into two classes, so each step is O of 1.
clips.script: This is counting DP over steps with a two-value state: d of k is walks of length k that end at D, o of k is walks of length k that end at any of eh, B, C. Symmetry collapses four vertices into two classes, so each step is O of 1.

clips.text: From D there are 3 moves, all into the other class; from each of A, B, C there is 1 move to D and 2 moves inside the class. So d of k is o of k minus 1 and o of k is 3 times d of k minus 1 plus 2 times o of k minus 1, starting from d of 0 is 1, o of 0 is 0, all modulo 10 to the 9 plus 7. Keep only the previous step: n is 10 to the 7.
clips.script: From D there are 3 moves, all into the other class; from each of eh, B, C there is 1 move to D and 2 moves inside the class. So d of k is o of k minus 1 and o of k is 3 times d of k minus 1 plus 2 times o of k minus 1, starting from d of 0 is 1, o of 0 is 0, all modulo 10 to the 9 plus 7. Keep only the previous step: n is 10 to the 7.

clips.text: Let d be the number of walks of the current length that end at D and o the number that end at A, B or C. One step maps (d, o) to (o, 3d plus 2o), starting from (1, 0), with each value reduced modulo 10 to the 9 plus 7. After n steps print d; n is 2 gives 3 and n is 4 gives 21, matching the samples. The loop is O of n with n is 10 to the 7, which is fast; keep two variables rather than arrays of length 10 to the 7, and do the multiplication in long long.
clips.script: Let d be the number of walks of the current length that end at D and o the number that end at eh, B or C. One step maps (d, o) to (o, 3d plus 2o), starting from (1, 0), with each value reduced modulo 10 to the 9 plus 7. After n steps print d; n is 2 gives 3 and n is 4 gives 21, matching the samples. The loop is O of n with n is 10 to the 7, which is fast; keep two variables rather than arrays of length 10 to the 7, and do the multiplication in long long.

clips.text: Look at the end of a tasty dinner of length i. If the last flower is red, what is left before it? If it is white, how many flowers at the end must be white together?

A tasty dinner is a sequence of blocks, each one red flower or exactly k white flowers, so counting them is counting DP over the length: ways of i is ways of i minus 1 plus ways of i minus k. Each query asks for a sum of ways over a range of lengths, which is exactly what prefix sums answer in O of 1.

Precompute ways of 0 is 1 and ways of i is ways of i minus 1 plus (i at least k? ways of i minus k: 0) modulo 10 to the 9 plus 7 for i up to 10 to the 5, then pre of i is pre of i minus 1 plus ways of i. Answer each test with (pre of b minus pre of A minus 1 plus MOD) mod MOD; O of 10 to the 5 plus t.
clips.script: Precompute ways of 0 is 1 and ways of i is ways of i minus 1 plus (i at least k? ways of i minus k: 0) modulo 10 to the 9 plus 7 for i up to 10 to the 5, then pre of i is pre of i minus 1 plus ways of i. Answer each test with (pre of b minus pre of eh minus 1 plus MOD) mod MOD; O of 10 to the 5 plus t.

clips.text: Split a tasty dinner at its last block: either one red flower or k white ones, so ways of i is ways of i minus 1 plus ways of i minus k with ways of 0, so 1 (the empty dinner) and the second term only when i at least k. Build ways and its prefix sums once up to 10 to the 5, then each test prints pre of b minus pre of A minus 1. After reducing modulo 10 to the 9 plus 7 the difference can be negative, so add MOD before the final mod. With t up to 10 to the 5 use fast I/O; total O of 10 to the 5 plus t.
clips.script: Split a tasty dinner at its last block: either one red flower or k white ones, so ways of i is ways of i minus 1 plus ways of i minus k with ways of 0, so 1 (the empty dinner) and the second term only when i at least k. Build ways and its prefix sums once up to 10 to the 5, then each test prints pre of b minus pre of eh minus 1. After reducing modulo 10 to the 9 plus 7 the difference can be negative, so add MOD before the final mod. With t up to 10 to the 5 use fast I/O; total O of 10 to the 5 plus t.

clips.text: The absolute time keeps growing, but whether a sleep is good depends only on the hour of the day. What is the smallest description of "where Vova is" after i sleeps?

Each sleep lasts exactly h hours, so Vova wakes at the same hour he fell asleep. The state is (number of sleeps so far, current hour mod h), and each sleep has two choices, A i or A i minus 1 hours: a DP over positions whose extra state is the clock. There are only n times h at most 4 times 10 to the 6 states, so try them all instead of guessing.
clips.script: Each sleep lasts exactly h hours, so Vova wakes at the same hour he fell asleep. The state is (number of sleeps so far, current hour mod h), and each sleep has two choices, eh i or eh i minus 1 hours: a DP over positions whose extra state is the clock. There are only n times h at most 4 times 10 to the 6 states, so try them all instead of guessing.

clips.text: dp of i, t is most good sleeps among the first i when sleep i starts at hour t, minus infinity if unreachable, with dp of 0, 0 is 0. For each reachable state and each d in A i plus 1, A i plus 1 minus 1, set t' is (t plus d) mod h and dp of i plus 1, t' is max(dp of i plus 1, t', dp of i, t plus l at most t' at most r). Print the maximum of dp of n, times; O of n times h.
clips.script: dp of i, t is most good sleeps among the first i when sleep i starts at hour t, minus infinity if unreachable, with dp of 0, 0 is 0. For each reachable state and each d in eh i plus 1, eh i plus 1 minus 1, set t' is (t plus d) mod h and dp of i plus 1, t' is max(dp of i plus 1, t', dp of i, t plus l at most t' at most r). Print the maximum of dp of n, times; O of n times h.

clips.text: Because each sleep lasts exactly h hours, the next sleep starts at (t plus A i) or (t plus A i minus 1) mod h, where t is the hour the previous sleep started. Let dp of i, t be the most good sleeps among the first i when sleep i starts at hour t, with dp of 0, 0 is 0 and minus infinity elsewhere; push every reachable state forward with both choices, adding 1 when l at most t' at most r. Print the maximum over t of dp of n, t. This is O of n times h is 4 times 10 to the 6 updates with two rolling rows; the minus infinity initialisation keeps unreachable hours from leaking into the answer.
clips.script: Because each sleep lasts exactly h hours, the next sleep starts at (t plus eh i) or (t plus eh i minus 1) mod h, where t is the hour the previous sleep started. Let dp of i, t be the most good sleeps among the first i when sleep i starts at hour t, with dp of 0, 0 is 0 and minus infinity elsewhere; push every reachable state forward with both choices, adding 1 when l at most t' at most r. Print the maximum over t of dp of n, t. This is O of n times h is 4 times 10 to the 6 updates with two rolling rows; the minus infinity initialisation keeps unreachable hours from leaking into the answer.

clips.text: LIS of the reversed array is the longest strictly decreasing subsequence of A. How many positions can a strictly increasing and a strictly decreasing subsequence of the same array have in common?
clips.script: LIS of the reversed array is the longest strictly decreasing subsequence of eh. How many positions can a strictly increasing and a strictly decreasing subsequence of the same array have in common?

clips.text: At most one, the peak where they meet. Each also uses any value at most once, so a value that occurs twice or more can serve both sides (one copy each), while a value that occurs once serves only one side, apart from that single shared position.

With d values occurring at least twice and s occurring exactly once, LIS(A) plus LIS(a′) at most 2d plus s plus 1, so the beauty is at most d plus ceiling of s over 2, and this bound is reachable (1 1 3 5 5, then 1 5 3 5 1 gives 3 both ways). Count frequencies and print d plus (s plus 1) over 2.
clips.script: With d values occurring at least twice and s occurring exactly once, LIS(eh) plus LIS(a′) at most 2d plus s plus 1, so the beauty is at most d plus ceiling of s over 2, and this bound is reachable (1 1 3 5 5, then 1 5 3 5 1 gives 3 both ways). Count frequencies and print d plus (s plus 1) over 2.

clips.text: A strictly increasing and a strictly decreasing subsequence share at most one position, and each uses every value at most once. So with d values that occur at least twice and s that occur once, LIS(A) plus LIS(a′) at most 2d plus s plus 1 and the minimum of the two is at most d plus ceiling of s over 2; a suitable arrangement reaches it, for example 1 1 3 5 5, then 1 5 3 5 1. Count frequencies with a map (or after sorting) and print d plus (s plus 1) over 2; O of n log n per test. Values that occur three or more times still count only once in d, because strictness lets each side use one copy.
clips.script: A strictly increasing and a strictly decreasing subsequence share at most one position, and each uses every value at most once. So with d values that occur at least twice and s that occur once, LIS(eh) plus LIS(a′) at most 2d plus s plus 1 and the minimum of the two is at most d plus ceiling of s over 2; a suitable arrangement reaches it, for example 1 1 3 5 5, then 1 5 3 5 1. Count frequencies with a map (or after sorting) and print d plus (s plus 1) over 2; O of n log n per test. Values that occur three or more times still count only once in d, because strictness lets each side use one copy.

clips.text: Which pairs of values does bubble sort ever swap? Try a few permutations: does 3 get an edge to 1 when 3 starts before 1? When 1 starts before 3?

Two values are swapped, and so joined by an edge, exactly when they form an inversion: the larger one starts on the left. A set with no edges therefore has no inversions, so its values appear in increasing order. The maximum independent set is the longest increasing subsequence.
Do not simulate bubble sort, which is O of n squared for n is 10 to the 5. Run the O of n log n tails method on the permutation with lower bound and print the length.

Bubble sort only swaps adjacent values that are out of order, and a pair that starts inverted can only change its relative order by being swapped directly, which must happen for the array to end sorted. So G has an edge exactly between the inverted pairs (i less than j, A i greater than A j). A set of vertices with no edge between them contains no inversion, so it is an increasing subsequence, and every increasing subsequence is independent; the answer is the LIS. Compute it in O of n log n with tails; the values are distinct, so strict and non-strict agree.
clips.script: Bubble sort only swaps adjacent values that are out of order, and a pair that starts inverted can only change its relative order by being swapped directly, which must happen for the array to end sorted. So G has an edge exactly between the inverted pairs (i less than j, eh i greater than eh j). A set of vertices with no edge between them contains no inversion, so it is an increasing subsequence, and every increasing subsequence is independent; the answer is the LIS. Compute it in O of n log n with tails; the values are distinct, so strict and non-strict agree.

clips.text: This is LIS with a stricter rule: the next element must be exactly one more than the previous. For an occurrence of v at position i, which earlier elements could come right before it?

Only an earlier occurrence of v minus 1. So the LIS-style state "longest chain ending at this element" needs no binary search: dp of v is the longest chain x, x plus 1,..., v ending at an occurrence of v seen so far, and reading v sets dp of v is dp of v minus 1 plus 1.

Scan left to right with a map of int, int dp (values reach 10 to the 9), updating dp of A i is max(dp of A i, dp of A i minus 1 plus 1) and remembering the best length k and its last value x. To print indices, scan from the right taking x, then x minus 1, and so on until you have k, then print them in increasing order. O of n log n.
clips.script: Scan left to right with a map of int, int dp (values reach 10 to the 9), updating dp of eh i is max(dp of eh i, dp of eh i minus 1 plus 1) and remembering the best length k and its last value x. To print indices, scan from the right taking x, then x minus 1, and so on until you have k, then print them in increasing order. O of n log n.

clips.text: Process the array in order and keep dp of v is the length of the longest chain x, x plus 1,..., v ending at an occurrence of v seen so far; reading A i sets dp of A i is max(dp of A i, dp of A i minus 1 plus 1). Let k be the best length and x its last value. Rebuild from the right: scan i from n down to 1 and take i whenever A i is the value you are waiting for (x first, then x minus 1,...), stopping after k picks, then reverse; taking the rightmost possible occurrence each time always leaves room for the rest. Use map, or a sorted copy of the values; unordered map can be slowed down by anti-hash tests. O of n log n.
clips.script: Process the array in order and keep dp of v is the length of the longest chain x, x plus 1,..., v ending at an occurrence of v seen so far; reading eh i sets dp of eh i is max(dp of eh i, dp of eh i minus 1 plus 1). Let k be the best length and x its last value. Rebuild from the right: scan i from n down to 1 and take i whenever eh i is the value you are waiting for (x first, then x minus 1,...), stopping after k picks, then reverse; taking the rightmost possible occurrence each time always leaves room for the rest. Use map, or a sorted copy of the values; unordered map can be slowed down by anti-hash tests. O of n log n.

clips.text: First throw away the envelopes the card does not fit into. Listing a chain from the smallest envelope up, in what order do the widths appear, and what does that suggest doing before anything else?

A chain is strictly increasing in both width and height. After sorting the envelopes by width, every chain appears in that order, so the task is a longest increasing subsequence where "j can come before i" means w j less than w i and h j less than h i. With n at most 5000 the O of n squared LIS handles this two-dimensional test directly.

dp of i is 1 plus max dp of j over earlier j (in sorted order) with w j less than w i and h j less than h i, recording par of i is the best j. Take the i with the largest dp, follow par back, reverse, and print the original numbers; print 0 if no envelope fits the card. O of n squared.

Keep only envelopes with w i greater than w and h i greater than h, remembering their original numbers, and print 0 if none remain. Sort them by width, so any chain is a subsequence of the sorted list, and compute dp of i is 1 plus max dp of j over earlier j with strictly smaller width and strictly smaller height, recording the parent. Follow parents from the best end, reverse, and print the numbers from the smallest envelope up. Equal widths end up next to each other but cannot nest, which is why the test compares widths explicitly; an O of n log n version sorts ties by height descending and runs a strict LIS on heights.
The coordinates are a distraction: a replanted plant can go anywhere. Think about the plants you never touch. What must be true of their species, read from left to right?

The untouched plants keep their order, and for the borders to exist that order must be all 1s, then all 2s, and so on: a non-decreasing subsequence of the species list. Any such subsequence can be kept (move every other plant into a free spot in its section), so the answer is n minus the longest non-decreasing subsequence.

Read s i and skip x i (read it as a string). Run the tails method with upper bound, because equal species may stay side by side, and print n minus length. O of n log n; O of n squared also fits for n is 5000.

A plant that is not replanted stays where it is, so the kept plants must already read 1...1 2...2... m...m from left to right, which is a non-decreasing subsequence of s. Conversely any non-decreasing subsequence can be kept, because real coordinates leave room to place each moved plant inside its own section. The answer is n minus LNDS(s), computed with tails and upper bound. Using lower bound computes the strictly increasing version and overcounts the moves whenever a species repeats (sample 3: species 1 2 1 3 1 1 needs 2 moves, not 3). The positions are never needed.
Describe each ray by its entry hole and its exit hole. When do two rays cross? Compare their order on the entry side with their order on the exit side.

Rays p and q cross exactly when their orders disagree: p enters before q but exits after it. List the rays in entry order and write down each one's exit position; a group in which every pair crosses is a strictly decreasing subsequence of that list, so the answer is the longest decreasing subsequence.

Store exitPos of ray from the third line, form b i is exitPos of x i for i, so 1 to n, and compute the LIS of minus b i with tails and lower bound. n is 10 to the 6, so the O of n squared DP is far too slow and input must be read with scanf or a fast cin.

Two rays cross exactly when their entry order and exit order disagree. Let b i be the exit hole of the ray that enters at hole i (b i is position of x i in the third line); a group of pairwise crossing rays is then a set whose exit holes strictly decrease in entry order, so the answer is the longest strictly decreasing subsequence of b. All b i are distinct, so strict versus non-strict does not matter; negate and run the O of n log n LIS. The O of n squared DP is too slow for n is 10 to the 6, and reading two million numbers needs fast input.
Two characters of the same colour can never swap past each other. So what must be true of the characters of one colour, read left to right, if the string is to end up sorted?

Each colour class must already be non-decreasing, and that is also enough: every adjacent inversion then has two different colours, so bubble sort can finish. The question is the fewest non-decreasing subsequences that cover the string, which by Dilworth's theorem is the length of the longest strictly decreasing subsequence: those characters all need different colours, and that many colours suffice.

Let dp of i is the length of the longest strictly decreasing subsequence ending at i, so 1 plus max dp of j over j less than i with s j greater than s i. Keep best of c is the largest dp at an earlier position holding letter c, so each step scans the letters above s i. Colour position i with dp of i and print the maximum; O of 26 times n.

A colour class keeps its internal order, so it must be non-decreasing; conversely, if every class is non-decreasing, any adjacent pair that is out of order has two colours and can be swapped, so the string can be bubble-sorted. The fewest non-decreasing classes is the longest strictly decreasing subsequence (Dilworth). Colour position i with dp of i, the length of the longest strictly decreasing subsequence ending at i: two positions j less than i with s j greater than s i always get dp of i greater than dp of j, so equal colours are non-decreasing, and the number of colours is max dp. With best of c over the 26 letters this runs in O of 26 times n.
For index i to lie on some longest increasing subsequence, the best increasing run ending at i and the best one starting at i must fit together. How long must they be together?

Compute f of i is the LIS ending at i and g of i is the LIS starting at i (the LIS ending at the matching position of the reversed, negated array). Index i is on some LIS exactly when f of i plus g of i minus 1 is L. In any LIS the k-th element has f exactly k, so i is on every LIS exactly when it is the only index on some LIS with its value of f.

Run the tails routine twice, on A and on the reversed minus A, reading f of i as the position lower bound returns plus one. Print 1 when f of i plus g of i minus 1 less than L; otherwise count cnt of f i over the indices that qualify and print 3 if cnt of f i is 1, else 2. O of n log n.
clips.script: Run the tails routine twice, on eh and on the reversed minus eh, reading f of i as the position lower bound returns plus one. Print 1 when f of i plus g of i minus 1 less than L; otherwise count cnt of f i over the indices that qualify and print 3 if cnt of f i is 1, else 2. O of n log n.

clips.text: f of i, the length of the LIS ending at i, is one more than the position lower bound finds in tails; g of i, the LIS starting at i, comes from the same routine on the reversed array with negated values. If f of i plus g of i minus 1 less than L, index i is in group 1. Every LIS takes exactly one index from each level f is 1 to L, and every qualifying index at level k extends to a full LIS, so a qualifying i is in group 3 exactly when it is alone at its level and in group 2 otherwise. O of n log n. Using upper bound breaks strictness when values repeat, and reversing without negating measures decreasing runs instead of increasing ones.
Every prefix of c was built from some prefix of A and some prefix of b. If c from 0 up to i plus j used exactly i characters of A and j of b, where can its last character have come from?
clips.script: Every prefix of c was built from some prefix of eh and some prefix of b. If c from 0 up to i plus j used exactly i characters of eh and j of b, where can its last character have come from?

clips.text: This is a two-sequence DP over prefixes, shaped like edit distance: the state (i, j) says how much of A and b is used, which fixes the position i plus j minus 1 in c. The "until one runs out" rule changes nothing, since appending the rest of the other string is also an interleaving.
clips.script: This is a two-sequence DP over prefixes, shaped like edit distance: the state (i, j) says how much of eh and b is used, which fixes the position i plus j minus 1 in c. The "until one runs out" rule changes nothing, since appending the rest of the other string is also an interleaving.

clips.text: dp of i, j is fewest changed characters in c from 0 up to i plus j, which is min(dp of i minus 1, j plus A of i minus 1 is not c of i plus j minus 1, dp of i, j minus 1 plus b of j minus 1 is not c of i plus j minus 1), with dp of 0, 0 is 0. Answer dp of the size of A, the size of b, O of the size of A times the size of b per test.
clips.script: dp of i, j is fewest changed characters in c from 0 up to i plus j, which is min(dp of i minus 1, j plus eh of i minus 1 is not c of i plus j minus 1, dp of i, j minus 1 plus b of j minus 1 is not c of i plus j minus 1), with dp of 0, 0 is 0. Answer dp of the size of eh, the size of b, O of the size of eh times the size of b per test.

clips.text: Let dp of i, j be the fewest changes so that c from 0 up to i plus j is an interleaving of A from 0 up to i and b from 0 up to j. The last character c of i plus j minus 1 came either from A of i minus 1 (cost 1 if it differs) or from b of j minus 1, so take the minimum of those two transitions, guarding i greater than 0 and j greater than 0 on the borders. The answer is dp of the size of A, the size of b; the length limits keep the total work across tests to about 2 times 10⁶ cells. Greedily matching c against whichever string fits fails when A and b offer the same letter.
clips.script: Let dp of i, j be the fewest changes so that c from 0 up to i plus j is an interleaving of eh from 0 up to i and b from 0 up to j. The last character c of i plus j minus 1 came either from eh of i minus 1 (cost 1 if it differs) or from b of j minus 1, so take the minimum of those two transitions, guarding i greater than 0 and j greater than 0 on the borders. The answer is dp of the size of eh, the size of b; the length limits keep the total work across tests to about 2 times 10⁶ cells. Greedily matching c against whichever string fits fails when eh and b offer the same letter.

clips.text: Fix where the substring x ends in s and where the subsequence y takes its last character in t. What must hold for the characters of x and y before those?

It is LCS-style counting over prefixes with an asymmetry: x is contiguous, so its previous character is exactly s of i minus 1, while the previous character of y can be at any earlier position of t. So the state should mean "x ends exactly at s of i" and "y lies inside t from 1 to j".

Let f of i, j count pairs whose substring ends exactly at s of i and whose subsequence uses only t from 1 to j. Then f of i, j is f of i, j minus 1 plus (s of i is t of j? 1 plus f of i minus 1, j minus 1: 0). Answer sum of ᵢ f of i, the size of t mod 10⁹+7, in O of the size of s times the size of t with two rows.

Define f of i, j as the number of pairs whose substring ends exactly at s of i and whose subsequence uses positions of t up to j. Either the subsequence does not use t of j (f of i, j minus 1), or it ends at t of j, which needs s of i is t of j: then it is the one-letter pair (s of i, t of j) or it extends any pair counted in f of i minus 1, j minus 1. Sum f of i, the size of t over all i. That is 25 times 10⁶ cells, so keep two int rows and reduce modulo 10⁹+7 at every step. Letting the s index also mean "anywhere inside s from 1 to i" counts subsequences of s as well and overcounts; the second sample exposes it.

Read the score 4 times LCS minus the size of C minus the size of D one character at a time along the alignment: what does a matched pair contribute, and what does a character left unmatched in C or D contribute?

A matched pair adds 4 minus 1 minus 1 is +2 and every unmatched character costs minus 1, so this is LCS with scores over substrings (local alignment). Substrings mean you may start fresh anywhere with score 0 and stop anywhere, taking the best cell.

Let dp of i, j be the best score of substrings ending at A of i and B of j: dp of i, j is max(0, dp of i minus 1, j minus 1, dp of i, j minus 1 minus 1, dp of i minus 1, j minus 1 plus 2 if A of i is B of j). The answer is the maximum over all cells, O of nm.
clips.script: Let dp of i, j be the best score of substrings ending at eh of i and B of j: dp of i, j is max(0, dp of i minus 1, j minus 1, dp of i, j minus 1 minus 1, dp of i minus 1, j minus 1 plus 2 if eh of i is B of j). The answer is the maximum over all cells, O of nm.

clips.text: For fixed C and D the score is the best alignment value with +2 per matched pair and minus 1 per other character, so maximising over substrings and alignments together gives the answer. dp of i, j is best value over substrings ending at A of i and B of j: leave A of i or B of j unmatched ( minus 1 from the left or upper cell), match them when equal (+2 from the diagonal), or start empty (0). Output the maximum over all cells, not dp of n, m. 2.5 times 10⁷ cells run fast; two rolling rows keep memory small.
clips.script: For fixed C and D the score is the best alignment value with +2 per matched pair and minus 1 per other character, so maximising over substrings and alignments together gives the answer. dp of i, j is best value over substrings ending at eh of i and B of j: leave eh of i or B of j unmatched ( minus 1 from the left or upper cell), match them when equal (+2 from the diagonal), or start empty (0). Output the maximum over all cells, not dp of n, m. 2.5 times 10⁷ cells run fast; two rolling rows keep memory small.

clips.text: First merge runs of equal colours, so neighbouring squares always differ. The component grows outwards from the starting square; when can one turn swallow a new run on both sides at once?

With m runs you need m minus 1 absorptions, and a turn takes two runs exactly when the runs bordering the component on the left and right have the same colour. Those saved pairs are nested around the start, so they form a palindromic subsequence: this is LCS of the run sequence with its own reverse.
Compress to m runs, compute L is LCS(A, reverse(A)) in O of m squared with rolling rows, and answer m minus 1 minus floor of L over 2.
clips.script: Compress to m runs, compute L is LCS(eh, reverse(eh)) in O of m squared with rolling rows, and answer m minus 1 minus floor of L over 2.

clips.text: After compressing equal neighbours into m runs, every turn absorbs at least one run, and absorbs one on each side exactly when the two bordering runs share a colour. The double turns pair up equal colours nested around the starting run, i.e. a palindromic subsequence, and L is LCS(A, reverse A) is the longest one. All floor of L over 2 of its pairs can be used, because after compression the innermost equal pair is never adjacent, so a starting run fits between them. Answer m minus 1 minus floor of L over 2 in O of m squared. Skipping the compression breaks inputs such as 3 3 3, whose answer is 0.
clips.script: After compressing equal neighbours into m runs, every turn absorbs at least one run, and absorbs one on each side exactly when the two bordering runs share a colour. The double turns pair up equal colours nested around the starting run, i.e. a palindromic subsequence, and L is LCS(eh, reverse eh) is the longest one. All floor of L over 2 of its pairs can be used, because after compression the innermost equal pair is never adjacent, so a starting run fits between them. Answer m minus 1 minus floor of L over 2 in O of m squared. Skipping the compression breaks inputs such as 3 3 3, whose answer is 0.

clips.text: Each permutation contains every number exactly once. For two numbers x and y, when can y come right after x in a common subsequence?

y can follow x exactly when x is before y in all k permutations. That relation has no cycles, so the longest common subsequence is a longest path in a DAG on n vertices, not a k-dimensional LCS table.

Store pos of t, v for every permutation. Walk the first permutation in order and set dp of v is 1 plus max dp of u over earlier u with pos of t, u less than pos of t, v for every t. O of n squared times k, about 5 times 10⁶ checks.

Record the position of each number in every permutation. A sequence is a common subsequence exactly when every consecutive pair (x, y) has x before y in all k permutations, so the answer is the longest path in that DAG. The first permutation is a topological order of it, so dp of i is 1 plus max dp of j over j less than i in the first permutation whose number precedes perm of 0, i in every other permutation. Answer max dp, O of n squaredk. A k-dimensional LCS table would have 1000⁵ cells; each value appearing once keeps the problem small.
Forget k for a moment: with any number of pieces of any length, what is the maximum total length? Then ask what extra information a cell needs so you can count pieces.

Without k this is plain LCS. With k, add a third index c is pieces used so far, and separate "piece c ends exactly at s of i and t of j" (the next equal pair may extend it, keeping c) from "the best anywhere inside these prefixes".

end of c, i, j is 1 plus max(end of c, i minus 1, j minus 1, best of c minus 1, i minus 1, j minus 1) if s of i is t of j, else minus infinity; best of c, i, j is max(best of c, i minus 1, j, best of c, i, j minus 1, end of c, i, j). Answer best of k, n, m, O of nmk about 10⁷.

Keep two tables per piece count c: end of c, i, j, the best total when piece c finishes exactly with s of i and t of j, and best of c, i, j, the best total within s from 1 to i and t from 1 to j. An equal pair either extends the current piece (end of c, i minus 1, j minus 1) or opens piece c after the best placement of c minus 1 pieces (best of c minus 1, i minus 1, j minus 1); best then also allows skipping a character of s or t. Answer best of k, n, m in O of nmk. Initialise everything to minus infinity except best of 0, times, times is 0, otherwise fewer than k pieces sneak in; rolling the i dimension keeps memory to a few small arrays.

A plain LCS table does not know which letters were chosen last, so it cannot tell whether the next letter completes the virus. What is the smallest summary of the chosen letters that answers that question?

The summary is the KMP state: the length of the longest prefix of the virus that is a suffix of the subsequence built so far. Add it as a third index of the LCS DP and forbid any transition that reaches state the size of virus.

Build the automaton go of state, letter from the prefix function. f of i, j, s is longest valid continuation from s1 from i to, s2 from j to in state s is max(f of i plus 1, j, s, f of i, j plus 1, s, 1 plus f of i plus 1, j plus 1, go s, c when s1 of i is s2 of j, which is c and go of s, c less than the size of virus). Answer f of 0, 0, 0 over about 10⁶ states, then walk the table to print it.

Precompute the prefix function of the virus and go of s, c, the state after appending letter c in state s.
