Fill f of i, j, s over suffixes so that reconstruction walks forwards from (0, 0, 0): take the common letter when s1 of i is s2 of j, the new state is below the size of virus and the value matches, otherwise step i or j to a cell with the same value. Print 0 if the best length is 0. Tracking only "how many virus letters are matched" without failure links is the common bug: for virus AAB, after AAA the state is still 2, not reset to 0 or 1.

The minimum number of moves is a standard table; the new part is printing moves whose positions are valid when each is applied. In what order can you emit them so that earlier moves never shift the positions used by later ones?

This is edit distance with reconstruction. Walking the table back from (the size of s, the size of t) and printing each operation as you meet it edits the string from right to left, so positions 1 to i still hold the original s from 1 to i.

dp of i, j is min(dp of i minus 1, j minus 1 plus s of i is not t of j, dp of i minus 1, j plus 1, dp of i, j minus 1 plus 1). Backtrack from (n, m): skip free diagonal steps, otherwise print REPLACE i t of j, DELETE i or INSERT i plus 1 t of j for the transition taken. O of nm with the full table.

Fill the standard edit distance table over prefixes, keeping all 1001 times 1001 cells. Backtrack from (the size of s, the size of t): a diagonal step with equal letters is free, a diagonal step costing 1 is REPLACE i t of j, coming from (i minus 1, j) is DELETE i, and coming from (i, j minus 1) is INSERT i plus 1 t of j. Printed in backtrack order, every later move sits at a position at most i, left of everything already changed, so its index refers to the untouched original prefix. Positions are 1-based; INSERT i plus 1 with i is the size of s appends at the end, which the statement allows.

The elements do not interact: turning 1 into b i takes some minimum number of operations, and you either spend all of them and collect c i or leave the element alone. What does that make each element?

Each element is a zero-one knapsack item with weight ops of b i and value c i, and k is the capacity. ops of v is at most 12 for v at most 1000, so k up to 10⁶ is a red herring: cap it at sum of ops of b i at most 12n.

Precompute ops of v for v at most 1000: for every A and x, set ops of A plus floor of A over x to ops of A plus 1 if that is smaller. Then run dp of cap is max(dp of cap, dp of cap minus w plus c) with cap going down from min(k, sum of w). O of 1000 squared plus 12n squared.
clips.script: Precompute ops of v for v at most 1000: for every eh and x, set ops of eh plus floor of eh over x to ops of eh plus 1 if that is smaller. Then run dp of cap is max(dp of cap, dp of cap minus w plus c) with cap going down from min(k, sum of w). O of 1000 squared plus 12n squared.

clips.text: Compute ops of v, the fewest operations to reach v from 1, by processing a in increasing order and updating ops of A plus floor of A over x for every x at most a (values only grow, so this order is safe). Each index i is then a zero-one item of weight ops of b i and value c i. Cap the capacity at min(k, sum of ops of b i), at most about 12n, and run the 1D knapsack with capacity sweeping downwards; the answer is dp at the capped capacity. Without the cap, 10⁶ capacity times 1000 items is too slow.
clips.script: Compute ops of v, the fewest operations to reach v from 1, by processing a in increasing order and updating ops of eh plus floor of eh over x for every x at most a (values only grow, so this order is safe). Each index i is then a zero-one item of weight ops of b i and value c i. Cap the capacity at min(k, sum of ops of b i), at most about 12n, and run the 1D knapsack with capacity sweeping downwards; the answer is dp at the capped capacity. Without the cap, 10⁶ capacity times 1000 items is too slow.

clips.text: Dough is used by every bun, stuffing i only by buns of type i. Which resource is the knapsack capacity, and what does a stuffing amount limit?
Dough is the capacity. Stuffing i only caps how many buns of type i you can bake, at most floor of A i over b i, so the stuffed buns are a bounded knapsack and plain buns are an unbounded item.
clips.script: Dough is the capacity. Stuffing i only caps how many buns of type i you can bake, at most floor of eh i over b i, so the stuffed buns are a bounded knapsack and plain buns are an unbounded item.

clips.text: dp of g is most money using at most g grams of dough. For each stuffing, for g from n down to 0, try every count q from 1 to floor of A i over b i with q times c i at most g. Then add plain buns with one upward sweep. O of n times m times 100.
clips.script: dp of g is most money using at most g grams of dough. For each stuffing, for g from n down to 0, try every count q from 1 to floor of eh i over b i with q times c i at most g. Then add plain buns with one upward sweep. O of n times m times 100.

clips.text: Let dp of g be the most money using at most g grams of dough. Each stuffing type is a bounded item: up to floor of A i over b i copies of weight c i and value d i, handled with a downward sweep over g that tries every copy count, so the type is used once as a group. Plain buns are unbounded, so one upward sweep dp of g is max(dp of g, dp of g minus c0 plus d0) adds them. Answer dp of n. Swapping the two loop directions either reuses stuffing that does not exist or allows only one plain bun.
clips.script: Let dp of g be the most money using at most g grams of dough. Each stuffing type is a bounded item: up to floor of eh i over b i copies of weight c i and value d i, handled with a downward sweep over g that tries every copy count, so the type is used once as a group. Plain buns are unbounded, so one upward sweep dp of g is max(dp of g, dp of g minus c0 plus d0) adds them. Answer dp of n. Swapping the two loop directions either reuses stuffing that does not exist or allows only one plain bun.

clips.text: Costs and salaries go up to 10⁸, so a table indexed by money is far too large. Which number in the input is small enough to index a DP by?

Total happiness is at most 10⁵, so swap the roles: dp of h is least money spent to collect exactly h happiness. It is a zero-one knapsack with value as the index and cost as the stored quantity, plus a budget check that depends on the month.

Process months in order; before month i you have earned x times (i minus 1). For h from H down to h i, if dp of h minus h i plus c i at most x times (i minus 1), set dp of h is min(dp of h, dp of h minus h i plus c i). The answer is the largest h with a finite dp of h. O of m times sum of h.

Index by happiness: dp of h is the least total spent on offers from the months so far that give exactly h happiness (infinity if impossible). Processing months in order, a purchase in month i only needs dp of h minus h i plus c i at most x times (i minus 1): earlier purchases were checked in their own months, and keeping the minimum spend only leaves more money for later. Sweep h downwards so each offer is used once, then print the largest reachable h. x times (i minus 1) reaches about 5 times 10⁹, so use 64-bit integers.
Bob pays for some items and steals the rest. If he pays for an item with time t, how many items in total does that one payment take care of?

A paid item with time t covers itself plus t stolen items, t plus 1 in all, and Bob can always arrange the order. So you want a set of items whose (t i plus 1) add up to at least n at minimum total price: a min-cost zero-one knapsack whose capacity is "items covered".

dp of j is least money to cover j items, with j capped at n. For each item, for j from n down to 0: dp of min(n, j plus t plus 1) is min(dp of min(n, j plus t plus 1), dp of j plus c). Answer dp of n, O of n squared with 64-bit costs.

If Bob pays for a set P, he has sum of t i seconds over P to steal the other n minus the size of P items, so the condition is sum of (t i plus 1) at least n over the paid items. That is a covering knapsack: dp of j is the least money for coverage j, capped at n because extra coverage is wasted. Process items with j going downwards and target min(n, j plus t i plus 1), then print dp of n. Prices reach 10⁹ and n is 2000, so the sums need long long.
The condition sum of a / sum of b is k is awkward because it is a ratio. Can you turn it into a condition on a single sum?

sum of A is k times sum of b means sum of (A i minus k times b i), so 0. So each fruit has weight w i is A i minus k times b i (possibly negative) and value A i, and you need a non-empty set with total weight exactly 0 and maximum value: a knapsack over a sum that can go negative, stored with an offset.
clips.script: sum of eh is k times sum of b means sum of (eh i minus k times b i), so 0. So each fruit has weight w i is eh i minus k times b i (possibly negative) and value eh i, and you need a non-empty set with total weight exactly 0 and maximum value: a knapsack over a sum that can go negative, stored with an offset.

clips.text: Weights lie in minus 999 to 99, so sums lie in minus 99900 to 9900. Use dp of sum plus OFFSET, minus infinity except dp of OFFSET is 0; sweep downwards for w at least 0 and upwards for w less than 0. Answer dp of OFFSET if it is positive, else minus 1. About 10⁷ steps.

Rewrite the ratio as sum of (A i minus k times b i) is 0 and run an exact-sum zero-one knapsack over w i is A i minus k times b i that maximises sum of A i. Sums can be negative, so store them at index sum plus OFFSET with OFFSET at least 100 times 999. For a non-negative weight sweep the index downwards; for a negative weight the source index s minus w lies above s, so sweep upwards (or copy the row) to use each fruit once. Every taste is at least 1, so dp of OFFSET greater than 0 exactly when a non-empty valid salad exists; otherwise print minus 1.
clips.script: Rewrite the ratio as sum of (eh i minus k times b i) is 0 and run an exact-sum zero-one knapsack over w i is eh i minus k times b i that maximises sum of eh i. Sums can be negative, so store them at index sum plus OFFSET with OFFSET at least 100 times 999. For a non-negative weight sweep the index downwards; for a negative weight the source index s minus w lies above s, so sweep upwards (or copy the row) to use each fruit once. Every taste is at least 1, so dp of OFFSET greater than 0 exactly when a non-empty valid salad exists; otherwise print minus 1.

clips.text: You pick a set of coins that sums to k, then a subset of that set. For a single coin, what are the possible fates, and which two totals do you need to track?

Each coin is unused, used only in the payment, or used in the payment and also in the sub-sum x. That is a zero-one knapsack with two capacities, the payment total s and the sub-sum x, both at most k.

can of s, x says some coins sum to s with a subset summing to x; start from can of 0, 0. For each coin c, for s from k down to c: can of s or-equals can of s minus c or (can of s minus c shifted left by c) with can of s a bitset over x. O of n times k squared over 64; print every x with can of k, x.

Let can of s, x be true when some subset of the processed coins sums to s and has a sub-subset summing to x. A new coin c can go nowhere, into the payment only (s plus-equals c), or into both (s plus-equals c, x plus-equals c); sweeping s downwards keeps it a zero-one choice. With can of s as a bitset over x the update is can of s or-equals can of s minus c or (can of s minus c shifted left by c), about 500 times 500 times 500 over 64 word operations. Output the set bits of can of k. Computing the reachable x over all coins independently of the payment is the usual wrong answer: x must come from the same coins that pay k.
Suppose you already know which items to save. In what order should you save them so that each finishes before it burns, if that is possible at all?

Save the chosen items in increasing order of d: swapping an adjacent pair that is out of order never makes things worse. Once the order is fixed by sorting, choosing the set is a zero-one knapsack over total elapsed time, where an item can be added only if the new time is below its d.

Sort by d. dp of i, T is max value from the first i items finishing at exactly time T: dp of i, T is max(dp of i minus 1, T, dp of i minus 1, T minus t i plus p i if T less than d i), with T at most 2000. Keep the whole table, walk back from the best T, and list the items in sorted order.

By an exchange argument the saved items can be taken in non-decreasing order of d, so sort by d and treat the items as a knapsack in which each new item is appended at the end. dp of i, T is the best value using some of the first i sorted items with total time exactly T, and taking item i requires T less than d i so it finishes before burning. Keep the 101 times 2001 table, choose the best T, and walk back: whenever dp of i, T differs from dp of i minus 1, T, item i was taken and T drops by t i. Print the chosen items in sorted order with their original indices; a single rolling row loses the information needed for this walk.
W and the counts go up to 10¹⁸, but there are only 8 distinct weights. Is there a number that every weight from 1 to 8 divides, so that groups of equal items become interchangeable?

L is lcm(1 to 8), so 840. Any 840 over i items of weight i weigh exactly 840, so all but fewer than 840 over i items of each weight can be treated as identical 840-blocks. The real knapsack is only over the loose remainder, whose weight is below 8 times 840.

dp of s is most whole 840-blocks available when the loose items weigh exactly s. For weight i try r is 0 to min(cnt i, 840 over i minus 1) loose items: s grows by r times i and the blocks grow by floor of (cnt i minus r) over (840 over i). Answer max over s at most W of s plus 840 times min(dp of s, floor of (W minus s) over 840). With s at most 8 times 840 is 6720, that is about 6721 times (840 over 1 plus 840 over 2 plus … plus 840 over 8) about 1.5 times 10⁷ steps.

Write the number of weight-i items taken as r plus q times (840 over i) with 0 at most r less than 840 over i; each group of 840 over i items weighs exactly 840, so only the remainders r need a real knapsack and everything else is a pool of identical 840-blocks. A bounded knapsack over the loose weight s at most 8 times 840 stores the largest number of blocks the leftover items can form. For each reachable s at most W, add as many blocks as fit, min(dp of s, floor of (W minus s) over 840), and take the best total. Keep r at most cnt i and use 64-bit arithmetic throughout.
They share exactly one cell. If Iahub enters that cell from above, from which side can Iahubina enter it without the two paths sharing a second cell?

Recognition: the answer is four ordinary grid path DPs glued at the meeting cell. Around that cell the four path pieces (Iahub in, Iahub out, Iahubina in, Iahubina out) are independent, so precompute the best sum from each of the four corners to every cell.

Approach: d1 is best sum from (1,1) to (i,j), d2 is from (i,j) to (n,m), d3 is from (n,1) to (i,j) moving up/right, d4 is from (i,j) to (1,m). For every interior cell take the larger of d1 of i-1, j plus d2 of i plus 1, j plus d3 of i, j-1 plus d4 of i, j plus 1 (Iahub vertical, Iahubina horizontal) and d1 of i, j-1 plus d2 of i, j plus 1 plus d3 of i plus 1, j plus d4 of i-1, j (the other way round). O of nm.

Fill four O of nm tables of best path sums: from the top-left, to the bottom-right, from the bottom-left (up/right moves) and to the top-right. At the meeting cell one of them passes straight through vertically and the other horizontally, otherwise they would share a second cell, so the answer is the max over 2 at most i at most n-1, 2 at most j at most m-1 of the two crossing sums d1 of i-1, j plus d2 of i plus 1, j plus d3 of i, j-1 plus d4 of i, j plus 1 and d1 of i, j-1 plus d2 of i, j plus 1 plus d3 of i plus 1, j plus d4 of i-1, j. The meeting cell itself is never added, and border cells can never be the meeting cell. Totals stay below 4 times 10 to the 8, but long long costs nothing here.

Every path visits exactly n plus m-1 cells, so the parity of its sum is fixed. After ruling out the odd case, ask what happens to the sum when you change a path at one corner (right-then-down becomes down-then-right).

Recognition: one corner flip swaps a single visited cell, so the sum changes by -2, 0 or +2, and flips can turn the minimum-sum path into the maximum-sum path step by step. Every even value between the two extremes is therefore reachable, and the extremes are plain grid DPs.

Approach: if n plus m-1 is odd, print NO. Otherwise compute mn of i, j is A of i, j plus min(mn of i-1, j, mn of i, j-1) and mx the same way with max, and print YES exactly when mn at most 0 at most mx at (n,m). O of nm per test.
clips.script: Approach: if n plus m-1 is odd, print NO. Otherwise compute mn of i, j is eh of i, j plus min(mn of i-1, j, mn of i, j-1) and mx the same way with max, and print YES exactly when mn at most 0 at most mx at (n,m). O of nm per test.

clips.text: A path has n plus m-1 cells of ±1, so an odd count can never sum to 0 (this also handles the 1 times 1 grid). Otherwise compute the minimum and maximum path sums with two grid DPs in O of nm. Flipping one corner of a path changes exactly one visited cell, so the sum moves by at most 2 and keeps its parity; since corner flips connect the minimum path to the maximum path, every even value in between occurs on some path, and the answer is YES exactly when min at most 0 at most max.
The last discrepancy d n is max - min of all speeds no matter what the order is. Which member should run last so that the first n-1 runners have the smallest possible spread?

Recognition: in some optimal order every new runner is a new minimum or a new maximum of those who already ran. After sorting the speeds, the first i runners are then always a contiguous block s from l to r of the sorted array, and the problem becomes an interval DP over that block.

Approach: sort s. dp of l, r is minimum sum of discrepancies when the runners so far are exactly s from l to r; dp of i, i is 0 and dp of l, r is s of r - s of l plus min(dp of l plus 1, r, dp of l, r-1). Fill by length; the answer is dp of 0, n-1. O of n to the 2.

Sort the speeds. Some optimal order always adds a runner who is a new minimum or maximum, so the runners so far form a sorted block s from l to r, and the discrepancy at that moment is s of r - s of l whatever order they ran in. Hence dp of l, r is s of r - s of l plus min(dp of l plus 1, r, dp of l, r-1) with dp of i, i, so 0, filled by increasing length, and the answer is dp of 0, n-1 in O of n to the 2 time and memory. Use 64-bit integers: the sum can reach about 2000 times 10 to the 9.

There are only about 12.5 million (l, r) pairs but up to 10 to the 6 queries, so precompute the answer for every substring. How does the count for s from l to r relate to the counts for the two substrings that drop one end?

Recognition: two interval DPs. First pal of l, r (is s from l to r a palindrome) from pal of l plus 1, r-1; then the count for s from l to r by inclusion-exclusion over s from l plus 1 to r and s from l to r-1, since every palindromic substring except possibly s from l to r itself lies in one of them.

Approach: cnt of l, r is cnt of l plus 1, r plus cnt of l, r-1 - cnt of l plus 1, r-1 plus pal of l, r. Fill by length (or l downward, r upward) and answer each query in O of 1. O of n to the 2 plus q.

Compute pal of l, r is (s of l is s of r) and (r - l less than 2 or pal of l plus 1, r-1) in order of increasing length. Then cnt of l, r is cnt of l plus 1, r plus cnt of l, r-1 - cnt of l plus 1, r-1 plus pal of l, r: the palindromes inside both shorter segments are counted twice and removed once, and the whole segment is the only substring in neither. That is O of n to the 2 time with a 5000 times 5000 int table (100 MB, within the limit; keep pal as bool). With 10 to the 6 queries, read and write with fast I/O or the time goes into scanf and printf.
Look at the first gemstone of a segment. It disappears in some second as part of some palindrome. Which other gemstone of the segment could sit at the opposite end of that palindrome?

Recognition: interval DP on dp of l, r is seconds to clear c from l to r. If gem l is not removed alone, it is the outer end of a palindrome with some later gem k of the same colour; everything between them is cleared first, and the last palindrome removed there can be extended by gems l and k at no extra cost.

Approach: dp of l, r is min of 1 plus dp of l plus 1, r; 1 plus dp of l plus 2, r if c of l is c of l plus 1; and dp of l plus 1, k-1 plus dp of k plus 1, r for every k at least l plus 2 with c of k is c of l. Empty segments cost 0; fill by length. O of n to the 3 with n at most 500.

dp of l, r is the answer for gems l to r on their own. Gem l either goes alone (1 plus dp of l plus 1, r), goes with an equal neighbour (1 plus dp of l plus 2, r), or wraps the final palindrome of an inner block: for each k greater than l plus 1 with c of k is c of l, clearing l plus 1 to k-1 ends with removing one palindrome, and adding gems l and k around it keeps it a palindrome, giving dp of l plus 1, k-1 plus dp of k plus 1, r. Fill by increasing length in O of n to the 3. The adjacent-pair case needs its own line because its inner block is empty yet still costs one second.
Trailing zeros of a product equal min(number of factors 2, number of factors 5). Can you avoid tracking both counts at once?

Recognition: run two separate min-sum grid DPs, one on the count of 2s per cell and one on the count of 5s. Every path has min(2s, 5s) at least min(best 2s, best 5s), and the path achieving the smaller optimum meets that bound, so the answer is the smaller of the two. The only twist is a 0 in the matrix.

Approach: factor each cell into its 2s and 5s, run both DPs with parent pointers and rebuild the better path. If some cell is 0 and the result is above 1, print 1 and a path through that zero instead. O of n to the 2.

Let A be the fewest 2s and B the fewest 5s on any path, each found by a min-sum grid DP in O of n to the 2; every path has at least min(A, B) trailing zeros, and the path that attains the smaller one has at most that many, so print it from parent pointers. A 0 makes the product 0, which has exactly one trailing zero: count a 0 as one 2 and one 5 in the DPs, and if a zero exists and min(A, B) greater than 1, print 1 with a path that goes down to the zero's row, right to the last column, then down. Missing the zero case, or giving a 0 no factors at all so that paths through it look free, is the usual bug.
clips.script: Let A be the fewest 2s and B the fewest 5s on any path, each found by a min-sum grid DP in O of n to the 2; every path has at least min(eh, B) trailing zeros, and the path that attains the smaller one has at most that many, so print it from parent pointers. A 0 makes the product 0, which has exactly one trailing zero: count a 0 as one 2 and one 5 in the DPs, and if a zero exists and min(eh, B) greater than 1, print 1 with a path that goes down to the zero's row, right to the last column, then down. Missing the zero case, or giving a 0 no factors at all so that paths through it look free, is the usual bug.

clips.text: Look at the first letter s of l of a segment. Either it is deleted by an operation of its own, or it is deleted together with some later equal letter. What has to happen to the letters between them first?

Recognition: an interval DP of the same shape as Zuma. If s of l goes together with s of k is s of l, the letters strictly between are cleared on their own, after which s of l joins whatever operation deletes s of k at no extra cost.

Approach: dp of l, r is min(1 plus dp of l plus 1, r, min over k in (l, r with s of k is s of l of dp of l plus 1, k-1 plus dp of k, r), with empty segments 0, filled by length. O of n to the 3 with n at most 500.

dp of l, r is the fewest operations to delete s from l to r. Either s of l is deleted alone (1 plus dp of l plus 1, r) or in the same operation as some s of k is s of l, k greater than l: first clear l plus 1 to k-1 independently (dp of l plus 1, k-1); then s of l is adjacent to s of k and rides along for free, leaving dp of k, r. Keep s of k inside the right part (dp of k, r, not dp of k plus 1, r) so it can still chain with later equal letters. O of n to the 3, roughly 2 times 10 to the 7 steps for n is 500.
Every element of the final array was formed from a contiguous block of the original array. When can a block become a single element, and is the value it becomes fixed?

Recognition: an interval DP followed by a prefix DP. Merging two v into v plus 1 keeps the sum of 2 to the A i, so a block that collapses has a forced value; an interval DP finds, for every A from l to r, whether it collapses and to what. Then cut the array into the fewest collapsible blocks.
clips.script: Recognition: an interval DP followed by a prefix DP. Merging two v into v plus 1 keeps the sum of 2 to the eh i, so a block that collapses has a forced value; an interval DP finds, for every eh from l to r, whether it collapses and to what. Then cut the array into the fewest collapsible blocks.

clips.text: Approach: val of i, i is A of i; val of l, r is val of l, k plus 1 if some split k has val of l, k is val of k plus 1, r is not -1, else -1 (by length, O of n to the 3). Then dp of 0 is 0 and dp of i is min over j less than i with val of j, i-1 is not -1 of dp of j plus 1; print dp of n.
clips.script: Approach: val of i, i is eh of i; val of l, r is val of l, k plus 1 if some split k has val of l, k is val of k plus 1, r is not -1, else -1 (by length, O of n to the 3). Then dp of 0 is 0 and dp of i is min over j less than i with val of j, i-1 is not -1 of dp of j plus 1; print dp of n.

clips.text: The final array is a partition of the original into contiguous blocks, each merged down to one element. A block collapses exactly when its last merge joins two collapsed halves with equal values, so val of l, r is val of l, k plus 1 for a split with val of l, k, which is val of k plus 1, r is not -1; since the sum of 2 to the A i is preserved, the value does not depend on the split, and any valid split will do. A prefix DP dp of i is min(dp of j plus 1) over collapsible blocks A from j to i-1 gives the answer dp of n. Total O of n to the 3 for n at most 500.
clips.script: The final array is a partition of the original into contiguous blocks, each merged down to one element. A block collapses exactly when its last merge joins two collapsed halves with equal values, so val of l, r is val of l, k plus 1 for a split with val of l, k, which is val of k plus 1, r is not -1; since the sum of 2 to the eh i is preserved, the value does not depend on the split, and any valid split will do. A prefix DP dp of i is min(dp of j plus 1) over collapsible blocks eh from j to i-1 gives the answer dp of n. Total O of n to the 3 for n at most 500.

clips.text: Every A i is at most 63, so the AND of any subsequence is one of only 64 numbers. What if you count subsequences grouped by their AND value instead of listing them?
clips.script: Every eh i is at most 63, so the AND of any subsequence is one of only 64 numbers. What if you count subsequences grouped by their AND value instead of listing them?

clips.text: Recognition: a DP whose state is a 6-bit mask, the AND so far. Going left to right, a subsequence either skips A i, starts at A i, or extends an existing subsequence whose AND v becomes v and A i.
clips.script: Recognition: a DP whose state is a 6-bit mask, the AND so far. Going left to right, a subsequence either skips eh i, starts at eh i, or extends an existing subsequence whose AND v becomes v and eh i.

clips.text: Approach: dp of v is number of non-empty subsequences of the prefix with AND exactly v. For each A: copy dp to nd, add 1 to nd of A, and add dp of v to nd of v and a for every v. Finally sum dp of v over v with popcount(v) is k, modulo 10 to the 9 plus 7. O of 64 times n.
clips.script: Approach: dp of v is number of non-empty subsequences of the prefix with AND exactly v. For each eh: copy dp to nd, add 1 to nd of eh, and add dp of v to nd of v and a for every v. Finally sum dp of v over v with popcount(v) is k, modulo 10 to the 9 plus 7. O of 64 times n.

clips.text: Keep dp of v for v in 0 to 63: the number of non-empty subsequences of the prefix whose AND is v. Adding A i keeps every old subsequence (skip A i), starts the new subsequence A i, and moves a copy of each old count dp of v to v and A i (append A i); write into a copy so A i is not used twice. The answer is the sum of dp of v over v with exactly k set bits. O of 64 times n per test; reset dp for each test case.
clips.script: Keep dp of v for v in 0 to 63: the number of non-empty subsequences of the prefix whose AND is v. Adding eh i keeps every old subsequence (skip eh i), starts the new subsequence eh i, and moves a copy of each old count dp of v to v and eh i (append eh i); write into a copy so eh i is not used twice. The answer is the sum of dp of v over v with exactly k set bits. O of 64 times n per test; reset dp for each test case.

clips.text: n at most 18. If you know which dishes Kefa has already eaten, what one extra fact do you need to score the next dish correctly?

Recognition: only the set of dishes eaten and the last dish matter, because a rule only fires for the dish eaten immediately before. That is the dp of mask, last state of a Hamiltonian-path DP, stopped at m dishes.

Approach: dp of mask, last is best satisfaction having eaten exactly mask and ending with last. Go to dp of mask or 2 to the nx, nx adding A nx plus c(last, nx). The answer is the max over masks with popcount m. O of 2 to the n times n to the 2, in long long.
clips.script: Approach: dp of mask, last is best satisfaction having eaten exactly mask and ending with last. Go to dp of mask or 2 to the nx, nx adding eh nx plus c(last, nx). The answer is the max over masks with popcount m. O of 2 to the n times n to the 2, in long long.

clips.text: Let dp of mask, last be the best satisfaction after eating exactly the dishes in mask, ending with dish last; start from dp of 2 to the i, i is A i. Appending an unused dish nx adds A nx plus c(last, nx), with c is 0 when there is no rule. Iterate masks in increasing order (an extension always has a larger mask) and take the max of dp over masks with exactly m bits. That is 2 to the 18 times 18 times 18 about 8.5 times 10 to the 7 simple steps; totals reach about 3.5 times 10 to the 10, so use 64-bit values.
clips.script: Let dp of mask, last be the best satisfaction after eating exactly the dishes in mask, ending with dish last; start from dp of 2 to the i, i is eh i. Appending an unused dish nx adds eh nx plus c(last, nx), with c is 0 when there is no rule. Iterate masks in increasing order (an extension always has a larger mask) and take the max of dp over masks with exactly m bits. That is 2 to the 18 times 18 times 18 about 8.5 times 10 to the 7 simple steps; totals reach about 3.5 times 10 to the 10, so use 64-bit values.

clips.text: You want the subset whose sum modulo m is largest. 2 to the 35 subsets is far too many, but 2 to the 17 or 2 to the 18 is small. What if you choose a subset of each half of the array separately?

Recognition: meet in the middle. List all subset sums modulo m of each half; the answer combines one sum x from the left with one sum y from the right, and since both are below m, (x plus y) mod m is either x plus y or x plus y - m.

Approach: sort the right list. For each x, binary search the largest y less than m - x and take x plus y. The wrapped case x plus y - m is always below x itself (the empty subset gives y is 0), so it never wins. O of 2 to the n over 2 times n.

Split a into halves of n over 2 and n - n over 2 elements and list all subset sums of each modulo m (at most 2 to the 18 each). For a left sum x the best right partner is the largest y with x plus y less than m, found by binary search in the sorted right list; y is 0 always qualifies, and a wrapped total x plus y - m is smaller than x, so it never beats that. The answer is the max of x plus y over all x, and it is 0 for the empty choice. O of 2 to the n over 2 times log time.
Forget the strings for a moment: for each pair of songs you only need to know whether they may stand next to each other. What object does that describe?

Recognition: songs are vertices, an edge joins two songs with the same genre or the same writer, and an exciting playlist is a path visiting each kept song once. With n at most 16 you want the largest set of songs that has a Hamiltonian path, which is dp of mask, last.

Approach: compare the strings once to build adj of i as a bitmask. ok of mask is bitmask of songs that can end a valid ordering of exactly mask; from each possible last, extend by any song in adj of last outside mask. The answer is n minus the largest popcount with ok of mask is not 0. O of 2 to the n times n to the 2.

Build the compatibility graph (same genre or same writer) by comparing strings once per pair, or after mapping each string to an integer id. A boolean dp of mask, last, stored as one bitmask of possible last songs per mask, marks which subsets can be arranged into an exciting order ending at last; extend from last to any unused neighbour. The answer is n - max popcount(mask) over reachable masks. The bound on the sum of 2 to the n keeps the total O of 2 to the n times n to the 2 small, as long as no 10 to the 4-character string comparison happens inside the DP loop.
At any moment the lake is described by the set of fish still alive. How many such sets are there, and does what happens next depend on how the lake got there?

Recognition: a probability DP over subsets. From a set of k alive fish, each of the k(k-1) over 2 pairs meets with equal probability, and the next state is the same set minus the fish that was eaten. Sets only shrink, so process masks from the full set downward.

Approach: p of full is 1. For each mask with k at least 2 fish and each ordered pair (i, j) of fish in it, add p of mask times A of i, j over (k(k-1) over 2) to p of mask without j. The answer for fish i is p of 2 to the i. O of 2 to the n times n to the 2.
clips.script: Approach: p of full is 1. For each mask with k at least 2 fish and each ordered pair (i, j) of fish in it, add p of mask times eh of i, j over (k(k-1) over 2) to p of mask without j. The answer for fish i is p of 2 to the i. O of 2 to the n times n to the 2.

clips.text: p of mask is the probability that at some moment exactly the fish in mask are alive. Starting from p of full is 1, visit masks in decreasing order (every meeting removes one fish, so it leads to a smaller mask): for each ordered pair i is not j both in mask, fish i eats fish j with probability A of i, j over (k(k-1) over 2), which moves that share of p of mask to mask without j. The answer for fish i is p of 2 to the i, and for n is 1 it is 1. About 2 to the 18 times 18 to the 2 about 8.5 times 10 to the 7 floating-point steps, fine in 3 s; print at least 6 decimals.
clips.script: p of mask is the probability that at some moment exactly the fish in mask are alive. Starting from p of full is 1, visit masks in decreasing order (every meeting removes one fish, so it leads to a smaller mask): for each ordered pair i is not j both in mask, fish i eats fish j with probability eh of i, j over (k(k-1) over 2), which moves that share of p of mask to mask without j. The answer for fish i is p of 2 to the i, and for n is 1 it is 1. About 2 to the 18 times 18 to the 2 about 8.5 times 10 to the 7 floating-point steps, fine in 3 s; print at least 6 decimals.

clips.text: Process the columns one at a time. When you fix a rotation for a column, decide which rows will take their maximum from this column. What is the only thing about earlier columns that later columns need to know?

Recognition: a DP over the set of rows already served. A column serves some subset s of the rows not yet served, and the most it can give them is its best rotation for exactly those rows; combining columns means splitting the full row mask into disjoint submasks, so this is a submask-enumeration DP.

Approach: for each column precompute best of s is max over the n rotations of the sum of the rows in s. Then nd of mask is max(dp of mask, max over non-empty submasks s of mask of dp of mask xor s plus best of s). The answer is dp of full. O(m times (3 to the n plus n to the 2 times 2 to the n)).

Assign each row to the column its maximum comes from; a column serving the row set s contributes best of s, the largest sum over its n rotations of the entries in rows s. Run dp over columns with state "rows already served": nd of mask is max(dp of mask, dp of mask xor s plus best of s) over non-empty submasks s, using s is (s - 1) and mask. An assignment can only underestimate the true row maxima, and the optimal answer is itself one assignment, so the DP is exact. With n at most 4 this is tiny; the hard version (n at most 12, m at most 2000) runs the same DP after keeping only the n columns with the largest maxima.

The traversal compares two kinds of neighbours: consecutive rows within a column, and the bottom row of one column with the top row of the next. For a pair of rows (i, j), can you summarise every comparison they cause with one number?

Recognition: precompute down of i, j is min over columns c of the size of A of i, c - A of j, c and wrap of i, j is min over c of the size of A of i, c - A of j, c plus 1. A row order is then a Hamiltonian path scored by its smallest down edge, plus one wrap edge from the last row back to the first: a dp of mask, last with the first row fixed.
clips.script: Recognition: precompute down of i, j is min over columns c of the size of eh of i, c - eh of j, c and wrap of i, j is min over c of the size of eh of i, c - eh of j, c plus 1. A row order is then a Hamiltonian path scored by its smallest down edge, plus one wrap edge from the last row back to the first: a dp of mask, last with the first row fixed.

clips.text: Approach: for each first row s, dp of mask, last is the largest possible minimum down edge over orders of mask that start at s and end at last; transition with min(dp of mask, last, down of last, nx). The answer is the max over s and last of min(dp of full, last, wrap of last, s). O of n to the 2 times m plus n to the 3 times 2 to the n.

Precompute down of i, j (row j directly below row i, min over all columns) and wrap of i, j (i is the bottom row and j the top row, min over c of the size of A of i, c - A of j, c plus 1) in O of n to the 2 times m. Fix the first row s and run dp of mask, last is max over orders of the min down edge, extending with min(dp, down of last, nx); the answer is the max over s and last of min(dp of full, last, wrap of last, s). That is about 16 times 2 to the 15 times 16 to the 2 about 1.3 times 10 to the 8 simple steps, fine in 4 s; a binary search on k with a boolean DP also works. When m is 1 there are no wrap edges, so wrap must start at infinity, and when n is 1 the answer is wrap of 0, 0.
clips.script: Precompute down of i, j (row j directly below row i, min over all columns) and wrap of i, j (i is the bottom row and j the top row, min over c of the size of eh of i, c - eh of j, c plus 1) in O of n to the 2 times m. Fix the first row s and run dp of mask, last is max over orders of the min down edge, extending with min(dp, down of last, nx); the answer is the max over s and last of min(dp of full, last, wrap of last, s). That is about 16 times 2 to the 15 times 16 to the 2 about 1.3 times 10 to the 8 simple steps, fine in 4 s; a binary search on k with a boolean DP also works. When m is 1 there are no wrap edges, so wrap must start at infinity, and when n is 1 the answer is wrap of 0, 0.

clips.text: x and y is 0 means every set bit of y is a zero bit of x. Describe the set of all valid y for a given x as one mask.

Recognition: y must be a submask of the complement of x within 22 bits (4 times 10 to the 6 less than 2 to the 22). So you need, for every mask, any array element that is a submask of it: a sum-over-subsets DP that keeps one witness instead of a sum.

Approach: f of mask is -1 everywhere, f of A i is A i; then for each bit b and each mask containing b, if f of mask is -1 copy f of mask xor (2 to the b). The answer for x is f of (2 to the 22 - 1) xor x. O of 22 times 2 to the 22.
clips.script: Approach: f of mask is -1 everywhere, f of eh i is eh i; then for each bit b and each mask containing b, if f of mask is -1 copy f of mask xor (2 to the b). The answer for x is f of (2 to the 22 - 1) xor x. O of 22 times 2 to the 22.

clips.text: y is compatible with x exactly when y is a submask of the 22-bit complement of x. Put each array value into f of A i, then run SOS DP over the 22 bits so that f of mask holds some array element that is a submask of mask, or -1. Each answer is f of full xor x; x can never be its own partner because x and x is x is not 0. About 9 times 10 to the 7 steps and a 16 MB table; use fast input and output for 10 to the 6 numbers.
clips.script: y is compatible with x exactly when y is a submask of the 22-bit complement of x. Put each array value into f of eh i, then run SOS DP over the 22 bits so that f of mask holds some array element that is a submask of mask, or -1. Each answer is f of full xor x; x can never be its own partner because x and x is x is not 0. About 9 times 10 to the 7 steps and a 16 MB table; use fast input and output for 10 to the 6 numbers.

clips.text: Draw the iterations as a tree: the 2 to the n numbers are the leaves and every later number sits above the two it was computed from. Which numbers change when one A p is overwritten?
clips.script: Draw the iterations as a tree: the 2 to the n numbers are the leaves and every later number sits above the two it was computed from. Which numbers change when one eh p is overwritten?

clips.text: This is a segment tree whose merge depends on the level: the level right above the leaves uses OR, the next XOR, and so on. Changing A p only changes its n ancestors.
clips.script: This is a segment tree whose merge depends on the level: the level right above the leaves uses OR, the next XOR, and so on. Changing eh p only changes its n ancestors.

clips.text: Store the tree in an array of size 2 to the n plus 1 with leaf i at 2 to the n plus i. To update, set the leaf and walk i /= 2 up to the root, recomputing t of i from t of 2i and t of 2i plus 1 with OR when the height above the leaves is odd and XOR when it is even. Print t of 1. O of n per query.

Build a segment tree over the 2 to the n numbers in which a node at height h (leaves at height 0) combines its children with OR when h is odd and XOR when h is even, which mirrors Xenia's iterations exactly, so the root holds v. A query changes one leaf, so recompute only the n nodes on its path to the root: O of 2 to the n plus m times n in total. A common bug is choosing the operation by distance from the root instead of from the leaves: the root uses OR when n is odd and XOR when n is even.
A triplet i less than j less than k with A i greater than A j greater than A k has a middle man j. Once j is fixed, do the choices of i and of k depend on each other?
clips.script: A triplet i less than j less than k with eh i greater than eh j greater than eh k has a middle man j. Once j is fixed, do the choices of i and of k depend on each other?

clips.text: They are independent, so the count for a fixed j is (stronger men to the left of j) times (weaker men to the right of j). Each factor is an inversion-style count that a Fenwick tree over the powers answers in O of log n.

Compress the powers to ranks 1 to n. Sweep left to right with j counted from 1: left of j is (j minus 1) minus (earlier ranks below rank j), the earlier men minus the weaker ones. Sweep right to left: right of j is later ranks below rank j. Add left of j times right of j in long long. O of n log n.

For each j multiply the number of i less than j with A i greater than A j by the number of k greater than j with A k less than A j and sum the products. Compress the powers (up to 10 to the 9) to ranks and get both counts with a Fenwick tree in two sweeps, O of n log n for n is 10 to the 6. The answer reaches about 1.7 times 10 to the 17, so the product and the sum must be long long, and the million numbers should be read with scanf or fast cin.
clips.script: For each j multiply the number of i less than j with eh i greater than eh j by the number of k greater than j with eh k less than eh j and sum the products. Compress the powers (up to 10 to the 9) to ranks and get both counts with a Fenwick tree in two sweeps, O of n log n for n is 10 to the 6. The answer reaches about 1.7 times 10 to the 17, so the product and the sum must be long long, and the million numbers should be read with scanf or fast cin.

clips.text: How many increasing subsequences of length len end exactly at position i? Express it through shorter subsequences that end at earlier positions.

cnt of len, i is sum of cnt of len minus 1, j over j less than i with A j less than A i. Among the earlier positions this is a prefix sum over values, so keep one Fenwick tree per length, indexed by value (the values are already distinct and between 1 and n).
clips.script: cnt of len, i is sum of cnt of len minus 1, j over j less than i with eh j less than eh i. Among the earlier positions this is a prefix sum over values, so keep one Fenwick tree per length, indexed by value (the values are already distinct and between 1 and n).

clips.text: Go left to right. For A i set cnt of 1 is 1 and cnt of len is prefix sum of tree len minus 1 up to A i minus 1 for len, so 2 to k plus 1, then add each cnt of len at index A i of tree len. The answer is the sum of all cnt of k plus 1. O of n times k times log n.
clips.script: Go left to right. For eh i set cnt of 1 is 1 and cnt of len is prefix sum of tree len minus 1 up to eh i minus 1 for len, so 2 to k plus 1, then add each cnt of len at index eh i of tree len. The answer is the sum of all cnt of k plus 1. O of n times k times log n.

clips.text: Let cnt of len, i be the number of increasing subsequences of length len ending at position i; it is the sum of cnt of len minus 1, j over earlier j with a smaller value. Keep k plus 1 Fenwick trees indexed by value: at position i query tree len minus 1 on the prefix A i minus 1, insert the result into tree len, and add cnt of k plus 1, i to the answer, O of n times k times log n in total. Counts for shorter lengths can exceed 2 to the 63 even though the final answer fits, so use unsigned long long: every operation is an addition, so wrapping mod 2 to the 64 still gives the exact final answer. k is 0 is allowed, and then the answer is n.
clips.script: Let cnt of len, i be the number of increasing subsequences of length len ending at position i; it is the sum of cnt of len minus 1, j over earlier j with a smaller value. Keep k plus 1 Fenwick trees indexed by value: at position i query tree len minus 1 on the prefix eh i minus 1, insert the result into tree len, and add cnt of k plus 1, i to the answer, O of n times k times log n in total. Counts for shorter lengths can exceed 2 to the 63 even though the final answer fits, so use unsigned long long: every operation is an addition, so wrapping mod 2 to the 64 still gives the exact final answer. k is 0 is allowed, and then the answer is n.

clips.text: Cake i may only go on an earlier cake with strictly smaller volume, and you maximise the total volume of the stack. Which subsequence problem is this, and what is different about it?

It is a longest strictly increasing subsequence in which each cake is worth its volume instead of 1: dp i is V i plus max dp j over j less than i with V j less than V i. The O of n squared transition becomes a prefix-maximum query on a Fenwick tree indexed by the rank of the volume.

Work with r squared times h as an exact integer (up to 10 to the 12) and multiply by π only when printing. Compress the volumes; for each cake in input order query the prefix max over ranks below rank(V i), set dp i is V i plus that max, and update position rank(V i) with dp i. O of n log n.

This is a weighted strictly increasing subsequence over the volumes in input order. Compress the integer volumes r squared times h, keep a Fenwick tree of prefix maxima over the ranks, compute dp i is r i squared times h i plus query(rank i minus 1) and then update rank i with dp i; print the largest dp times π with at least 6 decimals. Equal volumes share a rank, so querying rank minus 1 enforces the strict inequality. Comparing floating-point volumes π times r squared times h instead of the integers can make two equal volumes compare as different and break that strictness.

For one fixed string the longest correct bracket subsequence is greedy: scan with a counter of unmatched "(" and match each ")" when the counter is positive. What does a piece of the string leave unmatched after this greedy?
Every piece reduces to some matched pairs plus ")))…(((": unmatched closes followed by unmatched opens. Two such summaries combine in O of 1, which is exactly what a segment tree node needs.

Node is (pairs, open, close). Merging L then R: t is min(L.open, R.close); pairs is L.pairs plus R.pairs plus t, open is L.open plus R.open minus t, close is L.close plus R.close minus t. The answer is 2 times pairs of the merged range; keep the left-to-right order when combining the pieces of a query. O of n plus m log n.

Greedy matching shows that the best subsequence of a segment is twice the number of pairs a stack would match, and the unmatched rest looks like ")…)(…(". Store (pairs, unmatched open, unmatched close) in a segment tree; merging L then R creates t is min(L.open, R.close) new pairs. Each query merges O of log n nodes, so the total is O of n plus m log n for n up to 10 to the 6. The merge is not commutative: in an iterative bottom-up query keep a left accumulator and a right accumulator and join them in order at the end.
The query asks for a sum but the update is an xor. If you only know the sum of a range, can you tell how it changes after xor with x? What extra information per range would be enough?

Split by bits: a sum is sum of 2 to the b times (number of elements with bit b set). Xor with x flips bit b of every element in the range when bit b of x is 1, so that count becomes length minus count. With 20 per-bit counts in each node, a range xor is a lazy tag on a segment tree.

Each node stores ones of b for b less than 20 and a pending xor mask. Applying a mask sets ones of b is len minus ones of b for each set bit, and tags combine by xor. Push before descending, recompute from the children afterwards, and answer a sum as sum of ones of b times 2 to the b over the covered nodes. O of (n plus m) times 20 times log n.

Keep a segment tree in which each node stores, for each of the 20 bits, how many elements of its range have that bit set, plus a lazy xor mask. Applying x to a node replaces ones of b by len minus ones of b for every bit set in x and xors x into the tag; pushing hands the tag to both children. A sum query adds ones of b times 2 to the b over the O of log n covering nodes. This runs in O of (n plus m) times 20 times log n, and sums reach about 10 to the 11, so the answer needs long long.
Let dp of i be the best total for the first i elements and look at the last segment (j, i. Its value depends on the sign of its sum. How do prefix sums express that sign?

With prefix sums P, the last segment is positive when P of j less than P of i, zero when they are equal and negative when P of j greater than P of i. So dp of i is max of (max dp of j minus j over P of j less than P of i) plus i, (max dp of j over P of j is P of i) and (max dp of j plus j over P of j greater than P of i) minus i: three "best earlier value with a smaller, equal or larger key" queries.

Compress P from 0 to n. Keep a prefix-max Fenwick tree of dp of j minus j, a Fenwick tree over reversed ranks of dp of j plus j, and an array of the best dp of j per rank. Insert j is 0 with dp, so 0, then for i is 1 to n query all three, take the best and insert i. O of n log n per test.

dp of i is max over j less than i of dp of j plus sign(P of i minus P of j) times (i minus j). Splitting by the sign, the positive case needs max(dp of j minus j) over smaller prefix sums, the negative case max(dp of j plus j) over larger ones and the zero case max dp of j over equal ones; two max Fenwick trees over compressed prefix sums and one array give O of n log n. Include j is 0 with P of 0, so 0, keep prefix sums in long long (up to 5 times 10 to the 14), and size the structures by each test's n, since t can be 5 times 10 to the 5 and only the sum of n is bounded.
Both operations act on a whole segment. What would inc cost on a segment tree with only point updates, and how could a node avoid touching every element below it?

Range add with range minimum is a lazy segment tree: a node lying fully inside the update adds v to its minimum and keeps v as a pending tag for its children. The circular part is only input handling.

If lf at most rg use lf to rg; otherwise split into lf to n minus 1 and 0 to rg, apply an inc to both parts and take the min of both for rmq. Read each operation as a whole line and count its numbers (2 means rmq, 3 means inc). Use long long. O of (n plus m) log n.

Use a segment tree of range minima with an additive lazy tag: an inc covering a node adds v to its minimum and to its tag, the tag is pushed to the children before any descent, and the minimum is recomputed after the recursion. A circular segment with lf greater than rg is the union of lf to n minus 1 and 0 to rg. The operation type is the number of integers on the line, so read lines (getline, or fgets with sscanf) instead of a fixed number of tokens. Values reach 10 to the 6 plus 2 times 10 to the 5 times 10 to the 6, so use long long; O of (n plus m) log n overall.
From cell i there is exactly one portal, and it only moves you to the right. How many different routes can start at cell 1?
The portals form a directed graph in which every cell has one outgoing edge, so the cells reachable from 1 are a single chain 1, then 1 plus A 1, then …. Reachability here is following that chain.
clips.script: The portals form a directed graph in which every cell has one outgoing edge, so the cells reachable from 1 are a single chain 1, then 1 plus eh 1, then …. Reachability here is following that chain.

clips.text: Start at cur is 1 and repeat cur plus-equals A of cur while cur less than t. Print YES exactly when you stop on t. O of n.
clips.script: Start at cur is 1 and repeat cur plus-equals eh of cur while cur less than t. Print YES exactly when you stop on t. O of n.

clips.text: Follow the only path: cur is 1, then cur is cur plus A of cur while cur less than t. Every jump moves strictly right, so the walk either lands on t or jumps past it; print YES exactly when cur is t. O of n. A general DFS over the n minus 1 directed portal edges gives the same answer; the point is to read the portals as a graph.
clips.script: Follow the only path: cur is 1, then cur is cur plus eh of cur while cur less than t. Every jump moves strictly right, so the walk either lands on t or jumps past it; print YES exactly when cur is t. O of n. A general DFS over the n minus 1 directed portal edges gives the same answer; the point is to read the portals as a graph.

clips.text: When can Bajtek get from one drift directly towards another? Does it matter if a third drift lies between them?

Make each drift a vertex and join two drifts when they share an x or a y coordinate. A drift in between only splits the slide into two moves inside the same component, so "can get from A to B" means "same connected component".
clips.script: Make each drift a vertex and join two drifts when they share an x or a y coordinate. A drift in between only splits the slide into two moves inside the same component, so "can get from eh to B" means "same connected component".

clips.text: Count the components c with a DFS over the n at most 100 drifts (checking all pairs, O of n squared). The answer is c minus 1: a new drift at (x of one drift, y of another) merges two components.

Vertices are drifts, with an edge when x i is x j or y i is y j; a slide stops at the first drift in its way, which is in the same row or column, so reachability is exactly connectivity. Count components c by DFS in O of n squared and print c minus 1. A new drift is adjacent only to drifts in its row and its column, and each of those groups already lies inside one component, so it merges at most two components; placing it at (x A, y b) for drifts A and b in different components does merge two, so c minus 1 drifts are needed and enough.
clips.script: Vertices are drifts, with an edge when x i is x j or y i is y j; a slide stops at the first drift in its way, which is in the same row or column, so reachability is exactly connectivity. Count components c by DFS in O of n squared and print c minus 1. A new drift is adjacent only to drifts in its row and its column, and each of those groups already lies inside one component, so it merges at most two components; placing it at (x eh, y b) for drifts eh and b in different components does merge two, so c minus 1 drifts are needed and enough.

clips.text: The news spreads along friendships until it cannot spread further. So the answer for user x is the size of what?
It is the size of the connected component of x in the friendship graph. But a group of k users is a clique with k(k minus 1) over 2 edges, far too many to build when k is 5 times 10 to the 5.

You only need connectivity, not every friendship: join each group member to the next one in its list (k minus 1 edges). Label components with an iterative DFS (or DSU), record each component size, and print size of comp i. O of n plus sum of k.

Replace each group by a path through its members; a path connects the same users as the clique, so the components are unchanged and the graph has fewer than sum of k edges. Label components with an iterative DFS, count their sizes, and print size of comp i for every user. Groups with k is 0 or k is 1 add no edges. O of n plus sum of k; a recursive DFS can overflow the stack on a chain of 5 times 10 to the 5 users.
Look at a component that is a single cycle. What is the degree of each of its vertices? Does the converse also hold?

A connected component is a cycle exactly when every vertex in it has degree 2: a connected graph with all degrees equal to 2 is one closed ring, and without loops or multi-edges it has at least 3 vertices. So this is "find components, then check one property per component".
Store degrees, then run DFS from each unvisited vertex with a flag that becomes false if any visited vertex has degree other than 2. Count the components whose flag stays true. O of n plus m.

Label components with an iterative DFS; for each component check that all its vertices have degree exactly 2, and count the components that pass. All degrees 2 and connected means edges is vertices and a single ring; isolated vertices and paths fail the check. O of n plus m. Do not abandon the traversal when you meet a bad vertex: the unvisited rest of that component would later be counted as a new component.
Look only at the dots of one colour and the edges between side-adjacent dots of that colour. What does "a cycle of at least 4 dots" mean in that graph?

It is cycle detection in an undirected graph, and the length needs no check: a grid has no triangles (it is bipartite), so every cycle has at least 4 cells. A DFS finds a cycle exactly when it reaches an already visited cell that is not the cell it just came from.

For each unvisited cell run dfs(cell, parent) that moves only to same-coloured neighbours; if a neighbour other than the parent is already visited, print Yes. O of nm. Equivalently, count cells V and same-colour adjacent pairs E per component: a cycle exists exactly when E at least V.

Each colour class is an undirected graph on cells with edges between side-adjacent cells. Run a DFS that remembers the cell it came from; reaching a visited neighbour other than that parent closes a cycle, and every grid cycle has length at least 4 because the grid has no odd cycles. O of nm with n, m at most 50. The usual mistake is counting the step back to the parent as a cycle, which makes any two adjacent same-coloured dots look like a cycle.
Instead of choosing which k cells to wall up, choose which s minus k cells to keep. What kind of set of cells is always connected?

Any search from one empty cell discovers each new cell from a cell it has already discovered, so the first s minus k cells it discovers form a tree and are connected. (Equivalently: removing a leaf of a DFS tree never disconnects the rest.)
Count s, run DFS or BFS from any empty cell, and stop once s minus k cells have been discovered; turn every other empty cell into X. O of nm.

Run an iterative DFS or BFS from any empty cell and mark cells as kept when they are discovered, stopping after s minus k cells. Every kept cell after the first was discovered from an earlier kept cell, so the kept cells form a connected tree; print X for every other empty cell. Deleting the first k cells in DFS post-order (children before parents) works for the same reason. O of nm with up to 250 000 cells, so prefer an explicit stack or BFS to deep recursion.
Take any vertex v. If no directed path of length 2 may exist, can v have both an incoming and an outgoing edge?
Every vertex must be all-out or all-in, and every edge must go from an all-out vertex to an all-in vertex. That is a 2-colouring: an orientation exists exactly when the graph is bipartite.

2-colour the graph with DFS from vertex 1; if some edge joins two vertices of the same colour, print NO. Otherwise direct every edge from colour 0 to colour 1: character i is 0 if u i has colour 0, else 1. O of n plus m.

A path of length 2 needs a vertex with an in-edge and an out-edge, so each vertex is a pure source or a pure sink, and every edge joins a source to a sink: a bipartition. 2-colour the connected graph with an iterative DFS; an edge inside one colour (an odd cycle) means NO. Otherwise print YES and, for each edge in input order, 0 when u i is on side 0 and 1 otherwise. O of n plus m. The sample output is the mirror image of this orientation; any valid answer is accepted.
When is A plus b odd for A, b ∈ 1, 2, 3? What does that force for the two endpoints of every edge?
clips.script: When is eh plus b odd for eh, b ∈ 1, 2, 3? What does that force for the two endpoints of every edge?

clips.text: Each edge must join an odd number (1 or 3) and an even number (2), so the vertices split into an odd side and an even side with every edge going across: a 2-colouring. A component that is not bipartite makes the answer 0, and a bipartite component has exactly two colourings (swap the sides).

For each component, 2-colour it and count the vertices A and b on its two sides. If the first side is odd there are 2 to the a labellings (1 or 3 each, the other side all 2); if the second side is odd, 2 to the b. Multiply (2 to the A plus 2 to the b) over all components mod 998244353.
clips.script: For each component, 2-colour it and count the vertices eh and b on its two sides. If the first side is odd there are 2 to the a labellings (1 or 3 each, the other side all 2); if the second side is odd, 2 to the b. Multiply (2 to the eh plus 2 to the b) over all components mod 998244353.

clips.text: An odd sum means one endpoint is 2 and the other is 1 or 3, so a valid labelling is a 2-colouring in which the odd side has 2 choices per vertex. Colour each component with an iterative DFS; on a conflict the answer is 0. Otherwise a component with sides of sizes A and b has 2 to the A plus 2 to the b labellings (an isolated vertex gives 3), and the answer is the product over components mod 998244353 with precomputed powers of 2. There are up to 3 times 10 to the 5 tests, so allocate arrays of size n per test rather than resetting a maximum-size array each time.
clips.script: An odd sum means one endpoint is 2 and the other is 1 or 3, so a valid labelling is a 2-colouring in which the odd side has 2 choices per vertex. Colour each component with an iterative DFS; on a conflict the answer is 0. Otherwise a component with sides of sizes eh and b has 2 to the eh plus 2 to the b labellings (an isolated vertex gives 3), and the answer is the product over components mod 998244353 with precomputed powers of 2. There are up to 3 times 10 to the 5 tests, so allocate arrays of size n per test rather than resetting a maximum-size array each time.

clips.text: Each click turns the displayed number x into 2x or x minus 1, and every click costs the same. What graph are you walking on?

The numbers are vertices and the buttons are edges, so the fewest clicks is the BFS distance from n to m. The graph is infinite, but an optimal sequence never shows a number above max(n, 2m), so the numbers 1 to 2 times 10 to the 4 are enough.

BFS from n over 1 to 20000 with neighbours 2x and x minus 1 (staying at least 1) and print dist of m. Alternatively, work backwards from m: add 1 if it is odd, halve it if it is even, until it is at most n, then add n minus m; each step is one click.

Treat each number 1 to 20000 as a vertex with edges x to 2x and x to x minus 1, BFS from n, and print dist of m; the cap is safe because doubling a number that is already at least m only creates extra subtractions, so no optimal sequence goes above max(n, 2m). O of 10 to the 4. The backwards greedy (from m: +1 if odd, halve if even, until at most n, then add the difference) is the same search on the reversed operations, where the choice is forced.
The fire spreads one tree per minute in four directions, starting from K trees at once. When does a given tree start burning, in terms of the K starting trees?

A tree ignites at its distance to the nearest starting tree, so this is multi-source BFS: put all K burning trees in the queue at distance 0 and run a single BFS. BFS takes cells out in order of distance, so the last cell taken out is a correct answer.

Run that BFS on the N times M grid (up to 4 times 10 to the 6 cells) with flat int arrays for dist and the queue, and print the last cell dequeued. Read from input.txt and write to output.txt, as the statement says.

Push all K sources at distance 0 and run one BFS over the grid; the last cell dequeued has the largest distance to its nearest source. O of NM with N, M at most 2000; flat int arrays for dist and the queue (32 MB together) keep you under the 64 MB limit. With no obstacles, min over sources of the size of x minus x i plus the size of y minus y i for every cell (O of NMK) also passes. The most common mistake is reading standard input: this problem uses input.txt and output.txt.
For a fixed town v, what does it cost to bring goods of type t? You need that number for every pair (town, type).

The cost for (v, t) is the distance from v to the nearest town that produces t. A BFS from each of the n towns is too slow, but there are only k at most 100 types, and one multi-source BFS from all towns of type t gives that distance for every v at once.

Run k BFS passes, pass t starting from every town of type t, to fill dist of t, v. For each town take the s smallest of its k values (nth element or sort) and add them up. O of k times (n plus m) plus n times k.

For each type t, run a BFS seeded with all towns producing t, so dist of t, v is the cost of the nearest unit of type t for town v. The types are chosen independently, so the answer for v is the sum of the s smallest dist of t, v over the k types. That is at most 100 BFS passes over 10 to the 5 vertices and edges, about 2 times 10 to the 7 steps, plus nth element per town. dist takes k times n ints (40 MB), well within 512 MB.
Knowing only which cell Igor is in does not tell you whether his next move is a turn. What else must you remember?

Make the state (cell, direction he is moving). Stepping forward in the same direction costs no turn and changing direction costs one turn, so this is a shortest path on a state graph with edge costs 0 and 1.

Run 0-1 BFS from the four states (S, d) with 0 turns: forward steps go to the front of the deque, direction changes to the back. Print YES if some (T, d) needs at most 2 turns. 4 times n times m at most 4 times 10 to the 6 states, O of nm.

States are (cell, direction), 4 times n times m of them. From (c, d) you can step to the next cell in direction d if it has no road works (cost 0) or switch to another direction in place (cost 1); the four states at S start with cost 0. 0-1 BFS gives the minimum number of turns for every state, and the answer is YES exactly when min over d of turns(T, d) at most 2. O of nm. A plain BFS over (cell, direction, turns used at most 2) also works with 3 times as many states and no deque.
Suppose a path ends in column j after L moves left and R moves right. What is R minus L, whichever path you took?

R minus L is j minus c is fixed by the target column, so the path with the fewest left moves also has the fewest right moves. Up and down moves are free, so this is a shortest path where a left move costs 1 and every other move costs 0: 0-1 BFS.

0-1 BFS from (r, c), with left moves pushed to the back of the deque and up, down and right moves to the front, gives the minimum L for every cell. A cell counts exactly when L at most x and L plus (j minus c) at most y. O of nm for up to 4 times 10 to the 6 cells.

Because rights minus lefts is j minus c on every path to column j, minimising left moves minimises both counts at once. A 0-1 BFS (cost 1 for left, 0 otherwise) computes the minimum number of left moves L for every free cell; count the cells with L at most x and L plus j minus c at most y. O of nm. A plain BFS by number of steps is wrong: the shortest path to a cell may use more left moves than a longer detour that goes up and around an obstacle.
A BFS from every position i is O of n squared. But every odd-valued position is looking for the same kind of target. Can you search in the other direction?

Reverse the jumps: add an edge j to i whenever i can jump to j. The distance from i to the nearest even-valued position is then the distance from the set of all even-valued positions to i in the reversed graph: one multi-source BFS. Do it once with even sources and once with odd sources.

Build radj with i added to radj of i minus A i and radj of i plus A i (when in range). BFS from all even-valued positions at distance 0 and read the answer for the odd-valued ones; repeat with odd sources for the even-valued ones. Unreached positions get minus 1. O of n.
clips.script: Build radj with i added to radj of i minus eh i and radj of i plus eh i (when in range). BFS from all even-valued positions at distance 0 and read the answer for the odd-valued ones; repeat with odd sources for the even-valued ones. Unreached positions get minus 1. O of n.

clips.text: Each position has at most two jumps, so the reversed graph has at most 2n edges. A multi-source BFS from all positions with even A j on the reversed graph gives every position its fewest forward jumps to some even-valued position; record it for the odd-valued positions, then repeat with odd-valued sources for the even-valued ones. O of n. A BFS from the targets on the original (non-reversed) edges computes the wrong direction: it measures jumps from the targets, not to them.
clips.script: Each position has at most two jumps, so the reversed graph has at most 2n edges. A multi-source BFS from all positions with even eh j on the reversed graph gives every position its fewest forward jumps to some even-valued position; record it for the odd-valued positions, then repeat with odd-valued sources for the even-valued ones. O of n. A BFS from the targets on the original (non-reversed) edges computes the wrong direction: it measures jumps from the targets, not to them.

clips.text: Whether you may go from city v to city w depends on the city you were in just before v. What must a vertex of your search remember?

Make the state the last road taken, (u, v) with u the previous city. From (u, v) you may go to (v, w) for each neighbour w unless (u, v, w) is forbidden. Every road costs the same, so BFS over the 2m directed roads gives the shortest valid route, and a city may appear twice on it (sample 3).

Seed the queue with every road (1, w) at distance 1, keep the forbidden triples in a sorted vector of encoded integers, store a parent per state, and stop at the first popped state that ends in n; print minus 1 if there is none. Check whether (v, w) is already visited before looking up the triple.

BFS on directed roads: state (u, v) means "in v, arrived from u". Start from every road (1, w) at distance 1; from (u, v) move to an unvisited (v, w) unless (u, v, w) is forbidden; the first popped state with v is n gives the distance, and parent pointers rebuild the path. Checking visited first means at most k plus 2m triple lookups, and the remaining work is sum of deg(v) squared, at most about 1.2 times 10 to the 8 cheap array checks, fine in 3 seconds. A BFS on cities alone is wrong: the shortest way into a city may be blocked for the next step while a longer way in is not.
Can it ever help to use the portals twice? Compare jumping A to b and later c to d with jumping A to d directly.
clips.script: Can it ever help to use the portals twice? Compare jumping eh to b and later c to d with jumping eh to d directly.

clips.text: One portal jump is always enough: A to b then c to d costs A plus b plus c plus d, more than A to d. So the route is either a pure walk, or walk to a portal, jump once, and walk from another portal. Walking costs w per step, which is BFS from the start and BFS from the end.
clips.script: One portal jump is always enough: eh to b then c to d costs eh plus b plus c plus d, more than eh to d. So the route is either a pure walk, or walk to a portal, jump once, and walk from another portal. Walking costs w per step, which is BFS from the start and BFS from the end.

clips.text: BFS from (1, 1) and from (n, m) over free cells. Let bestS is min over portals p reachable from the start of distS(p) times w plus A p, and bestT the same with distT. The answer is min(distS(n, m) times w, bestS plus bestT), or minus 1. Use long long throughout. O of nm.
clips.script: BFS from (1, 1) and from (n, m) over free cells. Let bestS is min over portals p reachable from the start of distS(p) times w plus eh p, and bestT the same with distT. The answer is min(distS(n, m) times w, bestS plus bestT), or minus 1. Use long long throughout. O of nm.

clips.text: One portal jump always suffices, since two jumps A to b, c to d cost more than the single jump A to d. BFS from both corners gives step counts distS and distT; the answer is the minimum of distS(n, m) times w and min p(distS(p) times w plus A p) plus min q(distT(q) times w plus A q), each minimum taken over portals reachable from that side. If both minima pick the same portal the sum is still at least the walk through it, so no special case is needed. O of nm with long long: 4 times 10 to the 6 steps times 10 to the 9 overflows int, and 4 times 10 to the 6 numbers of input want fast reading.
clips.script: One portal jump always suffices, since two jumps eh to b, c to d cost more than the single jump eh to d. BFS from both corners gives step counts distS and distT; the answer is the minimum of distS(n, m) times w and min p(distS(p) times w plus eh p) plus min q(distT(q) times w plus eh q), each minimum taken over portals reachable from that side. If both minima pick the same portal the sum is still at least the walk through it, so no special case is needed. O of nm with long long: 4 times 10 to the 6 steps times 10 to the 9 overflows int, and 4 times 10 to the 6 numbers of input want fast reading.

clips.text: A subtree is balanced when (whites minus blacks) is 0. How does that difference for vertex u relate to the same difference for each of its children?

This is the simplest subtree DP: bal(u) is (+1 if u is white, minus 1 if black) plus sum of bal(child). Because A i less than i, every child has a larger label than its parent, so the labels already give a children-first order.
clips.script: This is the simplest subtree DP: bal(u) is (+1 if u is white, minus 1 if black) plus sum of bal(child). Because eh i less than i, every child has a larger label than its parent, so the labels already give a children-first order.

clips.text: Set bal of i is ±1, then for i from n down to 2 add bal of i into bal of A i; count the vertices whose final bal is 0. O of n per test case.
clips.script: Set bal of i is ±1, then for i from n down to 2 add bal of i into bal of eh i; count the vertices whose final bal is 0. O of n per test case.

clips.text: Store bal of i is +1 for W and minus 1 for B. Loop i is n down to 1: if bal of i is 0 count it, then (for i greater than 1) add bal of i to bal of A i. Since parents have smaller labels, each vertex is complete before it is added to its parent, so no DFS is needed. O of n per test case; reset the arrays for each of the up to 10 to the 4 test cases.
clips.script: Store bal of i is +1 for W and minus 1 for B. Loop i is n down to 1: if bal of i is 0 count it, then (for i greater than 1) add bal of i to bal of eh i. Since parents have smaller labels, each vertex is complete before it is added to its parent, so no DFS is needed. O of n per test case; reset the arrays for each of the up to 10 to the 4 test cases.

clips.text: Walking down from the house at vertex 1, what single number do you need to carry to know whether the path so far is still acceptable?

Carry the length of the current run of consecutive cats: it becomes run plus 1 at a cat vertex and resets to 0 at a cat-free one. This is a top-down DFS where each vertex's state depends only on its parent's.

Iterative DFS from vertex 1 with (vertex, parent, run), starting from run is A 1. If run greater than m, do not descend further. Count reached vertices with no neighbour other than their parent. O of n.
clips.script: Iterative DFS from vertex 1 with (vertex, parent, run), starting from run is eh 1. If run greater than m, do not descend further. Count reached vertices with no neighbour other than their parent. O of n.

clips.text: DFS from vertex 1 with run(1) is A 1 and run(child) is A child? run(parent) plus 1: 0. As soon as run exceeds m, prune that whole subtree, since every restaurant below shares the bad stretch. A reached vertex whose only neighbour is its parent is a restaurant; count it. O of n. Common mistakes: tracking the total number of cats on the path instead of the current consecutive run, and counting the root as a leaf when it has degree 1.
clips.script: DFS from vertex 1 with run(1) is eh 1 and run(child) is eh child? run(parent) plus 1: 0. As soon as run exceeds m, prune that whole subtree, since every restaurant below shares the bad stretch. A reached vertex whose only neighbour is its parent is a restaurant; count it. O of n. Common mistakes: tracking the total number of cats on the path instead of the current consecutive run, and counting the root as a leaf when it has degree 1.

clips.text: The command spreads exactly like a DFS that always picks the smallest child first. How does the order starting from officer u relate to the order starting from the commander?
